L’INSA Lyon a mis en place une procédure de contrôle systématique via un outil de détection de similitudes (logiciel Compilatio). Après le dépôt du manuscrit de thèse, celui-ci est analysé par l’outil. Pour tout taux de similarité supérieur à 10%, le manuscrit est vérifié par l’équipe de FEDORA. Il s’agit notamment d’exclure les auto-citations, à condition qu’elles soient correctement référencées avec citation expresse dans le manuscrit. [SOURCE: Page_3]

Par ce document, il est attesté que ce manuscrit, dans la forme communiquée par la personne doctorante à l’INSA Lyon, satisfait aux exigences de l’Etablissement concernant le taux maximal de similitude admissible. [SOURCE: Page_3]

Abstract [SOURCE: Page_14]

ix Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_14]

Abstract [SOURCE: Page_15]

In the context of global change, cities are moving towards more sustainable and resilient water practices. Nature-based solutions contribute to integrated water management approaches by locally managing wa- ter volumes and treating pollution, while bringing biodiversity and supporting socio-economic dynamics to the urban landscape at a reasonable cost. These solutions are flourishing around the world under dif- ferent terminologies and lack guidelines for their implementation. This challenge is addressed by the MULTISOURCE project, within which this thesis aims at the technical aspect of providing a pre-sizing of technological units developed for wastewater treatment. In particular, treatment wetlands face a lack of understanding of the relationship between the designs and the treatment processes involved, and a lack of comparable data on the systems. Current design models are simple and conservative, while data-driven models are unreliable. [SOURCE: Page_15]

This thesis proposes, as a first step, the development of an ontology to clarify terminological ambigui- ties, to unify knowledge on treatment wetlands and to better identify their main characteristics in terms of pollutant removal. The second step of this work proposes to homogenise data quality checks through a methodology for data validation with a quantitative assessment of the quality of the observations. In the third step, two methodologies of hybridisation of mechanistic and data-driven models are developed to provide design estimates based on both knowledge and data. Finally, this methodology is applied to the validated data set and design optimisation methods are developed to address the uncertainty inherent in decision making. [SOURCE: Page_15]

Keywords: Symbolic representation, ontology, hybrid modelling, mechanistic, empirical, decision-support [SOURCE: Page_15]

x Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_15]

Résumé [SOURCE: Page_16]

Dans le contexte du changement global, les villes s’orientent vers des pratiques plus durables et résilientes en matière d’eau. Les solutions fondées sur la nature contribuent aux approches de gestion intégrée de l’eau en gérant localement les volumes d’eau et en traitant la pollution, tout en préservant la biodiversité et en soutenant la dynamique socio-économique dans le paysage urbain à un coût raisonnable. Ces solu- tions fleurissent dans le monde entier sous de multiples terminologies et manquent de lignes directrices pour leur mise en œuvre. Ce défi est relevé par le projet MULTISOURCE, dans le cadre duquel cette thèse vise l’aspect technique du pré-dimensionnement des unités technologiques développées pour le traitement des eaux usées. En particulier, les filtres plantés sont confrontés à un manque de compréhension de la re- lation entre leur conception et les méchanismes de traitement impliqués, ainsi qu’à un manque de données comparables sur ces systèmes. Les modèles de conception actuels sont simples et conservateurs, tandis que les modèles basés sur des données ne sont pas fiables. [SOURCE: Page_16]

Cette thèse propose, dans un premier temps, le développement d’une ontologie afin de clarifier les ambiguïtés terminologiques, d’unifier les connaissances sur les filtres plantés et de mieux identifier leurs principales caractéristiques en termes d’élimination des polluants. La deuxième étape de ce travail propose d’homogénéiser les contrôles de qualité des données grâce à une méthodologie de validation des données avec une évaluation quantitative de la qualité des observations. Dans un troisième temps, deux méthodo- logies d’hybridation des modèles mécanistes et des modèles basés sur les données sont développées pour fournir des estimations de conception basées à la fois sur les connaissances et les données. Enfin, cette mé- thodologie est appliquée à l’ensemble des données validées, et des méthodes d’optimisation de la conception sont mises au point pour tenir compte de l’incertitude inhérente à la prise de décision. [SOURCE: Page_16]

Mots clés : Représentation symbolique, ontologie, modélisation hybride, modélisation mécaniste, modé- lisation empirique, aide à la décision [SOURCE: Page_16]

xi Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_16]

Resumen [SOURCE: Page_17]

En el contexto del cambio global, las ciudades avanzan hacia prácticas hídricas más sostenibles y resilien- tes. Las soluciones basadas en la naturaleza contribuyen a los planteamientos de gestión integrada del agua gestionando localmente los volúmenes de agua y tratando la contaminación, al tiempo que aportan biodiversidad y apoyan la dinámica socioeconómica del paisaje urbano a un coste razonable. Estas solu- ciones están floreciendo en todo el mundo bajo diferentes terminologías y carecen de directrices para su aplicación. Este reto se aborda en el proyecto MULTISOURCE, dentro del cual esta tesis tiene por objeto el aspecto técnico de proporcionar un dimensionamiento previo de las unidades tecnológicas desarrolladas para el tratamiento de aguas residuales. En particular, los humedales de tratamiento se enfrentan a una falta de comprensión de la relación entre los diseños y los procesos de tratamiento implicados, y a una falta de datos comparables sobre los sistemas. Los modelos de diseño actuales son simples y conservadores, mientras que los modelos basados en datos son poco fiables. [SOURCE: Page_17]

Esta tesis propone, como primer paso, el desarrollo de una ontología para aclarar las ambigüedades terminológicas, unificar el conocimiento sobre los humedales de tratamiento e identificar mejor sus princi- pales características en términos de eliminación de contaminantes. El segundo paso de este trabajo propone homogeneizar los controles de calidad de los datos mediante una metodología de validación de datos con una evaluación cuantitativa de la calidad de las observaciones. En el tercer paso, se desarrollan dos me- todologías de hibridación de modelos mecanicistas y basados en datos, para proporcionar estimaciones de diseño basadas tanto en el conocimiento como en los datos. Por último, esta metodología se aplica al conjun- to de datos validados y se desarrollan métodos de optimización del diseño para abordar la incertidumbre inherente a la toma de decisiones. [SOURCE: Page_17]

Palabras clave: Representación simbólica, ontología, modelización híbrida, modelización mecanicista, modelización empírica, apoyo a la decisión [SOURCE: Page_17]

xii Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_17]

Resum [SOURCE: Page_18]

En el context del canvi global, les ciutats s’estan orientant cap a pràctiques de gestió de l’aigua més sos- tenibles i resilients. Les solucions basades en la natura contribueixen a l’enfocament integrat de la gestió de l’aigua mitjançant la gestió local dels volums d’aigua i el tractament de la contaminació, alhora que fomenten la biodiversitat i donen suport a les dinàmiques socioeconòmiques del paisatge urbà a un cost raonable. Aquestes solucions estan proliferant arreu del món sota diferents denominacions i manquen de directrius per a la seva implementació. Aquest repte és abordat pel projecte MULTISOURCE, dins del qual aquesta tesi se centra en l’aspecte tècnic de proporcionar un pre-dimensionament de les unitats tecnològi- ques desenvolupades per al tractament d’aigües residuals. En particular, els aiguamolls construïts per al tractament de l’aigua pateixen una manca de comprensió de la relació entre els dissenys i els processos de tractament implicats, així com una manca de dades comparables sobre els sistemes. Els models de disseny actuals són senzills i conservadors, mentre que els models basats en dades són poc fiables. [SOURCE: Page_18]

Aquesta tesi proposa, com a primer pas, el desenvolupament d’una ontologia per aclarir ambigüitats terminològiques, unificar el coneixement sobre els aiguamolls construïts i identificar millor les seves prin- cipals característiques pel que fa a l’eliminació de contaminants. El segon pas d’aquest treball planteja l’homogeneïtzació dels controls de qualitat de les dades mitjançant una metodologia de validació de dades amb una avaluació quantitativa de la qualitat de les observacions. En el tercer pas, es desenvolupen dues metodologies d’hibridació de models mecanicistes i basats en dades per proporcionar estimacions de dis- seny basades tant en el coneixement com en les dades. Finalment, aquesta metodologia s’aplica al conjunt de dades validat i es desenvolupen mètodes d’optimització del disseny per abordar la incertesa inherent en la presa de decisions. [SOURCE: Page_18]

Paraules clau: Representació simbòlica, ontologia, modelatge híbrid, modelatge mecanicista, modelatge empíric, suport a la presa de decisions [SOURCE: Page_18]

In this introduction, we will present an overview of wastewater management throughout history, and a perspective on its evolution. We will see that water puts in relation science and decision-making, for being the source for life and a resource for human activities. We will thus present the interactions between science and decision-making, leading to the emergence of the research questions that this work aims to answer. Finally, we will present the project that coordinates and funds this work as well as our objectives and leads on how we plan to tackle these questions. [SOURCE: Page_25]

1.1      Water management overview Relationship to water in Europe is imbued with a ”cognitive dissonance”: in several areas worldwide, safe drinking water and proper sanitation are not accessible to everyone resulting in over a million cases of diarrhoeal diseases and deaths (WHO, 2019). Conversely, in Europe, defecating in drinking water is common practice. To gain insight into this complex relationship with water, let’s rewind time. [SOURCE: Page_25]

1.1.1 Historical elements Water has been a source of inspiration throughout history. In ancient times, water was seen as a sacred natural element that gave us the notion of purity, the source of dreams and life. In Rome, nine aqueducts channelled water to the city, notably to give life to the 591 marble fountains, and would flow across the city before returning into the Tiber river. In the Middle Age, cities developed along rivers, and their domestic water was reused, faeces and urine were valorised. However, at the beginning of the 19th century, cholera epidemics and the rise of the hygiene movement changed this attitude: used water was dirty and carried diseases. As roads were paved, sewer networks were extended underground to carry domestic wastewater and runoff from newly impervious surfaces, to a receiving water body. Urbanisation greatly impacted the water balance and runoff volumes (Fletcher et al., 2013). These networks, inspired by the double circula- tion of blood vessels in the human body, appeared in London in 1628 and in Paris in 1769. Nonetheless initially, and unlike in London, Parisians were reluctant to dump excrement into the Seine, which would lead to an economic loss if the resulting sludge was not used in agriculture (Illich, 1986). [SOURCE: Page_25]

Sewage discharges lead to the presence of pathogens in water resources, the development of eutroph- ication and the growth of cyanobacteria, which are threats that limit human uses. Measures were taken in France: the Water Law of 1964 introduced a water fee based on the polluter-pays principle to finance infrastructure for wastewater treatment. Another law in 1992, created bodies such as the Water Police and the urban planning schemes 1 , which are responsible for defining water quantity and quality objectives. In 2006, the right to water is acknowledged in that potable water should be economically accessible. The European Water Framework Directive [2000/60/EC] 2 was adopted in 2000 to improve water management, control emissions and diffuse environmental impacts and risks, by requiring and promoting technological and scientific progress and leaving it to each Member State to define appropriate measures. In Europe, wastewater is managed in a linear and centralised way, through a network of underground pipes: from ab- straction and potabilisation, to urban use at the housing level, treatment in wastewater treatment plants and discharge into a receiving water body. However, a sewerage network and centralised treatment is not a universal scenario, road-based conveyance may be involved, or an onsite treatment (Strande et al., 2023). For small communities 3 and rural areas, in particular in Central and Eastern Europe, a lower degree of centralisation is adopted and more extensive but affordable technologies such as treatment wet- lands are used. This context is not considered by European regulations 4 . In 2011, 13,000 mainly rural agglomerations covering 19% (3.3 million) of the population in France did not have a sewer network and relied on non-collective sanitation systems, of which more than one million did not comply with national regulations. 270 000 houses did not have indoor toilets and 1 100 000 houses discharged their waste water without treatment (de l’eau, 2011). [SOURCE: Page_25]

Meanwhile, good water quality and accessibility constitute a cornerstone of human dignity and is con- sidered in legally binding instruments, policy frameworks, and advocacy tools. The right to access potable water and to live in a balanced and healthy environment, is enshrined in the EU Charter of Fundamental 1 the SDAGE (Schéma Directeur d’Aménagement et de Gestion des Eaux) and SAGE (Schéma d’Aménagement et des Gestion des Eaux) 2 A Directive sets objectives for member States, and is transposed at the national level to be achieved through legislations and norms. 3 < 2000 Population Equivalent 4 A regulation is mandatory and directly applicable to all member States. [SOURCE: Page_25]

2 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_25]

Rights (2000), in the French Environmental Charter (2005), in the study A/HRC/6/3 of the High Commis- sioner for Human Rights (2007), the Declaration on Sanitation 5 , and the resolutions 6 of the UN Com- mittee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. This right covers drinking water and water sanitation (including collection, transport, treatment and disposal or reuse of waste water or human excreta) in terms of availability, quality, physical and economic accessibility and participation (i.e. information and consul- tation). This right has led to improved access to water and sanitation through the development of toilets in houses, workplaces, schools, recreational facilities, and of sewer networks. The EU’s Urban Waste Water Treatment Directive 91/271/EEC set out the substantive provisions of the right to water with water quality standards covering treatment, protection of sensitive areas, emission control and monitoring 7 . There is no explicit legal declaration on the right to water, neither within Spain nor ratified, but the decentralised management of drinking water and sanitation at the municipal level has been qualified as satisfactory (de l’eau, 2011). [SOURCE: Page_26]

1.1.2      Current Wastewater management Human activities require water, whether it be for recreational or industrial uses, thus putting pressure on water demand. Water restrictions are imposed in many regions, notably every summer, almost all French departments are subject to a restriction decree, and in 2024 in Catalonia, with a restriction of 200 L/day per inhabitant in Barcelona. In 2023, the daily consumption per inhabitant in Catalonia was in average of 117 L 8 , such that the higher consumption limit set in Barcelona may be explained by the tourism ac- tivities. Human activities also degrade aquatic ecosystems. Surface water quality is degraded mainly due to wastewater discharges from treatment plants (European Environment Agency, 2018). Moreover, sewer networks are ageing and leaking, and cities are reaching the point where centralising treatment is no longer cost-effective (Eggimann et al., 2015). In France, about 0.48% of sewer networks are replaced every year (Dequesne and Bréjoux, 2016) while their lifespan is of 100 years at most. [SOURCE: Page_26]

Urine and faeces, the golden resources of the past, are now diluted in wastewater drained away from cities and considered waste to be eliminated in treatment plants, see Figure 1.1. Agricultural irrigation has the highest demand for drinking water, consuming 80% of the volume abstracted, but requires fertilisers, while on the other hand wastewater treatment plants eliminate nutrients, so that in France only 50% of the phosphorus and 10% of the nitrogen content, two important sources of nutrients found in wastewater due to human urine and faeces, are reused by spreading sewage sludge on land in agriculture. The re- moval of nutrients prior to wastewater discharge aims to limit environmental risks such as eutrophication of aquifers due to the presence of N and P nutrients, in particular in a bioavailable form (Preisner et al., 2020). This paradigm of waste, excreta and water is most commonly associated with toilets that mobilise water for flushing. Other toilets exist, such as dry latrines that do not use flushing, or source separation toilets. The usage of water for cleaning also generates wastewater from personal washing, kitchens, wash- ing machines and dishwashers. In Europe, flushing accounts for about 20% of domestic water use, while drinking water accounts for less than 5%. Water used from households is known as domestic wastewater, and water used more globally from cities is known as urban wastewater. [SOURCE: Page_26]

Meanwhile, some regions suffer from a water stress or a lack of collection or treatment infrastruc- ture, leading to the common practice of reuse of untreated wastewater for agricultural purposes. Notably in a perspective of treated wastewater reuse, the practice presents sanitary risks due to the presence of pathogens (Feachem et al., 1983; Boutin, 2008; Beaupoil et al., 2010). These sanitary risks were illus- trated in March 2024 with the use of untreated wastewater for irrigation that led to the contamination of strawberries by hepatitis A, imported into Spain from Morocco. In addition, pharmaceuticals, plasticisers, cosmetics and, in particular, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and polyfluoroalkyl substances end up in 5 Declaration on Sanitation E/C.12/45/CRP.1 2010 6 resolutions 2010 64/292, 2013 68/157 and 2015 70/169 7 However, a court ruling in the autumn 2024 shows that the objectives are not being fully met in France, which has been condemned for failing to meet the requirements and deadlines of the Urban Waste Water Treatment Directive 91/271/EEC in 78 agglomerations of at least 2,000 population equivalents. These non conforming agglomerations include Le Lorrain, Le Robert, Saint-Esprit, Fort-de- France in Martinique, Trois-Rivières in Guadeloupe, Cilaeos in La Réunion and Galéria in Corsica. In Catalonia, in 2008, the treatment of wastewater was satisfactory for 92% of the population, but it corresponded to only 25% of the municipalities, from which we can conclude that rural areas lack resources or attractiveness for development, and should be looked after especially since they affect 4% of the wetlands, 24% of the rivers, 38% of the coastal waters and 38% of the underground waters (Agencia Catalana del Aigua: Water in Catalonia. Diagnosis and Proposals for Action, 2008). 8 Agencia       Catalana       del     Aigua,       https://aca.gencat.cat/ca/laca/campanyes-i-divulgacio/campanyes/ estalvi-i-eficiencia-de-laigua [SOURCE: Page_26]

waste water and constitute these contaminants of emerging concern that resist treatment. Water must be monitored. To the point where Ivan Illich 9 notes that: [SOURCE: Page_27]

H2O and water have become opposites: H2O is a social creation of modern times, a resource that is scarce and that calls for technical management. It is an observed fluid that has lost the ability to mirror the water of dreams. [SOURCE: Page_27]

Could water still bring us this unconditional joy? The Olympic Games in the summer of 2024 illustrate our conflicted relationship with it. To show the splendour of France and of this event, it was decided to hold the opening ceremony on and along the majestic and romantic Seine. But swimming in it? It had been banned since 1923. Due to a unified sewerage system combining sewage and run-off, heavy rainfall causes overflows into the river and generates sanitary risks. Making the Seine bathable again was therefore one of the symbolic goals set for the Olympic Games. Unfortunately, despite an investment of 1.4 billion euros for a better management of overflows, the water quality was still greatly impacted by a rain event, such that the swimming leg of the triathlon was postponed for a day to allow the concentration of E. coli to fall. [SOURCE: Page_27]

1.2      Evolution towards integrated water management Initially, wastewater treatment plants aimed to mitigate sanitary and environmental risks from wastew- ater discharge. The objectives were also to preserve natural resources, limit costs and improve urban resilience. Eutrophication of aquifers and accumulation of micropollutants in the environment due to wastewater discharges have been reconsidered with the revision in 2024 of the European Directive 91/271/EEC. Stringent treatment objectives have been set, with frequent monitoring and specified analytical method, detailed in the Table 1.1. They must be complied with by 2035 for secondary treatment, and by 2045 for tertiary treatment. We can note the addition of a new quaternary treatment step specific to micropollu- tants (pharmaceuticals, cosmetics). [SOURCE: Page_27]

Meanwhile, the 2018 IPCC 10 report predicts more frequent and intense floods and droughts, having consequences on all anthropogenic activities. Current challenges have thus led scientists and politics to manage water in an integrated and circular approach (Partnership, 2009), where wastewater is seen as a part of the anthropogenic water cycle, providing a source of water, nutrients and energy. Treatment plants should not only prevent eutrophication but also participate in food security and circular economy, or even 9 in his conference H2O and the Waters of Forgetfulness 10 Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, an intergovernmental body of the United Nations [SOURCE: Page_27]

4 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_27]

be considered in the full scope of interdependencies in the water-food-energy nexus, as highlighted by van Loosdrecht and Brdjanovic (2014). In this larger framework, technical aspects of wastewater management to ensure environmental and sanitary protection must now be considered together with social, economic, and legislative aspects for a sustainable and resilient management of water resources (Larsen and Gujer, 1997; Guest et al., 2009; Villarín and Merel, 2020; Wang et al., 2021a; Bakan et al., 2022), and this has been a challenge for the last thirty years as illustrated by the dates of publication of these reviews. This context creates situations known as wicked problems, where a solution to a given aspect can generate a problem for another aspect. Frameworks are developed to put together the multiple criteria, objectives and stakeholders covered by the scope of decision-making for circular approaches (Mendoza and Martins, 2006). [SOURCE: Page_28]

As an answer to current challenges, wastewater treatment plants are undergoing functional and struc- tural changes that we will develop below. [SOURCE: Page_28]

1.2.1 Functional changes Water management facilities endorse more responsibilities than solely technical treatment and handling of floods and droughts: they are considered in a full circular economy, with connections to irrigation, food and energy (Daigger, 2009). Water is indeed essential to energy production, while energy is necessary to water treatment and distribution. Nutrients are essential to agriculture and are found in wastewater, mainly due to urines as characterised by Kirchmann and Pettersson (1994); Rose et al. (2015). But they are currently eliminated in treatment plants to avoid eutrophication despite great potential for circular economy. The European regulation on treated wastewater reuse (UE) 2020/741 opens perspectives for the reduction of potable water consumption, and the valorisation of nutrients in agricultural irrigation, proposing a new paradigm for wastewater treatment plants (WWTP) as water resource recovery facilities (WRRF) and water reclamation plant (WRP) 11 . Going further, in 2018, the EU Bioeconomy strategy wrote that ”Cities should become major circular bioeconomy hubs” and defined in its action plan to ”Facilitate the deployment of new sustainable biorefineries”. WWTP could become biofactories or biorefineries, with an on-site and sustain- able processing of residual biomass into ”a spectrum of bio-based products and bioenergy” (International Energy Agency). The European Directive also states that ”Water is a primary good which belongs to every- one and is for everyone and which, as a natural resource that is essential, irreplaceable and indispensable to life, needs to be considered and integrated in its three dimensions: social, economic and environmental”. [SOURCE: Page_28]

Reuse of wastewater is informally practised in some regions experiencing scarcity of water, and oth- erwise when regulated, reuse of treated wastewater is most commonly found for irrigation of non-edible crops, recreational urban uses recharge of aquifers, or industrial process water reuse (Bixio et al., 2006; Lazarova et al., 2013). Fertigation is an irrigation using treated wastewater still rich in nutrients, but the wastewater requires treatment to mitigate the negative impacts on the soil and crops from its high rates in salts (Na, Ca, K) and in metals (Pb, Cd, Hg, As) (Poustie et al., 2020; Ofori et al., 2021). Reuse has been subject to a European regulation UE 2020/741 for agricultural irrigation with strong monitoring and 11 Web of Science has published 980, 1846 and 2854 scientific papers containing the term waste water treatment plant in 2010, 2016 and 2022, with a decreasing tail, and meanwhile 286, 856 and 2531 scientifics papers containing the term water resource recovery with an increasing tail up to these days. treatment objectives for pathogen removal. Different levels of water quality lead to different authorised practices based on the irrigation systems and types of crops. Reuse for potable water is also practised in some regions, requiring intensive treatment (Leverenz et al., 2011). Current Reuse practice is low in Europe, reaching 14 % of the wastewater volume in Spain, and 0.6 % in France, including all alternative water resources and uses together. In France, the application of the European Directive on the reuse of treated wastewater in agriculture tackles the management of pathogenic risks with stringent objectives and expensive monitoring, and illustrates a mismatch between regulatory objectives and current techno- logical performances reviewed by Guillaume-Ruty et al. (2024a). [SOURCE: Page_29]

It is also possible to valorise wastewater together with its nutrients, or to extract them as fertilisers (Martin et al., 2022). Phosphorus has been studied for the last thirty years notably with struvite precip- itation , potassium can be recovered together with phosphorus through struvite potassium, and concern emerges for nitrogen recovery due to the greenhouse gas that can derive from it (Kehrein et al., 2020; Mayer et al., 2016). Nonetheless, upscaling the technologies to an industrial scale remains a great chal- lenge notably due to market-related and value chain bottlenecks. Organic matter changed status from a source of degradation of aquatic ecosystems that needs to be eliminated, to a resource for sludge spreading in agriculture, energy recovery from incineration, or material extraction: cellulose fibres, biopolymers, no- tably bioplastic (Ruiken et al., 2013; Lotti et al., 2019; van Loosdrecht and Brdjanovic, 2014). [SOURCE: Page_29]

Finally, wastewater can be a source of direct and indirect energy (McCarty et al., 2011) : directly through the production of heat or biogas together with a digestate rich in nutrients, notably with anaero- bic digestion since a few decades. In the perspective of carbon footprint reduction, the revised European Directive has set the ambitious goal of reaching energy neutrality by the end of 2045 for WWTP of > 10 000 population equivalent, with the production of energy to be used on-site or outside. Research is still needed to increase energy production and nutrient recovery. Some studies recommend technical improve- ments such as the optimisation of operational parameters of the full treatment train, or coupling anaerobic digestion to membranes (McCarty et al., 2011), while other suggest a more radical change by separating ef- fluents at the source (Verstraete et al., 2009). We will now briefly present structural shifts that wastewater management follows. [SOURCE: Page_29]

1.2.2 Structural changes The main source of organic and nutrient pollution is human excreta in domestic wastewater. Dry latrines or separative toilets 12 are already practised in rural areas and experimented in urbanised sites or for events (Kirchmann and Pettersson, 1994; Joveniaux et al., 2022) and are an upstream and decentralised approach preventing the contamination of water. No water flush is used and excreta do not end up in a combined sewer together with grey water (from dish washers, laundry, showers) nor with rainwater. The treatment of water, on-site Reuse, or valorisation of urine and faeces are reported to be technically and economically feasible (Garrido-Baserba et al., 2022). Nonetheless, upstream separation is not a consensual topic and still faces challenges in terms of technical maturity of processes such as urine precipitation (Yan et al., 2021) or blackwater treatment (Eshetu Moges et al., 2018), social acceptance (Segrè Cohen et al., 2020; Simha et al., 2021), and economic perenniality due to great maintenance needs and 5 to 10 % higher construction costs (Garrido-Baserba et al., 2022). [SOURCE: Page_29]

Decentralisation, favoured in rural areas and developing regions, can be combined or not to upstream separation of pollution, and includes local collection, treatment and discharge of wastewater. A centralised management of wastewater using a sewer network that lead to a central WWTP is widely operated, but hits the limits of its economic, operational, and maintenance advantages in big cities, with issues such as ageing pipelines and overloaded WWTP. Therefore decentralised solutions are studied for urbanised areas and new neighbourhoods (Eggimann et al., 2015; Libralato et al., 2012; Wilderer and Schreff, 2000). Modu- lar and smaller-scale systems such as treatment wetlands can reduce sanitation costs and are more flexible to fit local constraints. They present market potential notably in rural areas, although it represents a chal- lenge in terms of monitoring and maintenance because facilities are scattered (Capodaglio et al., 2017; Eggimann et al., 2018). [SOURCE: Page_29]

Aligning with rural and developing contexts, the concept of nature-based solutions (NBS) has developed since 2008 for water management: water infiltration, mitigation of floods, on-site wastewater treatment, 12 dry latrines do not use flush water, and separative toilets separate urines and faeces [SOURCE: Page_29]

6 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_29]

Figure 1.2: Examples of Nature-based Solutions to manage urban water. Green roofs, trees, permeable paving and swales/trenches infiltrate and retain rainwater, green walls treat greywater, treatment wetlands treat wastewater, and ponds further treat treated wastewater. These volumes of water can then be reused in buildings or irrigation, or discharged. [SOURCE: Page_30]

local water reuse for non potable needs, see Figure 1.2. Notably for stormwater management in the preven- tion of combined sewer overflows, they are economically more advantageous than grey solutions (Lippera et al., 2025). For wastewater treatment, typical technologies include soil infiltration, willow systems (for evapotranspiration), stabilisation ponds, sludge drying reed beds and treatment wetlands. They rely on the use of plants and intensify natural bioprocesses that occur in natural wetlands to achieve higher per- formances of treatment. Less expensive, energy consuming, or maintenance demanding, Nature-based Solutions are however extensive and lack guidance on design conception as noted by Istenič et al. (2023). Nature-based Solutions are particularly appropriate to address urban circularity challenges related to not only water, but also nutrients recovery, biomass valorisation, living organisms maintenance and energy production (Langergraber et al., 2021b), notably valorising nutrients, biomass. They participate in this new integrated approach, delivering ecosystem services (Liquete et al., 2016) and necessitating exchanges between stakeholders from disciplines such as sociology, urban planning and engineering. Additional ben- efits associated with vegetation are a reduction in heat islands, the maintenance of a local biodiversity and nicer urban aesthetics promoting social and economical dynamics (Oral et al., 2020; Langergraber et al., 2021a; Chan et al., 2018; Panduro and Veie, 2013). [SOURCE: Page_30]

Finally, the European Directive on reuse of wastewater for agriculture introduces a multi-barrier ap- proach to manage collectively the risks. However it still needs to be assessed, as noted by Keraita et al. (2010). The approach relies on the distribution of the sanitary risks and management responsibilities along the reuse project and stakeholders rather than on a full and intensive treatment approach. The door is thus opened to alternative treatment technologies and barriers. Directives on multi-barrier practices (NF ISO 16075-2 AFNOR) are being revised to facilitate reuse practices, and lighten WWTP treatment requirements while ensuring sanitary protection. Decentralisation and reuse still face challenges related to costs, sanitary risks, ownership and governance, and is sometimes held back by conservative regulations (Fletcher et al., 2024). [SOURCE: Page_30]

7 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_30]

1.3       Science and decision making 1.3.1      Towards an informed choice... The role of science and number historically lies within society. Numbers were conceptualised well before writing, and were used for counting properties and agricultural products. In the 18th century in Germany and Italy, statistics are employed as a management technique to describe the situation of a State 13 . Statis- tics then integrated the mathematical vision that we have today from England. Science, both fundamental and applied, is not about scientists living in their own system, but being confronted to reality. Science has been historically driven conjointly with politics, as analysed by Bruno Latour 14 based on a letter writ- ten by Pasteur asking for funding to the ministry showing the importance of his research for society and economy, or as shown by Olivier Rey 15 on research programmes that set up research axes such as the Horizon 2020 Framework Programme for Research and Innovation 16 . Auguste Comte already declared in 1851 that ”the universe must be studied, not for itself, but for humans, or rather for humanity” 17 . More recently, Palmer et al. (2005) stated that ”ecologists must strengthen their role of providing ecological knowledge that is needed to inform decisions”. As regulations tackle water-related challenges (sanitation risks and environmental pollution) and set legal water quality objectives, interactions between decision- makers and scientists are also required, see the very technical Table 1.1 of the EU Directive. Governments reuse scientific productions to take operational and legal actions. In the context of integrated approaches, multiple types of sciences are gathered to support decision-making. Environmental Decision-Support Sys- tems (DSS) (Rosse et al., 2023) and Frameworks 18 are being developed to facilitate support to decision by expert knowledge. Specific to WWTP, Mannina et al. (2019) identified four main approaches employed in DSS that illustrate an evolution from mathematical to data-driven modelling, and from a restricted to an integrated scope: [SOURCE: Page_31]

• Mathematical modelling which is the most ancient and based on expert knowledge, [SOURCE: Page_31]

• Life cycle assessment which considers the conception, use and end-of-life impacts of a system or scenario on the environment, [SOURCE: Page_31]

• Multi-criteria decision-making that covers a wider scope with multiple environmental or economic objectives, [SOURCE: Page_31]

• Intelligent DSS that integrates artificial intelligence algorithms applied to large scopes. [SOURCE: Page_31]

They categorised the DSS into the following scopes: design, energy consumption, operational optimi- sation, improvement of the effluent quality and environmental sustainability. Mannina et al. (2019) con- cluded that efforts should be put in encouraging the adoption of innovative solutions in an interdisciplinary challenging context, notably with the development of better online DSS. The close relation to political ob- jectives and technique is observable with intellectual property on valorising research products, or with the goal of modelling often being to predict rather than to understand. Science meddles closely with technique, where the first aims to provide understanding by answering ”what” and ”why” questions, the second aims to answer the practical ”how” question. Technique immediately comes up as means to tackling the previous interrogations, while originating from the knowledge already produced by science. [SOURCE: Page_31]

1.3.2 ...or towards an imposed choice? It appears that technique, numbers and science have become to some extent the solution to challenges tackled by political objectives. Directives have been setting quantified objectives to wastewater treatment, based on scientific results and expert knowledge. Technique tends to dominate in decision-making pro- cesses as numbers tend to bear a status of being objective, impartial and neutral. However, numbers 13 By construction, statistics, or Staatskunde, or Statistik, actually means the science of the state. 14 in his conference for INRA Group Sciences en questions, Le métier de chercheur. Regard d’un anthropologue, given in 1994 15 in Réparer l’eau, 2021 16 One can read on the website: ”The objectives of Horizon 2020 were to strengthen the EU’s scientific and technological foundations, create a European Research Area with free circulation of researchers and knowledge, and drive the EU towards a knowledge society and competitive economy. Specific goals included implementing research, technological development, and innovation; promoting international cooperation; disseminating and optimizing research results; stimulating training and mobility; fostering better exploitation of industrial potential; and supporting the Europe 2020 strategy for smart, sustainable, and inclusive growth.” 17 in Système de politique positive, 1851 18 as an example, Wickenberg et al. (2021) developed a framework for urban planning, from a strategic planning, the implementation, the maintenance, to the evaluation of Nature-based Solutions [SOURCE: Page_31]

8 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_31]

and technique are constructions with choices made along the process. Supiot (2014) noted how numbers and technique have reached the political sphere through quantification and efficiency, such that political challenges appear to be technical questions that may evade debate more easily 19 . Metrics to assess the engagement in the environmental transition are developing such as resilience, ease of integration, im- plementation scale, and eco-efficiency or eco-effectiveness, as reviewed by Cornejo et al. (2019); Stanchev et al. (2017). The different metrics calibrate specific tools that have been developed such as GIS-based tools, multi-criteria analysis and life-cycle assessment, and ultimately support decision-making, see the studies of Dufossé et al. (2024); Garfí et al. (2017); Pons et al. (2008); Heimersson et al. (2014); Wang et al. (2013); van Afferden et al. (2015). Di Fiore et al. (2023) showed that quantification gives an illusion of certainty, with tools such as the life-cycle assessment, providing numbers with a high level of precision although uncertainty remains. AI is a good example of how much our decisions depend on algorithms, known as black boxes for their processes are not interpretable. Debates on the misuse of statistical tools show that scientists are not exempt from this risk, with the example of a tendency for binary conclusions on the significance of scientific results based on the calculation of a p-value rather than on an analysis and deliberation about uncertainties (Amrhein et al., 2019; McShane et al., 2019; Saltelli and Puy, 2023). And rightly so, Jacques Ellul deplored how technique and its focus on efficiency actually redefines cities and social order and dispossesses humans from their decision power 20 . More recently Bernard Stiegler made a similar analysis on digital technologies among which pharmakôn create dependencies in terms of memory, knowledge and know-how 21 . [SOURCE: Page_32]

1.4      Model hybridisation for reliable decision-making This introduction illustrates the shift of water from a topic of reflection to one of governance. Recent water uses and practices have increased pathogenic and pollution risks, leading to the development of wastewater management downstream to protect health and ecosystems. Disenchantment progressively occurred with the development of infrastructures and the techno-numerical turn taken by regulations on water manage- ment, setting for example quantitative objectives 22 . In the face of biodiversity decline and global change, integrated approaches for more sustainable, circular and resilient urban water management are devel- oped, within which nature-based solutions have become assets. Their peculiar status at the intersection of social, environmental and technological fields makes their study more difficult. Their implementations is promoted by decision-support tools, but in practice, their designs are still lacking scientific background to be optimised and more widely trusted (Meyer et al., 2015). We can also perceive how trust in numbers is at stake while the process of decision-making increasingly relies on science and delegates to techno- numerical approaches. Rightly so, research should be done rigorously within the boundaries of science, to support more reliable decisions. [SOURCE: Page_32]

1.4.1 Thesis context The new integrated approach to water management consists in targeting together multiple issues that stem from the same root. A wider scope appears, illustrated by the goals set for MULTISOURCE European- funded project 23 , ModULar Tools for Integrating enhanced natural treatment SOlutions in URban water CyclEs: [SOURCE: Page_32]

• Demonstrate enhanced nature-based systems in operational environments for a wide range of pol- luted urban waters [SOURCE: Page_32]

• Develop state-of-the-art guidance for Nature-based Solutions technology selection and preliminary design [SOURCE: Page_32]

• Engage urban water stakeholders in the development of urban water planning tools 19 see Governance by Numbers, 2007. We also observe that the interdisciplinary context of integrated water management involves governance rather than a government. Research is led on this governance as to the structure it should have: be adaptive (Hadjimichael, 2016), polycentric (Tzoulas et al., 2021) and collaborative (van der Jagt et al., 2021) 20 see his essays The Technological Society, 1954 and The Technological System, 1977 21 see Do Digital Technologies Kill Thought? (Le numérique empêche-t-il de penser?), Revue Esprit, January 2014 22 although we could argue that these measures are necessary to the re-enchantment of natural environments 23 This project is funded by the Horizon 2020 Framework Programme for Research and Innovation, in the category SOCIETAL CHAL- LENGES - Climate action, Environment, Resource Efficiency and Raw Materials [SOURCE: Page_32]

9 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_32]

• Improve urban governance and policies related to Nature-based Solutions and water reuse [SOURCE: Page_33]

• Provide comparative spatial environmental and economic scenarii for implementing Nature-based Solutions on a city-wide scale [SOURCE: Page_33]

The project focuses on decentralised management of water in urban contexts with the use of Nature- based Solutions. All urban waters are considered: raw wastewater, pre-treated wastewater, combined sewer overflow, greywater, road runoff, rainwater, and high-strength wastewater. In this context, experts from companies, municipalities, social and environmental sciences are gathered. The project aims at devel- oping an online decision-support tool (nat^4wat.icradev.cat) that facilitate the selection and pre-sizing of Nature-based Solutions, tailored to the context of the user. [SOURCE: Page_33]

1.4.2 Thesis outline Within the MULTISOURCE project, this work titled Model Hybridisation for Reliable Decision-Making contributes to an integrative approach by developing a decision-support tool. This tool incorporates pre- sizing models to aid in designing Nature-based Solutions, with a specific emphasis on treatment wetlands. For the final decision to be reliable, it requires the preceding constructed steps to be as well. Attaining this operational objective prompts scientific inquiry into the relevant criteria and suitable models. This thesis focuses on the design of treatment wetlands and aims to develop scientific methodologies ensuring reliability. With the concept of hybrid models, we will be interested in determining to what extent i. hybridisation of specialised symbolic representations, and ii. hybridisation of mechanistic and empirical numerical models, can help us reach a more accurate prediction of treatment wetland designs. To answer these questions, we will thus present in this work: [SOURCE: Page_33]

Chapter 2 State of the art We aim to make an overview of current advancement in the knowledge on treat- ment wetlands and the tools for their representation. We provide a description of treatment wetlands, and the state of the art of symbolic and numerical approaches in water management. We also provide a description of the numerical tools that participate in ensuring reliability of data and models, before presenting the emerging modelling methodologies of hybridisation. [SOURCE: Page_33]

Chapter 3 Objectives We present the challenges of MULTISOURCE project, and the research questions and objectives set for this work. [SOURCE: Page_33]

Chapter 4 Symbolic representation We aim to build a visual representation of treatment wetlands and to characterise key concepts. We first define the scope of MULTISOURCE project through its semantics and present the barriers to unification for better integrated research projects. We then focus on treatment wetlands to develop an ontology describing a treatment train using natural language and the support of a computer interface using the PO$_2$ Manager software. [SOURCE: Page_33]

Chapter 5 Data for modelling We aim to ensure the quality of data on which we will build our knowledge. We collect data on treatment wetlands based on their identified characteristics, targeting pollutant concentrations and technological designs. We propose a data validation workflow to automatise the check of data quality based on specific criteria, and to compute a data quality weight. We also describe the resulting dataset, focusing on pollutant concentrations, removal performances and associated factors. [SOURCE: Page_33]

Chapter 6 Hybrid numerical models We aim to compensate drawbacks of current numerical models in a combined approach. We model the relation between treatment wetland designs and pollutant re- movals. To do so, we develop a parallel and serial hybrid model based on Biopore mechanistic model, and machine learning models, trained on synthetic data as a proof of concept. We propose the deter- mination of a weighting parameter based on the trust in the machine learning model. [SOURCE: Page_33]

Chapter 7 Real case application We aim to apply the hybridisation to current design models for treat- ment wetlands. We apply the methodologies to the validated dataset, using NkC* empirical model and machine learning models. We use the data quality weight to train the data-driven models such that they rely mainly on the most trustworthy observations. Finally we study the uncertainties and design optimisation options based on pollutant treatment objectives and cost minimisation. [SOURCE: Page_33]

Chapter 2 [SOURCE: Page_34]

State of the art [SOURCE: Page_34]

”A thinking reed. - It is not from space that I must seek my dignity, but from the government of my thought. I shall have no more if I possess worlds. By space the universe encompasses and swallows me up like an atom; by thought I comprehend the world.” [SOURCE: Page_34]

Blaise Pascal, Thoughts, 1670 [SOURCE: Page_34]

We have previously defined how science relates to decision making and justified the ”model hybridi- sation for reliable decision making”. This chapter, a state of the art, introduces the remaining terms: modelling, hybrid models, reliability, and decision making. We provide key knowledge related to these terms, scientific advances and challenges for models applied to wastewater and treatment wetlands. We present two types of modelling: [SOURCE: Page_34]

• Symbolic representation: we look at the definition of important concepts and the representation of knowledge, identifying sources of misunderstanding. [SOURCE: Page_34]

• Numerical representation: we provide a brief historical background and evolution of numerical mod- els, describing how they mobilise knowledge and data, and the challenges faced by the modeller to ensure reliability. [SOURCE: Page_34]

In relation to the operational objective of decision making for treatment wetlands pre-sizing, we sum- marise the current mathematical tools available to assess and ensure model reliability. In fact, decision making occurs throughout the modelling process, through the selection of scope, data, model type, metrics and output type. [SOURCE: Page_34]

2.1       Treatment wetlands for wastewater treatment In this thesis, we will study the treatment of domestic wastewater with the use of treatment wetlands, which are flexible solutions. We will give a quick introduction to treatment wetlands, more details may be found in (Kadlec and Wallace, 2009). Treatment wetlands (TW) appeared in the 1960s from the work of the German wetland scientist Käthe Seidel for wastewater treatment. They have evolved into an essential nature-based wastewater treatment technology. Inspired by the biological processes of natural wetlands, these systems treat various types of wastewater - from stormwater run-off to industrial sources - while providing multiple co-benefits. They improve local biodiversity, biomass production, and carbon sequestra- tion, while mitigating the effects of urban heat islands, increasing permeability, and strengthening flood resilience as reviewed by Masi et al. (2018). Beyond their environmental impact, treatment wetlands con- tribute to the aesthetic and recreational value of urban areas, fostering social dynamics and overall well- being within communities. They are also cost effective compared to activated sludge treatments, in terms of construction, energy consumption, maintenance and sludge management, see (Rizzo et al., 2018; Garfí et al., 2017). For these reasons, these green systems, with complex interactions of microorganisms, plants, and biogeochemical processes, are now commonly operated around the world, providing a sustainable solu- tion for water management. In France, there are more than 5000 treatment wetlands in operation treating wastewater for small communities (< 2000 inhabitants or population equivalent 1 ), farms, and industries. [SOURCE: Page_36]

2.1.1 Description In this work, only subsurface flow treatment wetlands will be introduced and discussed. These systems are generally used to treat primary-treated effluents. They are generally characterised by the type of flow, which can be vertical or horizontal, the type of feeding (continuous or batch), and the level of water sat- uration. These conditions determine the aeration conditions and thus the biological processes that can occur. Typically, horizontal flow wetlands have saturated conditions that favour anoxic reactions (see Fig- ure 2.1), while vertical flow wetlands have unsaturated conditions favouring aerobic reactions. The type and granulometry of the substrate influence different removal processes 2 . For example, gravels between 2 and 4 mm are used to filter out suspended solids without inducing clogging in French treatment wetlands in tropical climates (Lombard-Latune et al., 2018). Materials with a high adsorption capacity can also be implemented to favour phosphorous and/or ammonium adsorption (Maleki Shahraki and Mao, 2022). [SOURCE: Page_36]

Figure 2.1: Horizontal and Vertical flow treatment wetlands, planted with reeds, illustration by Lide Jaurrieta (ICRA) [SOURCE: Page_36]

The type of plant (floating or fixed) is also a key element. The roots of macrophytes have been found to provide good support for biofilm growth, while the movement of their stems facilitate water infiltration and prevent sludge clogging. Phragmites australis, part of the Poaceae, is known as the common reed and is used in most cases in France and Europe. However, in other geographical contexts, reeds are considered invasive. Local plants must be used instead; Lombard Latune et al. (2017) identified several candidates: 1 1 PE corresponds in Europe to 60 g of BOD in the wastewater produced per inhabitant per day 2 The filtering medium of vertical flow wetlands is of great importance. It is composed of three layers of increasing granulometry: from the top filtration layer, the thickest between 30 and 80 cm deep, and composed of sand or fine gravel; the transition layer, which is 10-20 cm thick, and presents an intermediate granulometry; and finally the drainage layer, which is 10-20 cm thick too, and composed of large gravel. [SOURCE: Page_36]

13 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_36]

Heliconiaceae (in particular, the Bird of Paradise Flower Heliconia psittacorum), Cannaceae (Canna indica, Canna glauca), Marantaceae (Clinogyne comorensis), Cyperaceae (Cyperus alternifolius, involucratus, and papyrus), Typhaceae, and Poaceae (Hymenachne). [SOURCE: Page_37]

2.1.2      Pollutant removal Domestic wastewater is polluted by different chemicals and micro-organisms: organic matter, nutrients, and pathogens. Eme and Boutin (2015) showed that in France, urine only represents 1% of the wastewater volume, but accounts for 74% of nitrogen and 24% of phosphorus. Faeces represent 30% of the volume (with flush), and account for 28 to 39% of suspended solids and oxygen demands, 16% of nitrogen and 29% of phosphorus. Another category of pollutants is the micro-pollutants also referred to as pollutants of emerging concern. They include pharmaceuticals and personal care products. Synthetic molecules tend to be less easily biodegraded in biological processes, due to limiting functional group, as studied by Rich et al. (2022). [SOURCE: Page_37]

In the context of this work, the focus will be given to organic matter and nutrients. The pollutants of interest include particulate matter: TSS, carbonaceous matter: COD and BOD, and nutrients responsible for the eutrophication of aquatic ecosystems, nitrogen-based nutrients: NH$_4$-N, TKN, TN and phosphorus- based: PO$_4$-P, TP. They are degraded by various processes, see Table 2.1, notably biological with different types of bacteria: by aerobic or anaerobic biological processes. The presence of oxygen is a key factor to the occurrence of some processes. Globally, under aerobic conditions (here, unsaturated with a redox potential above 300 mV), oxygen is the main electron acceptor for microorganisms respiration, then nitrate is used for microorganisms facultative aerobic respiration (with a substrate redox potential of 300 to 100 mV). Aerobic conditions are found in vertical and unsaturated flow (VF) wetlands, which favour autotrophic nitrification of NH$_4$ to NO$_2$- and NO$_3$- through the following reactions: Nitritation: N H$_3$ + 1.5O$_2$ → biomass + H$_2$ O + NO$_2$− [SOURCE: Page_37]

Nitrification: 2NO$_2$− + O$_2$ → biomass + 2NO$_3$− [SOURCE: Page_37]

Anoxic or anaerobic conditions are found in horizontal and saturated flow treatment wetlands and favour the heterotrophic denitrification of NO$_3$- to N$_2$ and N2O in the presence of organic carbon, see (Langergraber et al., 2020a; Choudhary et al., 2011; Kadlec and Wallace, 2009; Wallace and Knight, 2005; Wallace, 2006): NO$_3$− + organic matter → CO$_2$ + H$_2$ O + N$_2$ [SOURCE: Page_37]

Under anoxic to anaerobic conditions (here, saturated) when water goes deeper in treatment wetlands or stays longer, the Redox potential of the substrate drops down from 200 to -100 mV, and other species must be used as electron acceptors such as manganese (Mn$_4$+ to Mn$_2$+), iron (Fe$_3$+ to Fe$_2$+), and then between -100 and -200 mV, sulphate (SO42- to S$_2$- ). Finally around -300 mV, anaerobic respiration or methanogenesis mobilises CO$_2$ to consume COD and NO$_3$-, producing methane and CO$_2$. Manganese, iron and sulphate can be interesting species to consider. Other mechanisms occur as well such physical and chemical processes: mineralisation, filtration and sedimentation (especially COD, BOD and TSS), see Table 2.1. These mechanisms occur simultaneously or in a cascade of reactions and are sensitive to the hydraulic design of the treatment plant, its operating conditions (type of water feed, temperature, oxygen availability). To go further, it is possible to consider additional pollutants and mechanisms such as clog- ging of the medium, metal uptake, removal of micro-pollutants (pharmaceutical products), see (Verlicchi and Zambello, 2014; Li et al., 2014; Ilyas and Van Hullebusch, 2020), and disinfection mechanisms, see the reviews (Wu et al., 2016; Donde and Xiao, 2017; Shingare et al., 2019). For example, the removal of the bacteria E. coli is the design criterion for maturation ponds using the Marais method. Although not intended for the design of treatment wetland, these removals are of great interest in the context of water reuse. [SOURCE: Page_37]

Overall, typical performance ranges for treatment wetlands are given in Table 2.2. Another system composed of two stages, and known as the French system, has been developed to treat raw wastewater directly. Intensifications are studied, such as the use of reactive media, like zeolite to treat ammonium, or apatite to treat phosphorus which presents the lowest removal. Artificial aeration may be added to [SOURCE: Page_37]

improve treatment performances and reduce the land footprint of treatment wetland, but this requires the installation of air blowers and the consumption of electricity. To a certain extent treatment wetlands designs, operational conditions, plants and geographical loca- tion influence the treatment performance of the systems in varying degree. Nan et al. (2023) and Wang et al. (2021b) reported that longer HRT (increased by the size, structure, distribution of depth, type of out- let and vegetation) improve pollutant and pathogen removals. López et al. (2019) reports that the removal of pathogens is correlated with organic matter and the particle size of the substrate. In France, Paing (2015) studied French systems and concluded to the absence of effect from hydraulic and organic loading rates (HLR and OLR) on treatment performances. Modelling studies such as Pucher and Langergraber (2019a) find filter material and OLR to have influence on the treatment performances for VF wetlands, and according to Sanchez-Ramos et al. (2017), more shallow depths to improve removal and surface ratio to have no influence for HF wetlands. [SOURCE: Page_38]

Knowledge exchange, data acquisition, and modelling are essential to research activities to better com- prehend treatment wetlands. However, we will see that these tasks remain challenging in the context of treatment wetlands due to their interdisciplinary appeal, their implementations worldwide, and their complex nature-based processes. 2.2       Modelling Reality is what scientists aim to describe or understand through quantification by measurements and through representations, i.e. modelling. For biochemists, biologists, and bioengineers, modelling can be a distant and daunting field. However, modelling is a broad subject, defined less subjectively as the process of building a simplified, informative, and abstract representation of a part of reality (a system, an object, a phenomenon). A model is a description that mobilises and links knowledge and/or data through the use of symbols and numbers. It is interesting to note that science is built from subjective points of view, but that the resulting representations can reach a form of objectivity, of knowledge that is independent of these rep- resentations. A model is always partial, based on hypotheses and simplifications, as well as on samples of reality, and therefore does not represent the truth. This observation led George E. P. Box to say in 1976 that ”all models are wrong, but some are useful”. As an example, clearly wrong but useful for pharmacokinetic studies, we can represent a human body by two compartments, one for human blood vessels and the other for human tissues. As a second example, graphs and gas molecule interactions can be used to represent social interactions and the propagation of opinions that can lead to the emergence of leaders (see the works of Nathalie Ayi). A model should be seen as a useful pretence, a partisan representation (Bouleau, 1999), an approximation to truth, an inference about truth (Burnham et al., 2002), or my favourite 3 : a metaphor of reality (Clark and Wokaun, 2003; Saltelli and Puy, 2023). In a practical way, Bourdieu defines that truth is the set of representations considered true because it is produced according to the rule that defines the production of truth 4 . [SOURCE: Page_39]

The inputs of modelling are knowledge and data. Intuition from knowledge, reflection, and deduction proceed a priori from reasoning with a more theoretical approach, while induction from data, perception, and sensation proceed a posteriori from observations and experiments. A model can aim at describing and understanding known cases, inferring (from probabilities), predicting unknown cases, or communicating. a posteriori knowledge from data may require more steps to be derived from experience. In particular, we need methods to make the world reliably observable, and analysis to build knowledge from perceptions and inductions. Starting with measurements and data, the modeller needs to extract information (descriptive statistics). Analysis and interpretation to give meaning to the information create individual knowledge 5 , and the aggregation of multiple sources of knowledge from multiple individuals creates a higher form, wisdom 6 , see Figure 2.2. Objectivity or universalisation in science is said to be ensured through scien- tific intersubjectivity 7 , or rather, cogito of mutual obligation 8 , according to Bachelard. Popper (1945) and Bourdieu (2001) speak in more liberal terms about sciences based on amicably hostile cooperation and mutual controls. Often, the source of knowledge is multiple and difficult to trace. However, science does not solely rely on the competition between multiple hypotheses but first of all on a common language (a use of symbols) and agreed practices, and on the combination of multiple sources of knowledge. We will see that symbolic modelling is a preliminary step in numerical modelling, whose methods vary with two forms of knowledge: a priori and a posteriori. In particular, a modeller needs to ensure that he can trust the observations and confirm that the reasoning is not only coherent, but close to the truth. Bachelard mentioned how science can only provide an approximation to truth through representations. Often, knowl- edge is confirmed when the multiple forms of knowledge are coherent and compatible, therefore, it may be necessary to use multiple approaches. Combining knowledge will be the focus of this thesis, and we will now introduce a great dream of a science of science. [SOURCE: Page_39]

2.3       Symbolic Representation 2.3.1 Unification of sciences Scientists from different disciplines felt the need to put their specialised knowledge on a common map, their partial understanding together to form a general picture. A plurality of specialised sciences is needed due to the ontological plurality of reality, and exchanges between the different disciplines are also needed. This unification of science has been a recurring goal throughout history: [SOURCE: Page_40]

• with René Descartes in the 17th century, who perceives the unity of science through the unity of the human mind 9 . He represented sciences as branches coming out from a tree rooted in metaphysics. The human mind, represented by this trunk, should follow a method, a mathesis universalis, such that thought operations follow an order and a measure, with the language of physics as the universal scientific language. [SOURCE: Page_40]

• with the Enlightement in France in the 18th century, to free and enlighten humanity thanks to knowledge 10 . [SOURCE: Page_40]

• with Auguste Comte in the 19th century to guide social progress 11 . He envisaged a historical clas- sification of sciences from the most general discipline to the most complex, with sociology as the culminating science. [SOURCE: Page_40]

• with the Circle of Vienna of logical positivism in the 20th century to make a universal science. [SOURCE: Page_40]

Can we unify sciences? Scientists are proof of an ontological plurality 12 to approach reality, however there exists a risk of reductionism because physics is the most appropriate to describe reality. Although criticised for proposing a reductionist vision, Descartes describes reality through its physical and mathe- matisable dimension, which is most directly accessible. The conciliation of these disciplines however faced difficulties due to the determination of a unifying language, the form of this unified science, and its final- ity. Typically in the 20th century, Carnap imagined a unified science described in the form of a deductive system with a phenomenalist-based language with practical finalities, while Neurath imagined an ency- clopedia with a physicalist-based language 13 , cross-references are made between things and words aiming to clarify the concepts, to establish connections between different disciplines studying the same object, and 9 Descartes, Règles pour la direction de l’esprit, 1628 10 D’Alembert, Discours préliminaire, 1751 11 Cours de philosophie positive, 1830-42 12 i.e. multiple manners, multiple levels 13 a unitary language without words considered dangerous [SOURCE: Page_40]

17 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_40]

to suggest analogies that may open new perspectives. The encyclopedia is an example of what we call symbolic representation, aiming to unify knowledge. Diderot defined encyclopedia as a chain of knowledge, aiming to ”bring together scattered knowledge, to explain the general system to the men with whom we live and to pass it on to the men who will come after us, so that the work of the past will not have been in vain for the centuries to come”. Symbolic representation is a way of modelling knowledge by using natural language, concepts and symbols such as words. The simplest example is how we speak, representing reality through our individual perceptions. Treatment wetlands can be described physically from their composi- tion and structure, procedurally in relation with other treatment steps and treatment mechanisms, and causally with reasoning. Communication and exchange of information are done through language, but the understanding from words is limited by: [SOURCE: Page_41]

• Backgrounds and references: collective symbolism and frequency of use of terms, including those used in science. In particular, knowledge is often relative to a place or a period of time, it evolves and may not coincide with the truth, [SOURCE: Page_41]

• Scientific jargons: lack of consensus between disciplines and the non-equivalence of definitions for certain common concepts, [SOURCE: Page_41]

• Language barrier: no literal translations between the different languages, [SOURCE: Page_41]

• Innovation and trends temporality: existence of homonyms (one term referring to two different con- cepts) and synonyms (several terms referring to a single concept). [SOURCE: Page_41]

As terms related to innovations in water management are marketed and overused 14 , the scientific literature is teeming with terms with unclear definitions, redundancy of homonyms and synonyms, thus scattering information and hindering its accessibility and comprehension. With a flourishing technology and terminology, and in the context of integrated research projects (i.e. involving multiple disciplines), we need a standardised and consensual representation of the field (especially treatment wetlands) that is clear and adapted enough for all stakeholders. We are here interested in bridging our different points of view with a more complex symbolic representation. There are different levels to organise knowledge using a symbolic and intersubjective 15 representation. These levels defined by Garshol (2004), see Figure 2.3, are successive steps that enrich this organisation of knowledge. Although it is possible to develop one type of representation without fulfilling the previous ones, some confusion and difficulties in communication may arise. The confusion is related to meaning, i.e. to semantics, and is reflected in the choice of terms, definitions and relations for given concepts (see the added elements in Figure 2.3). The main task therefore consists in elucidating the different elements directly associated with semantics. [SOURCE: Page_41]

2.3.2 Semantic approach to concepts Decision-making in an integrated water management approach stands at the crossroads of multiple dis- ciplines. Unlike French in which we take a decision, or German in which we meet a decision, English tells us that we make a decision. This verb highlights the anthropogenic construction process of decisions and illustrates how terms can influence our perception of and relation to concepts. Concepts are units of thought (ISO 25964-1, 2011), units used to reason and make sense of the world. We could probably say I use and relate concepts, therefore I am. Concepts are formulated by using terms and definitions. For example: ”The reed grows in water” mobilises the idea of a plant that looks like a long grass with feathery leaves called a reed, the action of increasing size represented by the term growing, and the transparent liquid found in natural aquifers called water. Terms are "words or phrases used to label a concept" (ISO 25964-1), and definitions are a representation of a concept through a description, a statement of its meaning that distinguishes it from other similar concepts (Vezina, 2009). They can be intentional (a set of properties) or extensional (a list of examples). We all have concepts in our minds, but we can doubt that things are the way they are perceived. All these terms and definitions are at the root of many misunderstandings men- tioned previously. These barriers are also accentuated by the effect of time and perspective in the context of integrated water management. [SOURCE: Page_41]
