2.3.3 Ontologies Properly providing a term and a definition for a concept seems to be a difficult task. Despite having differ- ent ideas about a term, we use the same words and perpetuate confusion, and conversely, no communication would occur between agents working on the same concept but using different terms. Therefore, knowledge representations based solely on terms and definitions seem inadequate. To a certain extent, data and knowledge can be handled by algorithms and computers, with applications to this physics-based approach. Nonetheless, they may also facilitate the organisation and elucidation of new understandings. Following on from this goal of unification of sciences, we will present a symbolic way to represent knowledge that we envisage for treatment wetlands, based on the support of computer tools. More complex structures such as thesauruses and ontologies (Figure 2.3) are of interest because of their ability to handle plurality (aspects, viewpoints) of a given concept, notably with the help of a computer-based implementation. [SOURCE: Page_42]

• A thesaurus contributes to the standardisation of terminologies by relating a concept (represented by a term) to synonyms, close matches and translations, and by providing a hierarchical classification of concepts in a given domain. [SOURCE: Page_42]

• From ontology, a branch of metaphysics that studies the nature of things, ontologies in computer and information science aim to represent concepts and model knowledge by characterising a concept: identifying its properties and its relationship to other elements. An ontology is an explicit, formal and shared representation of knowledge, (Uschold and Gruninger, 1996; Hepp et al., 2008). [SOURCE: Page_42]

The structure of the two representations may appear similar, but they are intrinsically different, and ontologies are more rigorous in establishing relationships, (Kless et al., 2015, 2012). Ontologies specify the type of relationship, whereas thesaurus hierarchies mix them all, notably is a part of and is a. An ontology relates concepts by pairs, in the form of semantic triples: [SOURCE: Page_42]

19 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_42]

predicate Sub ject −−−−−−−→ Ob ject where: [SOURCE: Page_43]

• Subject (as a node) is the resource to describe, • Predicate (as an arc or arrow) is a property (the nature of the relation, in the form of a verb), • Object (as a node) is another resource, actual data, or value of the property, • Subject and Object are also referred to as relata [SOURCE: Page_43]

A set of semantic triples where some concepts are related to several other concepts is called a semantic network or triple graph. [SOURCE: Page_43]

nota bene 1. Some clarification on the definition [SOURCE: Page_43]

• An ontology is a and not the representation, since there may be multiple representations of knowledge, depending on the scope, reasons and goals for its development. It does not aim to be exhaustive, but concise, [SOURCE: Page_43]

• It is shared because it is intersubjective and should be developed hand in hand with all stakeholders to be consistent and inclusive. This process will of course involve iterative discussions between stake- holders, [SOURCE: Page_43]

• It is formal and explicit because it is well structured and relates a concept to its main properties. [SOURCE: Page_43]

Ontologies can therefore describe a domain of knowledge by collecting and linking different forms of knowledge and domains. Concepts range from abstract to more tangible: more abstract concepts are called upper concepts and form the structure of the ontology. They can be applied to multiple cases, while most specific concepts are called instances and represent practical knowledge. Widely used in web applications 16 and the medical field 17 , ontologies facilitate communication between agents and interoperability be- tween technological devices. Concepts are also referenced by a universal reference identifier. Corominas et al. (2018) highlights that ontologies are a promising computational technique for application in wastew- ater treatment, and that they are currently in a trigger phase for academic expectations on the Gartner hype cycle curve (Dedehayir and Steinert, 2016), with existing ontologies for wastewater treatment plants aiming to facilitate decision support, technology selection and knowledge management. The hype cycle models the visibility of a technology over time by combining two curves: the hype level and the technical maturity. However, this model does not delve into the components of hype, which should be associated not only with innovation, but also with the media and social system (Dedehayir and Steinert, 2016). Their development is expected to increase. [SOURCE: Page_43]

Vocabulary Although ontologies aim to establish a vocabulary and semantic relationships for knowledge representa- tion and reasoning, they are themselves subject to the challenges they address. Readers may encounter different definitions of ontologies to which articles refer (Hepp et al., 2008; Baydaroğlu et al., 2022): [SOURCE: Page_43]

Musen (1992) A standardized lexicon that also includes information about how items are categorized and related to one another [SOURCE: Page_43]

Studer et al (1998), from: Borst (1997), Gruber (1993) A formal and explicit specification of a shared con- ceptualisation [SOURCE: Page_43]

Welty and Guarino (2001) A working application that is based on a conceptual model [SOURCE: Page_43]

Noy and McGuinness (2001) A formal explicit description of concepts in a discourse domain (classes, also called concepts), properties of each concept (slots, occasionally called roles or properties), and limits on slots (facets, sometimes called role restrictions) 16 For information search and agent interactions: the Resource Description Framework (1999), DARPA Agent Markup Language, taxonomies categorizing Web sites like Yahoo!, and for products and services terminology and categorization: the Amazon.com ontology and the United Nations Standard Products and Services Code ontology. 17 Medicine has developed two main ontologies to set a standard terminology: the Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine SNOMED (2000), and the semantic network of the Unified Medical Language System (1993). Bioinformatics have developed Open Biomedical ontologies such as the Gene Ontology. [SOURCE: Page_43]

20 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_43]

Smith (2003) A set of concepts written in a standard syntax with widely agreed definitions to produce a lexical or taxonomic framework for knowledge representation that can be shared across various information technology communities [SOURCE: Page_44]

Brank et al (2005) The fundamental data structure for comprehending knowledge [SOURCE: Page_44]

Raskin and Pan (2005) A formal representation of technical concepts and their interrelationships in a way that supports domain knowledge [SOURCE: Page_44]

Scholten (2008) An ontology is a concise and precise, formal specification shared by its (human or ma- chine) users and providing sufficient vocabulary such that a piece of knowledge can be formalized for its intended purpose [SOURCE: Page_44]

Guarino et al (2009) A special kind of information object or computational artifact [SOURCE: Page_44]

Garcia and Gil (2010) A clear alternative for formally representing content value chains and allowing copyright management solutions to be implemented on top of that formalization [SOURCE: Page_44]

Arp et al (2015) A representational artifact that includes a taxonomy and whose representations are in- tended to denote a set of universals, defined classes, and relationships between them [SOURCE: Page_44]

Nasution (2018) Foundation of semantic [SOURCE: Page_44]

Khider et al (2019) Formal means of representing objects and their properties, and it represents consensus knowledge that allows a community to explain major concepts in a domain using common language [SOURCE: Page_44]

Khadir et al (2021) The product of a shared body of information that has been organized in such a way that it can be read by machines and captures a specific conceptualization of the universe [SOURCE: Page_44]

The different definitions that have emerged over time point to the multiple advantages of ontologies: their ability to standardise and formalise knowledge about a given domain, and their interoperability for computer applications, while mobilising natural language. The conceptualisation of a domain (getting a general overview from concrete situations) and the abstraction (getting essential properties for each con- cept) are tasks that involve and target people at the same time. Developers and users should not be too different, otherwise the standardised and formalised representation may not be shared, agreed, consensual or universal for all. [SOURCE: Page_44]

The terminology concerning the elements that make up an ontology is also subject to synonyms (Oliva- Felipe et al., 2017; Ceccaroni et al., 2003; Scholten, 2008). They are defined below: [SOURCE: Page_44]

Classes Concept, entity, entity type, concrete representation of concepts/role categories/phenomenon cat- egories, elements, resources, subjects/objects [SOURCE: Page_44]

Subclass Subconcept, subtype y that inherits properties of class Y if y is a type of Y . [SOURCE: Page_44]

(Single) instances Most specific classes, specialisations of concepts, they cannot have subclasses [SOURCE: Page_44]

Relations (between classes) Relations, predicates, including taxonomic hierarchy between classes, rela- tions correspond to predicates pointing to another resource. Typical relations are is a, has, part of, property of, instance of, identical to, performed by, determined by, etc. [SOURCE: Page_44]

Properties Roles/slots of classes features, attributes. Properties correspond to predicates pointing to an actual value. [SOURCE: Page_44]

Facets Attribute, type of slot, restrictions on the slot, i.e. allowed values, cardinality [SOURCE: Page_44]

Norms Conditions, rules, constitutive or regulative conditions, formulae, sets of functions [SOURCE: Page_44]

Axioms Knowledge that cannot be proven [SOURCE: Page_44]

### 7. Documentation, guidelines

The most widely used language and software for implementing an ontology are Web Ontology Language (OWL) and Protege software. In practice, a semantic triple is also called a Resource Description Framework (RDF) Unit. This encoding structure is used to describe databases and metadata. RDF is associated with a syntax (e.g. turtle) and a vocabulary (e.g. Dublin Core vocabulary). An ontology is an abstraction, i.e. it is sufficiently independent of a given situation from which knowledge is extracted. It is therefore capable of covering multiple situations. An ontology is often divided into two parts, on the one hand the top level ontology, which consists of constitutional (or structural) knowledge, i.e. more abstract concepts, a tree, and on the other hand the domain ontology, which consists of operational knowledge, i.e. concepts relevant to a specific domain, a birch tree, a palm tree. The operational use of ontologies comes when they are fed with concrete data. Through knowledge engineering, ontologies can be incorporated into knowledge-based systems that can make inferences and solve problems or support decision making with artificial intelligence. The relationships implemented can help a user to identify relationships within data (variables), make inferences and thus transform data into knowledge (Corominas et al., 2018). They are more flexible than expert systems based on if-then rules to solve problems. [SOURCE: Page_45]

Existing works [SOURCE: Page_45]

There are several ontologies dealing with water, developed with different scopes, types of stakeholders and levels of detail. In the field of wastewater treatment, we have identified the following ontologies: [SOURCE: Page_45]

Cabezut-Boo and Sánchez-Aguilar (1999) began the work with the development of a knowledge base for activated sludge and a stabilisation lagoon facilities. Typical elements constituting these technologies were identified from interviews, standards and WWTP implementation, daily logs and experimental data. [SOURCE: Page_45]

Ceccaroni (2001); Ceccaroni et al. (2003) developed an ontology: WaWO, for wastewater treatment man- agement (with a focus on activated sludge plants) as well as for modelling of the treatment mech- anisms, see Figure 2.4. The classes are related to the WWTP (eg. descriptor core concept), the artificial intelligence (AI) control software (eg. state-WWTP core concept) and the microbial taxon- omy (eg. bacteria (superkingdom) core concept). WaWO has been developed for a decision support system: DAI-DEPUR+ and stored in the Ontolingua Knowledge System Laboratory Server. It has also been integrated into OntoWEDSS, which is implemented in the LISP programming language 18 , not widely used. [SOURCE: Page_46]

Oliva-Felipe et al. (2017) updated WaWO to WaWO+ in OWL and is still used and maintained. It describes physical, chemical and biological parameters and covers not only treatment, but also water quality (with quality classification) at a regional scale, the urban water cycle (representing mechanisms in drinking and waste water, water distribution and sewerage systems) and the social aspect (norms and regulations). Water transport, waste producers, treatment technologies, water quality, land use are also included. The ontology is divided into upper, core and river ontologies, each of which is further divided into upper terms and the instances of these upper terms. For nature-based solutions technological units, treatment wetlands are not considered, but lagooning is. [SOURCE: Page_46]

Scholten et al. (2004); Scholten (2008) developed an ontology to facilitate communication and modelling. It is based on the HarmoniQuA approach (a modelling support tool, MoST) consisting of a knowledge base and a policy toolbox. The ontology consists of the following ontological layers: the meta-ontology, the generic model knowledge (context, objectives), the mathematical knowledge (mathematical oper- ators, equations, variables and parameters), the simulation model knowledge, the generic simulation models for application domains and the specific simulation models for projects. [SOURCE: Page_47]

Chau (2007) developed a knowledge management system based on KArlsruhe ONtology and Semantic Web (KAON). It regroups several models for river flow and water quality. They characterised the inputs needed to select the models, the model parameters and the conditions of application of the parameters. [SOURCE: Page_47]

Elag and Goodall (2013) developed the Water Resources Component (WRC) ontology, which could facili- tate numerical modelling by identifying and coupling models that best describe mechanisms in water and earth disciplines, see Figure 2.5. The core concepts are grouped into four layers: resources (meta- data and case study: developer, development stage, organisation, project, data), scientific (mathemat- ical models: symbols, equation, units, mathematical classification, domain), coupling (application of models: modelling framework, architecture, standards interface, computational resolution) and tech- nical (implementation: programming language, operating system, number of processors, memory requirements). • The core concepts on which hierarchical relationships are built: Attribute, Component, Mate- rial, Method, Process, Scale and Step, see Figure 2.7, • a module for mapping the classes and data into the structure of a product transformation, process-oriented itinerary, with the core concept observation as well as other concepts reused from the SOSA/SSN, BFO and Time ontologies. PO$_2$ structure and core concepts allows the development of ontologies which are neither too specific nor too general. Ontologies are interesting tools for aggregating knowledge, but they still suffer from a lack of clear definitions and agreed terminology. Some have been developed to describe the large scope of wastewater management and river water quality, but do not include treatment wetlands. Modelling ontologies provide a description of mechanistic model concepts, but have a very detailed scope that is insufficient for non- specialists. Finally, The PO$_2$/TransformON ontology is one of the ontologies under development in PO$_2$ Manager software. It is applied to biomass transformation but would also fit the wastewater treatment train. However, the software is different than the typical P rote ge software used for ontologies. The ori- entation towards a preferred software favours standardisation, but the development of new software and encodings over time leads to the obsolescence of previous works, which is also aggravated by the absence of referees for the maintenance of ontologies, as illustrated by the translation and change of developer from WaWO in LISP to WaWO+ in OWL. [SOURCE: Page_49]

The standardisation of terminology is a necessity for better communication between stakeholders, es- pecially for wastewater management, where the correct definition of concepts and preferred terms is key for regulations. What is this? Is it the same as that? Semantics help to define objects, and a clear scope and description of the system constitute a crucial first step for good modelling. [SOURCE: Page_49]

26 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_49]

2.4       From symbols to numbers In this part, we will see how symbols (terms) are closely intertwined with numbers, and how we can easily move from a qualitative to a quantitative approach. [SOURCE: Page_50]

2.4.1      Defining the scope Setting the scope is an essential step of research, it contains the boundaries in which scientific results hold true. In this scope, conventions 19 are set as structural means to interpret scientific results, such as setting a referential in physics, or a geometrical framework in mathematics. Moving further, research also poses prior conventions of equivalence regarding the entities and attributes to be considered, slightly similar to the steps for the construction of definitions 20 . These conventions consist in defining categories of equiv- alence through a taxonomic operation (establishing categories from a set of common attributes) and an identification operation (assigning the entities to a given category). This is an important preliminary step at the crossroads of the nature of things, their sensory perception, and their quantitative characteristics. The various publications defining nature-based solutions and treatment wetlands differ in the choice of term used (preferred term) and in the characteristics set out in the definitions. Treatment wetlands are ambivalent concepts, both studied for their relation to society in the framework of nature-based solutions, and for their technological intensification of natural processes. Can ponds and treatment wetlands be studied together? Can horizontal flow and vertical flow treatment wetlands be studied together? Should air temperature or rainfall events be monitored? Should grain size or bacterial communities be identified along the treatment wetland? Unlike confined and controlled experiments where a direct cause-to-effect phenomenon is to be studied, multivariate analyses of uncontrolled systems require specific planning of the selection of cases suitable for the study and the potentially relevant characteristics to be monitored. Determining equivalence categories and criteria of categorisation has been crucial in the social sciences (Desrosières, 1992, 2006). Because the results depend on these choices, often intuitively and informally made, we believe the methodology would prove useful in modelling, by better identifying the scope, the assumptions made, and the domain of validity of a model. In the case of modelling, microorganisms, and in particular selected bacterial communities, may be considered equivalent or not when measuring pollu- tant removal. Engineers may be more interested in pollutant removal performances, assuming a global microbial community responsible for a unique biodegradation of a pollutant represented by a first-order kinetic rate k, while scientists may be more interested in understanding reactional pathways and assume different bacterial communities having interrelated but distinct activities represented by Monod kinetic rates. Among the pollutants considered, greenhouse gas production is generally not considered (Dufossé et al., 2024). Decision-making is not only a final step for the political sphere, but a task that scientists face throughout their research. A good assessment of the construction methodology and conditions of validity of a model lead to more interpretable results and participate in more reliable decision-making. [SOURCE: Page_50]

Water quality The evolution of the assessment of water quality illustrates the change of perspective in determining the factors relevant to assessing water quality. During the Roman republic, water quality was understood and assessed through perception. Vuorinen et al. (2007) retransmits these historical records: ”The quality of the water was examined by the senses: taste, smell, appearance and temperature. Also the health of the people and animals using a water source was considered (Vitruvius De Architectura. I,iv,9,10; VIII, iv,1,2). Throughout antiquity tasty or tasteless, cool, odourless and colourless water was considered the best, and stagnant, marshy water was avoided. These ideas were held until the end of antiquity as expressed by Palladius (5th century, Opus Agriculturae. I, 4) or Paulus Aeginata (7th century, Paulus Aeginata I.50)”. Rey (2021) has analysed how the symbolic environment of water has disappeared over time. In particular, with the hygienist period and scientific progress, our perception of water has changed to that of a resource that we see through toilet flushes and kitchen taps, and whose chemical structure and properties have been deciphered. Breaking down water into the concept of atoms may have been unthinkable centuries ago. Nowadays, the concept of quality of French tap water relies on the assessment of the presence of microorganisms, pesticides and nitrates. The quality estimate is directly dependent on the choice of the factors assumed relevant. The pesticide indicator is itself based on a specific set of molecules (metolachlo- rine, chloridazone, etc.), which was modified in 2021 to include pesticide metabolites in the assessments. This change in the construction of the pesticide category, i.e. in how chemical quality is modelled, resulted 19 Poincaré in The Value of science, 1905 20 see the previous section, Chapter 2.3.2 [SOURCE: Page_50]

27 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_50]

in a lower quality indicator for 2021 compared to the previous years: water pesticide quality compliance dropped to 82.6% in 2021 21 , as opposed to 94.1% in 2020 and 91.9% in 2019 22 . [SOURCE: Page_51]

Analysing the world with categorisation and quantification does not leave room for reveries, and instead creates a shift from the use of symbols to numbers 23 . In order to make things, objects, or concepts (here, water quality) commensurable, conventions must be set. Bachelard speaks about objectivation rather than objectivity to describe the construction activity of scientists 24 . In the face of this action arise epistemo- logical obstacles notably due to our inherited thought operations, our uncontrolled usage of words, and our reductionist quantification. There is a necessity of a qualitative definition and categorisation of the object of study (which pollutants to prioritise?), prior to any quantitative assessment, but the approach may involve a preliminary quantitative characterisation, notably for the identification operation with the thresholds determining when water has a good or bad quality. Because of this ambiguous and subjective identification and prior calculations, the convention of equivalence may be challenged at any time. Indeed, the selection of certain key factors and methods over others has the potential to influence our perception of an object, even though no physical change has occurred to it. This categorisation also leads to the need to define labels (or terms) for these categories. [SOURCE: Page_51]

Reliability, robustness, resilience Characterising the different objects starts with their definition and differentiation, and with the choice of a term. Words have a metaphorical power such that there exist terminological trends due to a porosity of language between scientific and common knowledge. Scientists for example use the concept of sponge cities 25 (Argent et al., 2008) to best convey the explanatory principle of more permeable cities for stormwa- ter management, and governments the concept of resilience (Juan-García et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2021a) which originated in 1970 from the field of ecology. Confusion may arise from possible gap between the imaginary conveyed by the terms, and their scientific definition. We will briefly describe the technical and quantitative definition of the concepts of reliability, robustness and resilience often encountered in both political and technological objectives. [SOURCE: Page_51]

Decision-making now particularly relies on quantitative assessments as mentioned in Chapter 1.3. If the objective of decision-making is to be reliable, what are its characteristics? What makes a decision trustworthy? We are interested in reliability in situations facing uncertainty. Considering urban wa- ter management, environmental, social and economic stresses constitute sources of uncertainties. What should be the characteristics of these assessments? They should be reliably produced, and the objects be- ing assessed should also be reliably characterised. Reliability constitutes an initial condition to the criteria of robustness and resilience. They are reported by Jones (2021); Hadjimichael (2016); Juan-García et al. (2017) as: [SOURCE: Page_51]

Reliability the ability of a system to meet its objective, the quality of consistently performing well. It is quantified as the probability that a system does not fail under defined conditions and over a defined period. Or inversely, it can correspond to the frequency of failure. [SOURCE: Page_51]

Robustness the ability of a system to maintain a satisficing state under expected but undesired condi- tions. It can also correspond to the range of these expected but undesired conditions outside the defined conditions that a system can face without failure. [SOURCE: Page_51]

Resilience the ability of a system to absorb, recover from and adapt to unanticipated failure, due to unex- pected conditions. It also correspond to the time needed or the speed for a system to absorb, recover from and adapt to a situation of failure. [SOURCE: Page_51]

Reliability in its technical definition may not be a sufficient criteria to deal with uncertainty, since by definition it does not consider out of scope or non forecasted situations. But in the context of global change, 21 82.6% of the population is served with water whose quality complies with regulation in 2021. The microorganisms and nitrates performance of indicators for other key factors remained stable. 22 Synthesis on French tap water quality, ARS, 2021 23 Merleau-Ponty in L’oeil et l’esprit, 1960 states that ”science manipulates things and gives up living in them”. He slightly qualifies further down with ”but classical science clung to a feeling for the opaqueness of the world, and it expected through its constructions to get back into the world” 24 Le Rationalisme appliqué, 1949 25 Bachelard actually studied the notion of sponge as an intuitive but inefficient image to represent physical phenomena, in La formation de l’esprit scientifique, 1934, Chapter: An example of a verbal barrier: the sponge. Over-extension of familiar images [SOURCE: Page_51]

Figure 2.8: Illustration by Cled’12 of the change of paradigm from a flowered city to a resilient city, showing a turn in the concept of cities, from a sensory perception to a technical assessment. [SOURCE: Page_52]

more intense and frequent droughts and floods constitute undesired but increasingly anticipated condi- tions 26 . Similarly to stormwater management which specifically relies on understanding and quantifying the uncertainty of rain events, decision makers need to characterise the uncertainty associated with these forecasted conditions. We are observing a reference shift in the scope of urban water management: where we may rather speak of resilience, we now need to consider a new reality that includes these undesired and expected damaging events. This shift and the range of possible scopes lead to confusion as to the correct concept to use. In a technical context, reliability is widely employed and corresponds to a quantitative assessment of systems (Jóźwiakowski et al., 2017; Marzec et al., 2019; Jucherski et al., 2017; Lombard- Latune et al., 2018; Manous and Stakhiv, 2021). Resilience assessment relies on four criteria: stressors, properties, metrics and interventions. However, Juan-García et al. (2017) reports that resilience does not have a consensual definition across disciplines, which hinders resilience assessment in wastewater man- agement. Wang et al. (2021a) showed that cities interpret the concept of resilient cities according to their needs, and suggested to better identify the main features. Olsson et al. (2014) also highlights the large scope covered by resilience theory, and the need to bridge two disciplines, resilience and transition man- agement scholars together. This may be hindered by the difficulty in reconciling different values, questions, methods and data. [SOURCE: Page_52]

nota bene 2. For modelling, uncertainty comes from the modelling process and data management. The reliability of data and of a model will be presented in the Section 2.6. [SOURCE: Page_52]

I had the opportunity to have a live illustration for a presentation of my PhD thesis by Cled’12. He illustrated this change of paradigm with the term resilient city in Figure 2.8, showing the tendency to rec- oncile multiple visions of wastewater management, but still under the influence on one side, of subjective ideals, and on the other, of a techno-scientific and quantitative approach. [SOURCE: Page_52]

2.4.2 Consensus and compromise Decision making is a process of comparison and selection of one option among multiple possibilities, which often is based on multiple criteria and performed collectively, in the face of certainty, risks, uncertainty, and conflicts (Poch et al., 2012). It requires information on which to base thinking, and time to consider it. The interdisciplinary status of Nature-based Solutions and integrated water management lead to the collaboration of stakeholders from different disciplines. Can different perspectives be unified? A common categorisation of Nature-based Solutions and treatment wetlands meets obstacles starting with terminol- ogy. Consensus on terminology already faces difficulties, as illustrated by the fact that ’treatment wetland’ is a term employed by engineers in the book of reference (Kadlec and Wallace, 2009), but neither identified nor used by the classifications of the interdisciplinary works by Castellar et al. (2021) and Anderson and Gough (2022). It illustrates the lack of porosity between research fields, and how terminology can affect bibliographic research and analysis. It also shows how the search for consensus on terminology can lead to very different preferred terms depending on the methodology and the stakeholders chosen. [SOURCE: Page_52]

26 2018 IPCC report [SOURCE: Page_52]

29 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_52]

Stakeholders, and in particular experts, can be selected on the basis of different criteria, which are given in (Mauksch et al., 2020)’s Table 2.3. Open discussions and workshops can be held with direct in- teractions between stakeholders or anonymously to reduce the influence of known stakeholders. There are several methods to reach consensus, often in the form of an iterative process of collecting individually argued responses, compiling and confronting responses, collecting new individually argued responses, etc., until a final aggregation of responses, (Pérez et al., 2018; Perez et al., 2014; Del Moral et al., 2018; Bourree et al., 2008). The aggregation of responses is often an undiscussed step, despite the large variability it brings. It is likely that no real consensus will emerge when dealing with terminology. Selecting preferred terms on the basis of their occurrence in the literature (assuming initial knowledge of all existing nomen- clatures) is an alternative to seeking active multi-agent consensus, although dominant terms may result from a few authors publishing frequently or from insufficient understanding. One problem with seeking consensus is the over-representation of the project leader’s opinion. He or she takes the initiative and is the decisive actor, from the selection of the experts to the aggregation of the results in the consensus process. Instead, finding out the evolution of concepts and terms and how they are perceived by different stakeholders can help to identify potential biases and stratifications in semantics and better connect all visions. [SOURCE: Page_53]

Method                                        Definition/explanation Social acclamation                            Peer nomination Political influence                           Selecting experts with potential political impact Personal involvement                          Selection on the basis of personal interest in the subject External Cues                                 Assessment based on externally available criteria, eg years on the job, job position, certification, publications, etc. Self-ratings                                  Self-assessment of expertise Past performance                              Selection based on past performance Knowledge tests                               Selection based on verifiable knowledge Psychological traits                          Cognitive tests assessing expertise [SOURCE: Page_53]

Table 2.3: List of expert identification method identified by Mauksch et al. (2020) [SOURCE: Page_53]

Especially in the context of integrated approaches, the notion of multi-criteria decision making is sim- ilar to that of consensus or voting systems: several criteria and opinions have to be aggregated, possibly with some trade-offs, and only one option is selected. What kind of Nature-based Solutions should be implemented? What dimensions should the solution have? Is cost, biodiversity or efficiency more impor- tant? Proposals can be selected, ranked or scored (grades) based on one or more criteria (e.g. scientific relevance, collective symbolism), with one or more iterations and using a specific metric (max, min, mean, median). The IDEA protocol 27 (Hemming et al., 2018a,b; Castellar et al., 2021) and the Delphi method 28 (Beiderbeck et al., 2021) are often used in the water sector. Decisions can be made by humans, but also by algorithms. In a quantitative approach, statistical tools have been developed to support decision mak- ing. Multiobjective or Pareto optimisation aims to find the optimal option, i.e. the one that satisfies the objectives of multiple criteria. For example, each option is compared to the objective set by each criterion, and its deviation can be represented by an objective function f (also known as a cost function). So how do you aggregate multiple criteria? By using an optimisation method that sums these objective functions and selects the lowest or highest sum. Weights and constraints can be applied to the function. Often there are multiple solutions that minimise or maximise the function, corresponding to the Pareto front along which one optimised criterion offsets another, see Figure 2.9. Multiobjective optimisation has been used in the management of coastal aquifers (Saad et al., 2022) or in the calibration of a hydrological model (Jung et al., 2017). [SOURCE: Page_53]

2.4.3 Metrics Providing a quantitative information, we use metrics to measure characteristics of concepts and objects, notably resilience. Metrics, also called efficiency criteria, are indicators that help answer the questions: 27 Investigate, Discuss, Estimate, Aggregate 28 The name Delphi historically derives from the Oracle of Delphi, the method assumes that structured group judgments are more accurate and valid than individual or unstructured group judgments. How different are these objects? Which system or which model is better? Many metrics have historically been established using water as a reference: grams, degrees Celsius, calories. These allow us to compare elements in a standardised way. For modelling and data analysis, the metrics used are not those mentioned above, but translations of better as closest to reality, or presents the least distance between its estimates and observations. [SOURCE: Page_54]

When describing a dataset or selecting relevant variables for a model, one is interested in how the variables evolve with respect to each other, say the pair X i and X j . This co-variation is measured by the covariance, which can be interpreted as the direction of an assumed linear relationship between the variables: 1 X   N Cov(X i , X j ) =          (x ik − X̄ i )(x jk − X¯ j ) N − 1 k=1 A data set is usually described by a correlation matrix that quantifies the degree of linear covariation. It standardises the covariance matrix by dividing it by the product of the standard deviations of the variables, which is more practical and interpretable since the correlations (also known as Pearson coefficients r) take values in [−1, 1]: Cov(X i , X j ) Corr(X i , X j ) = σX i σX j [SOURCE: Page_54]

nota bene 3. An alternative to the linear correlation assessment is the Spearman correlation, which quantifies the degree of monotony of the relationship. This is done by replacing the values of the variables with their ranks R[X i ] and R[X j ]. [SOURCE: Page_54]

For modelling, the regression coefficients or the models performances are determined by optimising or calculating a metric. The objective is to reduce the gap between the observations and the predictions. If we consider a target and aim for the middle (the observations), see Figure 2.10, the model needs to predict close to the centre (accuracy) and to be consistent in its predictions (precise). A variety of metrics have been studied, the most common of which are presented below considering a set Y of p characteristics on n observations and its estimate Ŷ : [SOURCE: Page_54]

The metric is sensitive to large differences (errors, outliers), which are emphasised by the square. [SOURCE: Page_54]

2.5      Numerical representation We will present several types of models which are used for treatment wetland numerical representation, and we will see to what extent they can be used, in particular for pre-design purposes. Numerical modelling consists of building a representation of reality using mathematical operators. Numerical modelling finds its linchpin wih Descartes (17th c.) who considers that human bodies function like machines and can be described through mathematics and physics. He suggested to break down complex problems into simpler subparts. Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651) extrapolates this idea to thoughts and perceptions: they are matter in motion that can thus be explained like mechanistic processes. The models can approximate reality by incorporating knowledge or data. Data corresponds to a set of real case studies, we will refer to this set as a ’sample’, or a set of observations or individuals, and the total number of cases, which may not all have been studied, is referred to as the population. From the reliance on knowledge and data, we can distinguish several types of models under various terminologies (Psichogios and Ungar, 1992; Schneider et al., 2022), which present a decreasing level of human intervention against an increasing autonomy of algorithms, and are reminiscent of the rationalist and empiricist views of how we acquire knowledge, as illustrated in Figure 2.11: [SOURCE: Page_57]

Mechanistic models These models are designed a priori, from theoretical and expert knowledge, and gen- erally describe major phenomena. The relationships between variables are physically interpretable and may involve causality with the dependent variable. These models include the following terms: first principles, conceptual models, a priori models, process-based models, expert-driven models, de- ductive models, white-box models, parametric models, ascending models. [SOURCE: Page_57]

Empirical models These models describe mechanisms by assuming a structure derived from knowledge, but whose parameters are estimated empirically from data and specific experiments. They are also called phenomenological models. [SOURCE: Page_57]

Statistical models they assume a certain structure in the relationships between variables, but they do not guarantee causality or physical meaning. The parameters are estimated by optimisation on data. These models are also known as grey box models or global conceptual models. [SOURCE: Page_57]

Data-driven models These models are built solely from data, a posteriori. They do not represent causal relationships but correlations, and relationships between variables are not known or explicit in the models. These models are also known as: learning models, machine (and deep) learning models, a posteriori models, inductive models, black box models, non-parametric models, descending models. [SOURCE: Page_57]

These categories are not consensual, but a clear nomenclature and definition seems necessary to under- stand the nature of the models. In particular, the term ’empirical models’: Schneider et al. (2022) includes them in mechanistic approaches, while IWA (2020) includes them in data-driven approaches. Grey-boxes also include hybrid models. Statistical models are also considered by some researchers as empirical models (see presentations from the IWA MIA SG webinar on 10 November 2020, (IWA, 2020)) or learning models, in the same category as machine learning models. The review by Defo et al. (2017) on treatment wetlands models considers that Monod, time-dependent retardation, NkC*, first-order and regression models end up being black-box models, just like neural networks, due to their global scope ’input-output’. The term parametric is also quite confusing, as Schneider et al. (2022) notes. The distinction is whether parameters have a physical meaning or not. In statistics, however, parametric refers to models with a finite number of parameters that assume normality, such as linear regression or one-way ANOVA models. [SOURCE: Page_57]

We propose to think of the set of different types of models as a discrete gradient between dependence on knowledge and dependence on data, and between explainability and accuracy, as shown in Figure 2.12. Grey-box models may be physics-based, but have a global and non-detailed approach/understanding. In the same domain, hybrid models combine mechanistic and data-driven models and are also only partially interpretable. [SOURCE: Page_57]

The current design of treatment wetlands is often based on simple and rather imprecise a posteriori models, values summarised by Dotro et al. (2017): [SOURCE: Page_57]

the rule of thumb based on the population equivalent. With PE expressed as BOD load according to the European definition, a vertical flow treatment wetlands typically requires an area of 2 to 5 m^2 .PE −1 and a horizontal flow treatment wetlands 5 to 10 m^2 .PE −1 . More in detail: VF wetlands used as [SOURCE: Page_57]

the mass loading charts based on expert knowledge. They impose constraints on annual (cross-sectional) organic loading rates (g.m−2 .d −1 ) and hydraulic loading rates (m^3 .m−2 .d −1 ). The area is calculated from the allowable areal mass loading rate (g.m−2 .d −1 ) derived from a mass loading chart. For VF wetlands, the maximum OLR is of 27 g COD /m^2 d against 20 g COD /m^2 d for Germany and Austria. For HF wetlands, the maximum OLR is of 6 g BOD 5 /m^2 d with a surface HLR of 20 mm/d in Spain, while in the US, the maximum OLR is of 4-8 g BOD 5 /m^2 d with a surface HLR of 20 to 50 mm/d. In practice however, the method is sometimes employed for the pre-design of treatment wetlands with conditions outside of the validity bounds of the loading charts. These models are conservative, i.e. they tend to over-size the treatment wetlands to ensure that the pollutant removal performances comply with treatment objectives based on typical data. Over-sizing is a major drawback for these extensive systems, requiring large and sometimes expensive available footprints compared to activated sludge (0.12-0.3 m^2 .PE −1 , (Dotro et al., 2017)). Moreover, the models do not predict the actual treatment performances which fluctuate between case-studies and over time (see the values reported in Table 2.2, such that there is a need for both a more optimised design model and a need to have access to the corresponding treatment performances. We will investigate to what extent a numerical representation, based on knowledge or data, can improve the design predictions. [SOURCE: Page_59]

2.5.1 Mechanistic models We will present mechanistic models more into details with an example on the historical comprehension and model development of population growth in biology, which can be applied to many species and situations. Indeed, the main phenomena in treatment wetlands are the separation of liquid and solid phases, and the biodegradation of pollutants by micro-organisms for their growth, in particular, bacterial communities. Population growth corresponds to the evolution of the number of individuals with respect to time, which can be represented mathematically with an ordinary differential equation. The evolution could also be considered with respect to other variables, and when it depends on multiple variables, it can be represented with partial differential equations. Mechanistic modelling is a long-standing dialogue as illustrated below: [SOURCE: Page_59]

• Malthus with his population dynamics described by a linear exponential growth model that he devel- oped in an essay published in 1798: dN(t) = rN(t) dt represents a system of a population N that grows infinitely with a growth rate r and no one dies. [SOURCE: Page_59]

• Verhulst, who introduced the non-linear logistic model by adding a threshold to the Malthusian model, in 1848: dN(t)              N(t) = rN(t)(1 −      ) dt               K so that the population becomes mortal, and mortality increases with the size of the population, as seen in − N K. [SOURCE: Page_59]

• Gompertz, who introduced an age-dependent component into the model to make individuals unequal in the face of mortality. [SOURCE: Page_59]

• Lokta and Volterra with their first-order nonlinear predator-prey differential equations to describe the dynamics of two interacting species, in 1925: dN(t)            N(t) ( dt = rN(t)(1 − K ) − α N(t)P(t) dP(t) dt = −µP(t) + β N(t)P(t) [SOURCE: Page_59]

where interaction with a predator P results in an additional cause of mortality −αP for the popula- tion N. [SOURCE: Page_59]

Bacterial growth from Activated Sludge models These mechanisms have been described for activated sludge models (ASM) and reused in treatment wet- lands models (Langergraber et al., 2009). The numerical models have been subjected to notation standard- isation based on the recommendations of Corominas et al. (2010) and Henze et al. (1982). In experimental studies, the substrates or pollutants of interest are specific molecules or intersections of chemical groups, which are the components most frequently monitored: COD, BOD, TKN, TN, TP, TSS. These compounds can be further subdivided according to additional criteria. They have been categorised and standardised by Corominas et al. (2010) based on several works for activated sludge and anaerobic digestion modelling. The notation associated with the pollutant fractions is based on the following characteristics: [SOURCE: Page_59]

Main symbol [SOURCE: Page_59]

• Particle size: particulate X, colloidal C, soluble S [SOURCE: Page_59]

36 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_59]

Subscript [SOURCE: Page_60]

• Degradability: undegradable U 30 , biodegradable B, abiotically convertible A • Organic/inorganic: Org, Ig • Name: compound organism • Specifications: internal cell compound, origin, location, compartment, degradation rate, units [SOURCE: Page_60]

Biokinetic reactions are described by the CWM$_1$ model developed by Langergraber et al. (2009) for HF wetlands, and by the CW2D model developed by Langergraber and Šimůnek (2005) for VF wetlands. The variables are the concentrations of chemical (substrate) and biological species (bacteria), not at the component level, but at the more detailed fraction level. For example, COD is broken down into more or less degradable soluble fractions SF, SA, SI and particulate fractions XS and XI. These concentrations evolve on the basis of the kinetic reactions in which they are involved and the stoichiometric coefficients that weight the fraction that actually reacts. 17 reactions are described in the model, added successively to better fit reality, see Table 2.5: [SOURCE: Page_60]

• first, we consider the aerobic growth of heterotrophic organisms X H on S O$_2$ , S S , and S I , [SOURCE: Page_60]

• then, to avoid infinite growth, the lysis of these organisms, reducing X H to produce more S S , but the oxygen consumption does not fit true variations, [SOURCE: Page_60]

• aerobic hydrolysis of X S is introduced and represents the breaking down of molecules into smaller molecules, producing more S S (but the sludge production is underestimated), [SOURCE: Page_60]

• non-biodegradable particulate X I is therefore considered in the lysis, but the oxygen consumption becomes too low, [SOURCE: Page_60]

• nitrification of S N H$_4$ to S NO$_3$ by autotrophic organisms X A is therefore considered, participating in X A aerobic growth and lysis, [SOURCE: Page_60]

• finally, denitrification is also considered, for anoxic growth of X H and anoxic hydrolysis. [SOURCE: Page_60]

These reactions are associated with process rates that determine their amplitude and the influences of the different variables. The process rate amplitude for the aerobic and anoxic growth reactions corresponds to the maximum growth rate r max = µ of the bacteria multiplied by their concentration. However, other chemical species can alter this value depending on their concentration. The influence of the components on the state of the process rates is introduced using switch functions (Gooijert, 2010). These changes are like weights, taking values between 0 and 1. If a species S is a limiting factor (i.e. low concentrations lead to a low process rate), its influence on the process rate is expressed by K S+S . Conversely, if a species S is an inhibiting factor (i.e. high concentrations lead to a low process rate), its influence on the process rate is expressed by KK+S . K is the saturation inhibition coefficient of S expressed in mg − S/L. For example, the aerobic growth of heterotrophic bacteria X H by consuming fermentable, readily biodegradable soluble COD S F is ρ = µH X H , where µH is the maximum aerobic growth rate of X H on S F . Since low concentrations S of S F can limit growth, the process rate then becomes ρ = µH ( S +FK ) = X H , and S F is consumed with a F   SF stoichiometric yield coefficient of − Y$_1$ . H [SOURCE: Page_60]

The mechanistic model CWM$_1$ is described with: [SOURCE: Page_60]

• a Gujer stoichiometric matrix representing the reaction or production of compounds for each process, see Table 2.4, [SOURCE: Page_60]

• a list of process rates, see Table 2.5, [SOURCE: Page_60]

• a list of kinetic, stoichimetric and composition parameters. [SOURCE: Page_60]

The impact of the mechanisms on each component concentration is the sum of the process rates multi- plied by the stoichiometric coefficients, using the Gujer matrix. [SOURCE: Page_60]

Treatment Wetlands models [SOURCE: Page_63]

Mechanistic models for treatment wetlands are developed in a similar way to activated sludge, with the main difference that activated sludge reactors are considered completely stirred tank reactors (CSTR) while treatment wetlands tend to behave like plug-flow reactors (PFR), i.e. they do not homogenise pollu- tants concentration between the inflow and outflow. They incorporate additional mechanisms (see Table 2.1) to better fit reality, although depending on the objective, some are designed to understand single mech- anisms and others are simplifications for operational use (Meyer et al., 2015). Dehghani Tafti et al. (2024) describes treatment wetlands models as integrated models composed of sub-models that interact with each other: hydrodynamic + sedimentation + filtration + water chemistry + biokinetic + biofilm models. Treat- ment wetlands with saturated subsurface flow can be represented by a hydraulic flow through a porous medium, transporting particulate and dissolved elements, which can then be degraded by bacteria for their growth, see Figure 2.13. The different submodels to employ vary with the type of Nature-based Solutions considered and with the modelling objective (or Nature-based Solutions use case). Fortunately, models have been developed for each of these mechanisms, which are combined and numerically implemented in simulation software such as those listed in Table 2.6. [SOURCE: Page_63]

Figure 2.13: Three mechanisms occurring in treatment wetlands and described in COMSOL. First, the water hydraulics are represented by the Richards equation model, then, the transport of pollutants is represented by the Darcy equation model, and finally, the biodegradation of the pollutants is represented by the CWM$_1$ model. [SOURCE: Page_63]

In practice, the determination of the most appropriate design for treatment wetlands is conservative and based on the compliance of the different effluent concentrations with regulatory effluent standards. Nitrogen removal is often the limiting process requiring larger treatment wetlands areas. The design ob- tained for N H$_4$ − N is usually prioritised due to its more stringent treatment requirements compared to BOD in order to meet its treatment objectives (Langergraber et al., 2020a). In this perspective, the repre- sentation of nitrogen dynamics in treatment wetlands has been addressed using mechanistic models (Tan et al., 2021; Morvannou et al., 2014), which underlined the importance of calibration that might be difficult to achieve for complex mechanistic models. They must rely on experimental studies such as the work of Pálfy and Langergraber (2014); Langergraber et al. (2007). [SOURCE: Page_63]

There are descriptive and predominantly process-based models that capture the complexity of mecha- nisms within treatment wetland, but their practical utility for design purposes remains challenging (Samsó and Garcia, 2013; Meyer et al., 2015). They require the calibration of numerous parameters such as degra- dation kinetic rate k, background concentration C ∗ , temperature coefficient θ , a process often dependent on specific contextual and scoping considerations. [SOURCE: Page_63]

2.5.2 Empirical Models Empirical models describe mechanisms from knowledge or assumptions about variables, while still relying on data to define their parameters, (Schneider et al., 2022). For treatment wetlands design purposes, long-term simulation models are required and simplifications are made to reduce the computational cost of mechanistic models. We will describe the NkC* model in detail because it is widely employed, notably for design purposes (Kadlec and Wallace, 2009), and we will therefore use it in our research. [SOURCE: Page_63]

NkC* model [SOURCE: Page_64]

To address the need for treatment wetlands design, the tank-in-series model is an empirical model devel- oped for HF wetlands, associated with a first-order kinetic rate for pollutant degradation and a background concentration. The resulting NkC* model predicts the effluent concentration of a given compound in the effluent using the following characteristics: surface area, inflow rate and inflow concentration of the com- pound (Von Sperling et al., 2023; von Sperling et al., 2023; Kadlec and Wallace, 2009), see Figure 2.14. The hydraulics are represented by a series of continuously stirred tank reactors, which enable to emulate what happens between a fully mixed reactor and a plug flow reactor, see Figure 2.15. In order to derive an analytical model, the NkC* model is assumed steady-state with all reactors having the same volume. [SOURCE: Page_64]

They compared kinetic rates k following first order kinetics and k Monod kinetics. They concluded that first order kinetics can be used robustly when the contaminant concentration is less than the Monod half saturation constant. Constant kinetics with values from the literature will therefore be used in our research. [SOURCE: Page_65]

Temperature dependence Removal kinetics are known to be temperature dependent, assuming higher values as temperature in- creases. The Van’t Hoff-Arrhenius law expresses the temperature dependence of the kinetic rate of chemi- cal transformation: Ea k = k o × e RT with : k is the reaction term, T the temperature in K, E a the apparent energy of activation, in mol.L−1 , R = 8.314 the gas constant, in J.K −1 .mol −1 (or Boltzmann constant). [SOURCE: Page_65]

This law has been simplified in (Metcalf and Eddy, 2003), into a new one that takes a reference tem- perature to determine the reaction kinetic constant k as a function of temperature. See the Appendix A.2 for the detailed calculations. [SOURCE: Page_65]

k T = k 20 θ (T −20) A linearised version can be obtained: [SOURCE: Page_65]

log(k T$_2$ ) − log(k T$_1$ ) = log(θ ) T$_2$ − T$_1$ So θ can then be calculated as θ = 10slope . [SOURCE: Page_65]

A curious observation for BOD$_5$ is that the θ found is less than 1, so the kinetics increase with decreas- ing temperature (for horizontal, aerated and batch wetlands). Allen et al. (2002); Stein and Hook (2005) propose an explanation with a higher rhizome aeration in cold winter conditions. The study shows that in summer, SO42− is used as electron acceptor and reduced to sulphide, while in winter, O$_2$ is used as it is more available and has a stronger redox potential. Dotro et al. (2017) commented on the difficulty of interpreting θ values less than 1.00, as this would be different from other biological treatment processes [SOURCE: Page_65]

42 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_65]

and would suggest that removal efficiencies could actually deteriorate with increasing liquid temperature. Dotro et al. (2017) considered this to be counter-intuitive and inconsistent with reports in the literature, as recognised by Kadlec and Wallace (2009). However, this could be possible if one considers that as the water temperature decreases, the internal cycling of certain parameters (such as BOD) also decreases. Another point that may have caused difficulties in the derivation and interpretation of θ values from operational wetlands is the fact that with an increase in temperature there may also be an increase in water loss by evapotranspiration. This water loss causes an increase in the measured effluent concentrations and there- fore an incorrect calculation of the removal efficiency, which can potentially lead to an incorrect decrease in the calculated value of θ as the water loss occurred during a period of high temperature. [SOURCE: Page_66]

Calibration The kinetic rates are determined by performing respirometry tests (Morvannou et al., 2011), but some parameters can also be determined from existing data. The number of tanks in series N has generally been determined arbitrarily for the TIS model or from tracer test studies. The number of tanks N is determined from tracer tests (Kadlec and Wallace, 2009). Recently, based on tracer test data, von Sperling et al. (2023) derived a relationship between N and the ratio between length and the depth of treatment wetlands: L N = 0.686( )0.671 h Background concentrations have also been determined empirically based on C in , with a power relation- ship for BOD background concentration C ∗ determined in a course from Aarhus University, September 2021: C ∗ = 0.6 + 0.4C 0.55 in [SOURCE: Page_66]

These equations are obtained by regression methods on data. These are described in the following part. [SOURCE: Page_66]

2.5.3 Data-driven models - statistical models Moving from mechanistic to statistical modelling, d’Ockham (14th c.) proposes as methodology to apply the principle of parsimony, i.e. to always consider the smallest number of hypotheses and parameters, and to ”shave away all that is unnecessary”. Then Claude Bernard (19th c.) introduced the experimental study of the pair cause to effect and Fisher (20th c.) upgraded the pair to multiple causes involved but not all con- trolled and multiple effects, leading to design experiments and randomness in statistical models. Statistics flourished in contexts with few observed individuals n and few measured variables p. Statistical models can be thought of as mathematical structures, and the expert selects the most appropriate one based on knowledge and the models’ fit to the data. A statistical model finds relationships between variables based on the data it is trained on. This approach is therefore a posteriori, so that without experts, causality cannot be inferred directly from the relationships found. Modellers opted for a parsimonious methodology, with carefully chosen variables to form a limited set of explanatory features, and hypothesised and exper- imented accordingly, steps that Burnham et al. (2002) recommends to take before data are collected. A proper methodology should avoid what Corominas et al. (2018) calls data graveyards, i.e., unused or un- usable data that may result from incomplete metadata for interpretation and analysis, or improper data storage practices. [SOURCE: Page_66]

Typically, it is possible to establish an empirical relationship to predict the outflow concentration or load of a pollutant P out , relative to the inflow concentration or load P in and flow rate q. The simplest forms considered by Rousseau et al. (2004) for HF wetlands are the following typical regressions: [SOURCE: Page_66]

• multi-linear P out = α + β1 P in + β2 q + ², β • power P out = αP in^1 qβ2 + ², [SOURCE: Page_66]

• or even an exponential relation with temperature T: P out = α e−βT + ². [SOURCE: Page_66]

With β i and α as regression coefficients and ² as residual variance. Different scales are used for the units: g and kg of pollutants, per day and per year. The parameters of these models can then be calibrated to specific cases, as was done by Son et al. (2010), which evaluated the area-based first-order kinetic rate constants k 20 for BOD, TP, TN and TSS. [SOURCE: Page_66]

In an Environmental Decision Support System (EDSS) developed in the framework of a COST action 31 (Acuña et al., 2023), the design equations relating the outflow loads L out to the treatment wetlands surface areas S T were the following: [SOURCE: Page_67]

• linear: L out = βl S T + ² β • power: L out = S Tp + ² [SOURCE: Page_67]

• exponential: L out = α e eβ e S T + ² [SOURCE: Page_67]

2.5.4      Data-driven models - machine learning models According to Hobbes, (Leviathan, 1651), intellectual activity was similar to calculations, with speech and actions as results. In 1950’s, Turing was dreaming of a thinking machine that would be considered as so when a man is not capable to distinguish who is human, when talking to another man and to a machine. At the same time rises Polanyi’s Paradox that people know more than they can actually express. Based on Hobbes’ vision of thinking process and with the goal to overcome Polanyi’s Paradox, Artificial Intelligence (AI) emerges. It is a term invented by John McCarthy and Marvin Lee Minsky. AI emerged much earlier than what public perception would tell: due to technological limits, its application had to wait for more powerful computing processors (Venkatasubramanian, 2019). Symbolic AI to formalise reasoning appears in 1940-50’s, followed by the development of expert systems and multi-agent systems in 1980-95’s, and eventually, numerical AI arose with machine learning and in particular deep learning with neural net- works, in 1990-2005’s. Modelling and statistics take a turn with the possibilities offered by AI, powered by computers and with the rise of Big Data, characterised by the 3V: volume generated, velocity of production, and variety of formats. The explosion of data, real-time monitoring and storage capacity (especially omic data), and better computer processors are opening up a new era for modelling. Artificial intelligence relies solely on data, and this field of research studies ”how to make computers do things that man is currently better at” (E. Rich 1983). [SOURCE: Page_67]

A given individual can be characterised by many variables that are monitored without a prior exper- imental design. This situation, where often n ≃ p or n <<< p (few to no degrees of freedom), poses a dilemma for statistical models because too many features could explain too little variability. A common in- dicator of a reliable model is the degrees of freedom (n − p), Zhu et al. (2023) uses the sample size to feature size ratio (SFR) and recommends a minimum SFR of 10 and ideally above 100. Data mining tools, machine learning models, many algorithms based on correlations, variable transformations, statistical operations and automated calculations have started to strive (Corominas et al., 2018). These models are particularly suited to the current challenges of modelling complex situations, i.e. multivariate situations. Legay (1997) considers that we are currently voluntarily exploring modelling of complex systems, in particular related to environmental challenges. Although legitimately criticised for relying on obscure processes, artificial intelligence allows an act of humility from scientists to rely on it when the mind cannot seize a too complex reality. Depending on the algorithms, the amount of data required varies from a few hundred observations to millions for deep learning models such as neural networks. The key difference with statistical models is the ability to tune the model, i.e. change the shape of the model itself to fit the data, rather than testing which model has the best shape. While statistical models have parameters to calibrate, based on a certain metric, machine learning models similarly have additional hyperparameters that modify the structure of the model and that the modeller can tune (Zhu et al., 2023). [SOURCE: Page_67]

Machine learning models are categorised according to their reliance on labelled data for training (the equivalent of calibration in mechanistic models): supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement; their objec- tive: descriptive and predictive; and the type of data and output: classification and regression, as illus- trated by Figure 2.16. The objects (concepts) involved in a supervised model (the model must provide an output) can be categorised into: [SOURCE: Page_67]

• the dependent variables: the variables to be estimated from other objects (it does not imply causality); target, outcome, output, endpoint [SOURCE: Page_67]

• the independent variables: the variables used to estimate; predictors, features, covariates. [SOURCE: Page_67]

Description [SOURCE: Page_68]

A typical machine learning model for describing and visualising data is the Principal Component Analysis (PCA). It describes variables in a new space whose basis consists of linear combinations of the variables: principal components. More precisely, these principal components correspond to the eigenvectors derived from the covariance matrix computed for the variables. The first component is oriented along the largest variability, the second is orthogonal to the first and captures as much residual variability as possible, and so on. The proportions of variance they capture correspond to the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix. To avoid bias (if there are different scales between variables), all variables are normalised. PCA helps with dimension reduction and information synthesis by projecting observations and variables along these principal components, often in two dimensions: along PC$_1$ and PC$_2$. The variables are represented as vectors within a circle of radius 1, with the same origin at the centre of the circle. The closer the norm of the vectors is to 1, the more they are represented by the principal components; and the closer they are to each other, the more they are correlated, while they are uncorrelated when their scalar product is close to zero. [SOURCE: Page_68]

Prediction [SOURCE: Page_68]

In supervised learning, prediction models are based on regression (quantitative output) and classification (categorical output). The methods developed are numerous, and in terms of implementation, ML methods have flourished so much that the caret R package (http://topepo.github.io/caret/) counts 50 types of ML methods, with about 10 different versions for each. Below are some examples of typical machine learning algorithms (excluding deep learning) for prediction: [SOURCE: Page_68]

Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) This is a type of multivariate regression model that seeks to minimise the sum of the squared differences between the observation and the predic- p tion: Σni=1 [yi − (β0 + Σ j=1 β j x i j )]2 . To do this, a penalty is added so that the coefficients β j must be [SOURCE: Page_68]

optimised to minimise the sum of the absolute values of β j (L$_1$ norm). All regression coefficients start with β i = 0. The β i of the variable x i that is most correlated with the dependent variable increases towards β i,OLS until another variable xk is correlated with the residuals of y on x i . Some of the coefficients may be 0 (reducing the complexity of the model), hence the other name for this method: L$_1$ regularisation. [SOURCE: Page_69]

Support Vector Machine (SVM) This algorithm is used for supervised classification and consists in iden- tifying a hyperplane that best divides a data set into two. To do this, the hyperplane with the max- imum margin relative to (the distance to or the number of) threshold observations is selected, and these boundary observations are called support vectors. For non-linear cases, SVM artificially in- creases the number of features by taking polynomial functions of the features to find relationships in higher dimensions. For regression, the model identifies instead the hyperplane that best fits the data. [SOURCE: Page_69]

k nearest neighbours (KNN) Used mainly for supervised classification, this algorithm is a local method that selects the k nearest neighbours of a new individual to predict its class. To do this, and to avoid bias, all variables are normalised and the k nearest neighbours are the k observations with the closest Euclidean distance (L$_2$-based or Manhattan distance, L$_1$-based) to the new individual. The class is then determined based on the modality that has the highest number of neighbours (a sum calculated using the Kronecker delta δ). For regression, the value of the prediction is the mean of the k nearest neighbours. [SOURCE: Page_69]

Random Forest (RF) This algorithm is an ensemble method, i.e. based on the aggregation of the results of several decision trees, here by averaging the results. It targets the reduction of variance. Each decision tree T i is trained on a subset of data and features, and provides a small part of the output. They successively cut each variable value range into two based on a threshold, so that each group is as homogeneous as possible. The homogeneity of each cut (leaf node with parameter µ i, j ) is measured by entropy or Gini index. To reduce variance and prediction correlation between trees, k < n observa- tions and m < p features are drawn for each tree based on bootstrapping. Each tree is characterised by a depth, splitting variables and splitting rules. See Figure 2.17. [SOURCE: Page_69]

Gradient Boosting (BOOST) It is similar to random forest, but the trees are grown sequentially to correct the predictions based on the residuals of the previous tree and on different subsets, such that the re- sults are summed and slightly more interpretable than for random forest. This sequential correction of the previous trees targets the reduction of bias but presents higher risks of overfitting. See Figure 2.18. [SOURCE: Page_69]

Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) Similar to random forest, but the parameters characterising the trees are regularised to avoid overfitting using prior distributions. An interesting output is the presence of credible intervals associated with the model’s predictions. [SOURCE: Page_69]

With the exception of LASSO (regression), these models can be used for both classification and re- gression. The over-representation of trees in the methods may not be a greenwashing campaign by AI, but an illustration of the better performance achieved by these tree-based methods. Indeed, data-driven approaches are often trained together and compared against each other using multiple metrics, and tree- based methods were found to perform best in (Münch et al., 2023; Nguyen et al., 2022, 2021). Nguyen et al. (2021) predicted nitrogen removal by treatment wetlands from 11 features and 755 observations using the Cubist algorithm, which is an ensemble regression method based on trees. Nguyen et al. (2022) also found the Cubist algorithm to be the best performer for subsurface treatment wetlands design, based on 10 features and 618 observations for NH$_4$-N and COD. Münch et al. (2023) used Random Forest to study CO$_2$ solubility in food, based on its composition and temperature, with 362 observations. These models were developed mathematically some 30 to 60 years ago, as illustrated by some of the publications listed in the Table 2.7. Because k iter and I MCMC are high, BART model may take much more time to train. If the number of observations is high, then SVM may take much more time to train. Their algorithmic im- plementations with computers are now flourishing, with the compilation packages scikit-learn in Python (https://scikit-learn.org/stable/) and caret in R (https://topepo.github.io/caret/). [SOURCE: Page_69]

Deep Learning Also inspired by nature, in particular human neurons, neural networks thrive particularly well in the con- text of wastewater treatment plants, which provide time-series data, and in hydrology (Sit et al., 2020). [SOURCE: Page_69]

Neural networks are composed of interconnected neurons, which are individual models or functions with p variables x i mobilising simple activation functions g (typically the identity and logistic functions in re- p gression and classification models, respectively) such that y = g(α0 + Σ i=1 α i x i ). Neurons are only connected between successive layers in such a way that each layer is a linear combination of neurons from the pre- vious layer, and only the first and last layers are readable by the modeller. Numerous modifications and improvements have led to new algorithms such as long short-term memory (LSTM) networks. These LSTM networks were found to have the best performance by Yang et al. (2023) for predicting COD, N H$_4$ − N and TP effluent concentrations in treatment wetland, from 10 variables and 186 observations, and by Hwangbo et al. (2021) for predicting N$_2$ O emissions from WWTP, from 6 variables and 750 000 observations. Akratos et al. (2008) has modelled the removal of BOD and COD by HF wetlands using neural networks, after de- termining the characteristics from a PCA run on a 2-year period of experimental data. [SOURCE: Page_70]

2.5.5      Limitations Models take different forms and depend on their intended applications (Dotro et al., 2017), relying on different contributions of data and knowledge. Mechanistic models can quickly become complex and com- putationally expensive. Learning models, on the other hand, rely solely on data and tend to overfit the data used for training. Their nickname ’black box’ is often justified by the lack of understanding in the calcula- tion of the outputs, especially when there is no equation associated, just a list of fitted hyperparameters. Thriving in other disciplines, AI models are reported by Liu et al. (2023) to have great potential in WWTP fault detection, diagnosis and prognosis, but according to Bahramian et al. (2023) industrial developments in WWTP are lacking, developments which may be hindered not only by the quantity but also the quality of data. [SOURCE: Page_71]

Is there a way to mobilise the advantages of both types of models while avoiding their disadvantages? Hybrid models are one solution that researchers have begun to explore. But first, a brief digression on the statistical tools used to improve individual empirical and data-driven models. [SOURCE: Page_71]

2.6       Data and model reliability Data-driven modelling consists in providing relationships between variables from observations of reality. The validation of the model compared to reality is done through the comparison to knowledge and data. Data, with its quantity and quality, therefore plays a central role in the development and reliability of the models. We assumed that reliable decision-making depends on reliable models and modelling processes. Its [SOURCE: Page_71]
