reliability is thus directly linked to the reliability of expert knowledge and experimental data. Before mov- ing on to validation methodologies, we first recall the specificity of numerical modelling. In 1991, Popper introduced the principle of falsifiability or refutability, which states that it can only be shown that a theory is false. In a more pragmatic approach adopted by Kuhn, he also develops the notion of verisimilitude 32 , which is the degree of closeness to truth. Validating a model has been a recurring challenge, because it is difficult to determine to what extent the data and the modelling methodology are reliable. A framework showing the modelling process and assessment is shown in Figure 2.19. Numerical modelling requires a translation from the conceptual and mathematical modelling to the computational implementation as an algorithm (corresponding to the computerised model, or computational model - model code - model). A similar methodology should be envisaged for data-driven models. [SOURCE: Page_72]

Model qualification                                               Model confirmation [SOURCE: Page_72]

Conceptual                                                  Conceptual REALITY                                                                REALITY Analysis                model                                     Analysis          model [SOURCE: Page_72]

Model validation                           Code verification [SOURCE: Page_72]

Computer simulation        Programming                          Simulation                        Programming Model validation                               Model verification [SOURCE: Page_72]

Computerised                                        Model                           Model code Model set-up model [SOURCE: Page_72]

Model calibration [SOURCE: Page_72]

Figure 2.19: Relation between theory, modelling and simulation process, and its terminology, evolution from Schlesinger et al. (1979) to Refsgaard and Henriksen (2004) representation. The dashed arrows are actions to execute to pass from one element to the other, and the full lines to actions to assess the arrows. [SOURCE: Page_72]

Von Sperling et al. (2020); Poch et al. (2012) consider equation-based models, and both include in the modelling steps calibration of the model to experimental data and validation (or evaluation) using addi- tional data. They also point to the need to iterate the modelling process by looping back from one step to a previous one. For data-driven models, the calibration step corresponds to model tuning and selection. The most recent framework from Figure 2.19 emphasises the need to calibrate the model to the case study, which is distinct from the need to confront the model with reality in order not only to validate the model on the application case study, but also to validate the underlying theory. Model validation, verification or evaluation still raises many questions, especially in relation to data-driven models that consider correla- tions rather than causality and do not require hypotheses or theories. Let us note the risk associated with data-driven methods that consists of the search for significant patterns in data. Known as data dredging, it poses risks when conclusions are drawn from patterns identified on the basis of a unique data set, or when data collection and analysis are carried out without a prior hypothesis, which is deplored by Burnham et al. (2002). Data dredging is also known as post hoc data analysis, data snooping or data mining. Ronald Coase, a British economist, is said to have given the following warning: ”If you torture data long enough, it will confess to anything.” Ignorance of pitfalls and best practices contributes to the mishandling of data and leads to false conclusions. To what extent can data be trusted? [SOURCE: Page_72]

For data reliability, modelling workflows are numerous and do generally involve data management. David Ikumi reports in the Source 33 , July 2023 that a typical modelling workflow includes the following steps: [SOURCE: Page_72]

1. data collection 32 Bachelard speaks of an approximation to truth 33 the International Water Association magazine [SOURCE: Page_72]

49 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_72]

2. data pre-processing 3. data storage and access 4. data mining 5. modelling (development, training, including data-driven, mechanistic and ML components) 6. comprehension of model results 7. proposed action Model validation tools can be understood as assessments of fidelity to reality as observed through mea- surements. In this part we will introduce methods and statistical tools for handling data in the training of statistical and data-driven models, typical metrics used to compare quantities, criteria related to reliability, and methods to assess uncertainties associated with predictions. [SOURCE: Page_73]

2.6.1      Validation and pre-processing of experimental data Data validation is a routine part of the analysis of experimental data. Data validation consists in identi- fying erroneous values and outliers with respect to expectations. Erroneous values result from a faulty or dysfunctional data production and measurement process, while outliers occur as exceptional values from a reference range in a given context. These types of observations are not intrinsically flawed, but affect the reliability of a data-driven model, particularly its range of validity. ? notes that ”data validation is a goal-driven process” that relies on objectives and subjectivity. Depending on the model objectives, data variability, errors and uncertainties are treated differently. Two publications address this challenge and propose a data validation workflow for time series data: (?) for metrology in urban drainage and stormwa- ter management, and (Rieger, 2012; Rieger et al., 2010) for activated sludge, with a modelling purpose. With on-site and real-time data, it is possible to reconcile data with knowledge of the system and to correct for operating conditions or instrumentation. Using mechanistic and data-driven approaches, Villez et al. (2024) also proposes an automated workflow for data quality assessment. These data validation workflows consider: • Data collection and preliminary analysis: data visualisation, grouping and description. • Data pre-processing: outlier detection, missing data handling, time series filtering and smoothing, and data transformations. • Quality assessment: outliers and erroneous data are reconciled on the basis of expert-based checks or statistical methods and additional experiments in (Villez et al., 2024; Rieger et al., 2010; Rieger, 2012) and on the basis of quality categorisation and data imputation in (?). In addition to data cleaning and matching, some data pre-processing may be required specifically before training data-driven models: feature selection (when the relevant variables are not known), dimension reduction, data scaling and transformation, and feature engineering (Bahramian et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2023), see variable requirements in Table 2.7. They are associated with the following topics: Correlation The assumption that features used to predict a dependent variable are independent of each other is not always verified. If two features are correlated, it is important either to remove one of them from the model (to avoid the variance explained by both features being randomly attributed to one or the other), or to transform one of them to decorrelate them. Disparity Often, variables take values in different ranges or even orders of magnitude. In the case of large scale disparities, especially in PCA and KNN, some variables with high magnitude values have more weight than the others in the calculation of distances. To make the variables comparable, they can be normalised, i.e. reduced and centred, by subtracting the mean from the observations yi and dividing y − ȳ by the standard deviation iσ . Missing data Often missing data cannot be handled by the algorithms, so methods to eliminate them are needed beforehand. Heteroscedasticity Homoscedasticity, i.e. the variance between observations is homogeneous, is an as- sumption before fitting regression models. If the variance increases with the size of the values taken by a variable, it may be necessary to transform the variable to artificially homogenise the variance by gradually reducing it. The transformation may consist of taking the logarithm of its values or weighting the values by the inverse of their residual errors obtained after fitting the model. [SOURCE: Page_73]

50 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_73]

Handling outliers Outliers can be identified as such by expert knowledge, i.e. they do not fit into the typically expected ranges or categories. Outliers can also be identified statistically, i.e. not by physical meaning but by math- ematical metrics. It is important to note that outliers are not necessarily faulty or erroneous, but may correspond to another category or situation. When data can be compared to reference values, outliers are easily identified. Instruments and analytical tools provide a limit of detection and quantification or a limit of saturation. Outliers are sometimes removed or replaced by these limits. However, this method has been shown to introduce bias in the data sets (Villez, 2017). [SOURCE: Page_74]

Statistically, without assuming distributions, a dataset is described using non-parametric descriptors: median and quartiles. Outliers are defined as values below Q 1 − 1.5IQR and above Q 3 + 1.5IQR, where IQR is the interquartile range (between the 25th percentile of Q$_1$ and the 75th percentile of Q$_3$). Often a dataset is assumed to follow a normal distribution and outliers are defined based on their probability of occurrence under a fitted normal distribution. Relying on this method to identify outliers, two implementation tests are used (Mercoiret, 2009): [SOURCE: Page_74]

• Chauvenet’s criterion, output: the probability of occurrence of a given value, or the expected number of observations that would reach at least or at most a given value, [SOURCE: Page_74]

• the Z-score, output: the distance from the mean, expressed in number of standard deviations, it is actually used for normalisation. [SOURCE: Page_74]

They are assumed to be robust, so the assumption of a normal distribution is often made even though it is known that the observations do not follow it. The resulting statistical outliers are usually removed from the data sets. [SOURCE: Page_74]

Handling missing values Dealing with missing data is a common situation faced by scientists. Several scenarii are possible. If the dataset is large enough, the entire sample containing the missing data is removed. Otherwise, especially in the case of time-series data, the missing data is interpolated from anterior and posterior values or replaced by a typical value (mean, median). Finally, the value can be imputed with additional information, in particular from other variables. There are three types of missing values, the patterns of which provide insight into the situation to be characterised for imputation: [SOURCE: Page_74]

missing completely at random (MCAR) : missing values occur randomly across measurements and vari- ables, [SOURCE: Page_74]

missing at random (MAR) : missing values occur randomly but with different frequencies between the variables, [SOURCE: Page_74]

missing not at random (MNAR) : missing values are due to (unknown) factors for given variables. [SOURCE: Page_74]

In the case of MCAR or MAR, Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn (2011) 34 proposed an imputation method available in the R package MICE: predictive mean matching (PMM). It consists in randomly draw- ing the value y of another observation from a set of donors, generally 3 to 10. These donors are determined by their distance from the case to be imputed. This distance is calculated as follows: a linear regres- sion model is fitted to the observed full cases and selected predictor variables x i such that ŷ = β̂0 + Σ x i β̂ i . We get the coefficient estimates β̂ and the coefficients β̇ drawn from their posterior distribution. Then |Σ x i β̂ i − Σ xmissing, j β̇ j | is evaluated. [SOURCE: Page_74]

This method has the advantage of introducing uncertainties associated with missing data, and it is possible to generate multiple imputed datasets to account for them. [SOURCE: Page_74]

2.6.2 Bias-variance tradeoff Once the data pre-processing and the data itself are trustworthy, the models need to be developed and verified. A major difficulty in data-driven models is known as the bias-variance trade-off 35 , where the 34 see the website online: https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-idconcepts.html#sec:notation 35 The razor of Ockham, or principle of parsimony is an example of bias-variance trade-off, opting for simple models. A simple model is easier to interpret, but tends to underfit the data used, leading to high bias (a large error is introduced between what is modelled and the [SOURCE: Page_74]

51 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_74]

model is optimised to reduce its total error, defined as the sum of the squared bias, variance and irreducible error: E[(y − ŷ)2 ] = Bias( ŷ)2 + V ar( ŷ) + σ2² [SOURCE: Page_75]

Bias Bias( ŷ) = E[ ŷ] − y: It corresponds to the systematic or consistent error between reality and a mea- surement, or between an observation and its prediction by a model. In modelling, a high bias (or low accuracy) corresponds to a situation of underfitting caused by the model being too simple to capture the true relationship between input and output variables. [SOURCE: Page_75]

Variance V ar( ŷ) = E[ yˆ2 ] − (E[ ŷ])2 = E[E[ ŷ] − ŷ)2 ]: It corresponds to the variability of the measurement with respect to reality, or of the model prediction with respect to the data. In modelling, a high variance (or low precision) corresponds to a situation of overfitting, where the model is too complex and sensitive to noise in the training data. [SOURCE: Page_75]

An ideal model has good precision 36 and good accuracy 37 , see Figure 2.20. So in practice, in order to mobilise more features, the more data available the better, such that for statistical models, their reliability increases with the degrees of freedom (ν = n observations − p f eatures − 1 for linear regressions), or the ratio of sample size to feature size (SFR = n/p, Zhu et al. (2023) recommends a safety minimum of 10). The two criteria are often difficult to reconcile and one or the other may be favoured depending on the objective of the model. We will assume that a reliable model aims to have both a low bias and a low variance. [SOURCE: Page_75]

Data sampling Once the data have been collected, it may happen that the values of a variable are heterogeneously dis- tributed. Or, in the case of a categorical variable, the categories may not be present in the same proportions. Depending on the objective of the model, there are several ways to sample the data set for modelling or training models, which will lead to different results. Sampling of observations can be random, but may result in the under-representation or absence of some value ranges or categories that are present with few individuals in the initial population. Stratified sampling consists in taking into account a given charac- teristic (variable or strata) when drawing the individuals at random, see Figure 2.21. Proportional sam- pling preserves the initial proportions of the population in the sample, whereas disproportional sampling equalises the proportions of the different categories by drawing equal numbers of individuals from each. [SOURCE: Page_75]

An alternative to stratified sampling is clustering, in which clusters of individuals are drawn at random. In multivariate contexts, one way to ensure a good representation of the variability in a population is to model). The complexity of a model increases with the number of features, and the risk associated with high complexity is that for a given number of observations, with more features mobilised, less variance is available to be explained. A complex model has the advantage of being flexible, but tends to overfit the data used, resulting in high variance (the model would change significantly if we used a different dataset). 36 it presents a low variability, a low dispersion related to the risk of overfitting, i.e. a low variance 37 it reaches a value close to reality, i.e. a low bias [SOURCE: Page_75]

use Latin hypercube sampling. It consists of dividing each variable range into m intervals containing the same probability (or density of individuals), and sampling m individuals in such a way that each individual is the only one belonging to a given hyperplan, i.e. at most one individual is sampled in each interval for all variables. In 2D and with uniform densities, this would be equivalent to picking a given number in a Sudoku grid. [SOURCE: Page_76]

Cross Validation The reliability and flexibility of a data-driven model is low if it is built once, on the whole dataset. When evaluating statistical or data-driven models, the reliability, or rather, the robustness of a model must be tested on new data. The data set used should be divided into a validation set and a training set, see the first case in Figure 2.22. The test set (typically 20% of the initial data, (Zhu et al., 2023)) corresponds to data on which the model has not been trained and helps to assess the accuracy of the predictions, and the extent to which the model is generalisable. However, when the dataset is split in half, the developed model is less reliable as it is based on fewer observations and the error of the model is therefore overestimated. Also, the error varies with the distribution of data points between the two sets, as some points have a higher or lower weight in the model depending on their values. There are several methods to validate and improve a model based on this idea, depending on the partitioning of the global dataset. [SOURCE: Page_76]

Leave-one-out CV The validation set consists of one observation each time the model is trained, so there are as many models as there are observations. This is computationally expensive, but no randomness is introduced. [SOURCE: Page_76]

k-fold CV The set is shuffled and divided into k sets. One validation set at a time is removed as the model is built on the rest of the data, and k models are obtained. It has more bias than LOOCV but less variance. k = 5 or k = 10 is typically used, see the last case of Figure 2.22. [SOURCE: Page_76]

Bootstrap This method is similar to k-fold CV, but the set is divided into training and validation sets several times with replacement, i.e. with the possibility to select data points again. It is mainly used to estimate the variability of the result. [SOURCE: Page_76]

In the case of time-series data, cross-validation as such cannot be applied because of the time-dependency, the successive observations are correlated with each other and the training and validation sets should be defined on the basis of time periods. Cross-validation consists in multiple iterations of the following steps, changing the composition of the dataset used for training: [SOURCE: Page_76]

• dividing the training set into a training and a validation set of defined sizes, [SOURCE: Page_76]

• fitting the model on the training set, [SOURCE: Page_76]

• predicting the validation set, [SOURCE: Page_76]

In LOOCV and k-fold CV, the process is iterative, and the unseen data changes n or k times. [SOURCE: Page_77]

• calculating efficiency metrics. [SOURCE: Page_77]

For statistical models, a mean and an uncertainty interval for the model coefficients can be derived from the folds. For machine learning models, cross-validation helps to tune their hyper-parameters (see the list in Table 2.7), i.e. to find the hyper-parameter values that give the best average metric value for the validation sets. A final model is then estimated with these hyper-parameter values, and on the whole dataset. [SOURCE: Page_77]

2.6.3      Sensitivity Analysis and Uncertainty Propagation In particular because we are interested in models that are more complex than the conservative rules- of-thumb or mass loading charts, optimising the surface design of the treatment wetlands means that incertitude arises with respect to the pollutant treatment performances. Incertitude includes uncertainty, ambiguity and ignorance 38 . Here, we only consider the quantifiable uncertainty, i.e. the risk or the extent to which treatment performances may not comply with the objectives, due to identified variables. Andy Stirling recalls that ”models are about different ways of making sense, not definitive ways of asserting pre- cise predictions” (Scoones and Stirling, 2020), and that ”each technique routinely delivers its answers with formidable levels of precision. Yet the resulting impression of accuracy is deeply misplaced. For behind the scenes, the same calculations typically yield a variety of equally-rigorous but different possible answers, ranging across many orders of magnitude.” 39 . The modelling methodology often imposes the selection of specific processes or parameter values such that the prediction, often a number, is not neutral, but the re- sult of a construction. We saw earlier that a model itself is not absolute, processes can be added or removed, data can be handled in many ways, and models can be compared using different metrics. This impossibility to account for everything is known as the Garden of Forking Paths where in a tree of successive decisions, only one branch has been selected from several possibilities. The risk of not exploring everything is to miss a relevant possibility. But in real and uncontrolled environments, a large variability can be expected for many of the characteristics defined in a model. What effect will an air temperature of 10 °C, rather than 25, have on the performance of a treatment wetland? How can we be sure that all the choices made have not affected the prediction? A "deterministic" prediction is always associated with a degree of ignorance: the uncertainty due to the variability of the model inputs, as well as the uncertainty associated with some approximations, parameters, knowledge gaps. [SOURCE: Page_77]

Fortunately, there are tools that integrate stochastic mechanisms into a deterministic model. [SOURCE: Page_77]

Sensitivity Analysis Sensitivity analysis assesses the effect of the variability of individual features on the model output Y . This impact can be quantified using correlation coefficients, the ANOVA method based on an experimental design, or the Sobol index S i , which measures the variance due to a single variable X i : it is the ratio of the variance of the output when X i is fixed to the total variance of the V ar(E[Y | X ] output, S i = V ar(Y ) i . [SOURCE: Page_77]

38 Andy Stirling, 2019, in a blog-post https://steps-centre.org/blog/politics-in-the-language-of-uncertainty/ 39 in 2019, on https://steps-centre.org/blog/how-politics-closes-down-uncertainty/ [SOURCE: Page_77]

54 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_77]

Uncertainty Analysis Uncertainty analysis assesses the impact of the uncertainties associated with the features on the model output and quantifies it in terms of probability. This analysis is also called uncertainty propagation or cascading. Monte Carlo simulation is a method of uncertainty propaga- tion that consists of defining theoretical distributions for parameters and variables according to the modeller’s knowledge and confidence, and running several thousand simulations randomly drawing values from these distributions, see Figure 2.23. It is based on the central limit theorem, which states that the distribution of the normalized sum of n independent random variables, each with finite mean and variance, converges to a normal distribution as n tends to infinity. In uncertainty propagation, this implies that the combined uncertainty of independent sources often approximates a normal distribution, even if the individual uncertainties are not normally distributed. The method produces several predictions following this normal distribution, from which a mean and a standard deviation are determined. [SOURCE: Page_78]

Sensitivity Auditing Sensitivity auditing covers all types of uncertainty, including those associated with the model structure itself and the assumptions made in defining its scope. [SOURCE: Page_78]

Sensitivity analysis is considered in mathematical modelling by Von Sperling et al. (2020) and uncer- tainty analysis in decision making by Poch et al. (2012). In the context of anaerobic digestion modelling, uncertainty analysis was carried out to compare predictions with observational uncertainties, and sensitiv- ity analysis was carried out to identify parameters to be calibrated in the priority (Ossiansson and Lidholm, 2008). Global sensitivity analysis and Monte Carlo simulations are recommended by Flores-Alsina et al. (2010) for modelling activated sludge designs, as they help to determine the impact of each variable and assumption used in the models. Saltelli and Puy (2023) advocates the use of these tools, which ”improve the transparency, adequacy and fairness of numbers in quantitatively oriented disciplines”. These tools shed light on the variability of the prediction, which is an additional piece of information. Depending on the objectives of the model, data variability, errors and uncertainties are treated differently and the resulting decisions may not be the same. [SOURCE: Page_78]

2.7      Hybrid models It may happen that, despite all the precautions mentioned above, single mechanistic or data-driven models are difficult to develop due to insufficient knowledge or data, leading to unreliable predictions. Hybrid models consist of combining different types of models and sources of knowledge to compensate for each other’s shortcomings and to get closer to the truth. This type of modelling is gaining visibility in the wastewater sector as a key challenge addressed by the IWA Specialist Group on Modelling and Integrated Assessment and the Water Resources Recovery modelling 2021 conference in Arosa, Switzerland. Typical combinations are: [SOURCE: Page_79]

• a mechanistic/empirical and an empirical/data-driven model to balance the oversimplification due to hypotheses and the overfitting to data, see the review by Schneider et al. (2022), [SOURCE: Page_79]

• two types of data-driven models, with high dependence on data quantity and quality, see the review by Bahramian et al. (2023) and applications to wastewater, (Borzooei et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2018), [SOURCE: Page_79]

• a high and a low fidelity model to complement a detailed and accurate representation with a simple one, see the review by Asher et al. (2015), [SOURCE: Page_79]

• a numerical and a symbolic model, which is an emerging topic in food processing (Münch et al., 2022) and gas path fault diagnosis (Chen et al., 2022). [SOURCE: Page_79]

We focus here on the first type of hybridisation: the first type has the advantage of being interpretable and describing the main mechanisms that occur, while the second type provides little understanding and no causality, but can additionally capture unknown side mechanisms. The different types of model hy- bridisation are distinguished by the nature of their inputs and outputs. The data-driven models mobilised are supervised because of the predictive objective. Schneider et al. (2022) mentions several terms and synonyms associated to hybrid models in the literature 40 . [SOURCE: Page_79]

2.7.1 Parallel Models Parallel modelling consists of running and training the mechanistic and data-driven models separately, see Figure 2.24. The models can take the same or different inputs (the data-driven model can capture implicit relationships from the data), with additional observations of the target variable to train the data-driven model. Their outputs are then combined and the mechanistic model acts as a regulariser of the data- driven model, i.e. it prevents large deviations from the main mechanism identified. This hybridisation is also called corrective or additive. [SOURCE: Page_79]

2.7.2      Serial Models Serial hybridisation means that the models are run consecutively, using the output of the first model as input, so that the second model is dependent on the first. A synonym for serial is compositional hybridi- sation, the individual models account for different phenomena and are generally fitted and trained with different sets of features. [SOURCE: Page_80]

Calibration of mechanistic parameters with a data-driven model An interesting structure is to use the data-driven model to calibrate a parameter of the mechanistic/em- pirical model to best fit the observations, see Figure 2.25. This allows the parameter to incorporate effects from variables whose explicit relationship to the parameter has not yet been determined. [SOURCE: Page_80]

Estimation of unmeasured process parameters is done using neural networks by Psichogios and Ungar (1992), the output is then used in a first-principle model of a fedbatch bioreactor. Shape-constrained spline functions are used by Thürlimann and Villez (2017) for the purpose of fault detection in data on resource recovery from urine. [SOURCE: Page_80]

Completing the unknown with a data-driven model If the mechanistic model describes only one or a few phenomena, there may be a large residual variance be- tween predictions and observations made in an uncontrolled environment. The serial hybrid model in this case consists of predicting the observations with the other model predictions as input. Another possibility is to predict the residual variance directly 41 . By training the data-driven model to predict the residual variance, it can incorporate complementary factors to explain this residual variance, see Figure 2.26. This hybridisation can also be seen as a way of adding understanding to the data-driven model by providing a variable that accounts for the relationships with the mechanistic set of features. [SOURCE: Page_80]

Here, the two models are intertwined to explain a given mechanism, and the outputs generated at time t are used to generate the outputs at time 41 In terms of terminology and vision, this hybridisation is sometimes considered parallel because of the models predict different variables, but modelling residuals depends on the prior use of another model. • dx dt = m(x)e(x) [SOURCE: Page_81]

The first case has been implemented by Mašić et al. The use of partial derivative equations with neural networks is referred to as physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). They are widely used in engineering contexts to implement digital twins (Kar- niadakis et al., 2021), and are being further developed. Lawal et al. (2022) reviewed recent proposals for improvement: extended PINNs, hybrid PINNs and minimised loss techniques. De Jaegher et al. (2021) develops PINNs using case 2 to predict membrane fouling, replacing the attachment efficiency coefficient by neural networks following a collision event between the membrane and colloids. PINNs are developed like case 3 by Quaghebeur et al. (2020) to predict pollutant effluent concentrations from a WRRF under dry and rainy weather, and by Thompson and Kramer (1994) on sparse and noisy data on cell biomass and metabolite formation in a fermentation process. The 2nd and 3rd cases are considered by Quaghebeur et al. (2021) with three examples of academic models. [SOURCE: Page_81]

2.7.4      Surrogate Models A surrogate model aims to simplify the calculations when a mechanistic model is too complex to run casu- ally. There are three types of surrogate model, but only the last is of interest here: [SOURCE: Page_81]

• Projection-based surrogates, which project the equations onto a subspace of fewer dimensions. They are also called reduced order, reduced basis and model reduction methods. [SOURCE: Page_81]

• Multifidelity based surrogate models that simplify the representation of the processes or reduce the numerical resolution. They are also referred to as multiscale, hierarchical and physics-based meth- ods, see for example (Christelis and Hughes, 2022) on hydrogeological system modelling, (Zheng et al., 2019) on subsurface flow modelling and (Zhang et al., 2018) on hydrological system modelling. [SOURCE: Page_81]

• Data-driven surrogate models that do not predict real observations, but the predictions obtained by a complex mechanistic model, see Figure 2.28. This simplifies the mapping between input and mechanistic predictions and is computationally faster. The resulting model consists only of the data- driven model structure, but because a mechanistic model was involved in the process, surrogate models fit into a broader definition of hybrid modelling. They are also referred to as meta-models, surrogate models, emulators, and response surface models, as reviewed by Schneider et al. (2022); Asher et al. (2015). [SOURCE: Page_81]

2.8      Challenges This state of the art aimed to describe existing symbolic and numerical models and tools applicable to treatment wetlands. The transversal aspect of treatment wetlands, which are not only technologies but also promoters of a more circular and resilient city, shows the need for interdisciplinary interactions: re- search projects on the topic are integrated, i.e. they mobilise several actors from different disciplines. Unifying specialised disciplines is however a difficult task and therefore slows down a deeper knowledge discovery. Access to knowledge may be hampered by limited consensus on nomenclature, the creation of new terms or the emergence of innovations. For modelling objectives, what and how to model are two im- portant questions. Depending on the objectives, the modeller needs to consider which treatment wetlands to model, identify relevant properties and processes, criteria for prioritisation (for design purposes, is it cost, efficiency, biodiversity?), and the available knowledge and data. The difficulty in characterising and implementing treatment wetlands in urban planning stems from a lack of understanding of the natural processes involved in wastewater treatment and a lack of comparable data of sufficient quantity and qual- ity. [SOURCE: Page_82]

Aiming to better understand and describe treatment wetlands and water management has relied on a physics-based approach with the quantification of their characteristics and numerical modelling. Mech- anistic models, which accurately describe the hydraulics, contaminant transport and contaminant degra- dation, are complex models, but some have limited accessibility, as they have to be acquired through the purchase of a licence, and the computation time is long (several hours to days), while the risks of drift in- crease with the runtime, as some long-term phenomena are not considered. These models are therefore not used for treatment wetlands design, and regulations now opt for overly simplistic and conservative design rules. In this context, statistical and data-driven approaches are gaining interest but stringent methodolo- gies must be followed to ensure reliable models. In particular, data-driven model outputs may be sensitive to data scale, data partitioning, measurement uncertainties, or the choice of the main processes and vari- ables considered to be involved. Saltelli and Puy (2023) therefore warns that due to these decisions and assumptions, ”results from models and other instances of quantification reflect the interests, disciplinary orientations, and biases of their promoters”, such that a single number as an output is unlikely to be re- liable. The variability of outputs is an additional source of information that provides its uncertainty. The most competitive deep learning models can hardly be used for treatment wetlands modelling due to the insufficient amount of data available and the varying quality of the data. From a scientific point of view, another weakness of data-driven models is that they are hardly interpretable, i.e. they would not help to gain more understanding and knowledge. [SOURCE: Page_82]

Hybrid models are proving to be an interesting compromise and have begun to flourish in wastewater treatment modelling. The different combinations of models presented have been shown to improve model predictions while improving understanding through data. However, the methodology has yet to be applied to treatment wetlands cases and still faces many obstacles. There are multiple combinations to evaluate and multiple ways to handle data, especially for time series data. Indeed, Verhaeghe et al. (2024) shows that using the same or different data sets to calibrate the mechanistic and train the data-driven model yields different predictions. Research may take 10 to 15 years to obtain proper modelling methodologies with hybrid models (mechanistic and data-driven, symbolic and numerical) in particular for wastewater treatment (Venkatasubramanian, 2019). [SOURCE: Page_82]

3.1      Project challenges The MULTISOURCE project aims to address a broad challenge by developing a planning tool for integrated urban water management. Nature-based solutions are ambivalent concepts at the intersection of multiple challenges across disciplines. Nature-based solutions, and in particular treatment wetlands, allow us to answer new challenges with more flexibility combined with existing conventional treatment technologies: they can be decentralised, located within cities, and implemented from household to industrial scale. More stakeholders should be involved in the paradigm shift, broadening the technical scope to include social, en- vironmental, and economic aspects. However, the collection and exchange of knowledge can be an obstacle: [SOURCE: Page_84]

• Innovations in Nature-based Solutions and treatment wetlands technologies have led to a plethora of new terms, with possible overlaps between technologies or between terms, creating confusion and difficulties in communication. The terminology for treatment wetlands used to treat wastewater has not been standardised, [SOURCE: Page_84]

• A great quantity of data is collected along the studies of these technologies but not fully standardised, hence data is difficult to compare due to heterogeneity of data types, formats and units and due to missing but relevant pieces of information on the systems studied. There are many case studies that may not be comparable, starting with the types of wastewater encountered, [SOURCE: Page_84]

• New objectives have been set for nature-based solutions covering large scopes, in city-wide scenarii: pollutants of emerging concern may need to be monitored, and beyond typical technical developments, quantitative social, environmental and economic assessments are expected. [SOURCE: Page_84]

Meanwhile, decision-making supported by this planning tool also covers specialised technico-scientific fields, and relies on quantitative assessments, such as the pre-sizing estimates of Nature-based Solutions. The specific challenges encountered in modelling lead to scientific discussions occurring, for example, with the 8th IWA WRRmod^2022+ (Water Resource Recovery Modelling Seminar) conference, held in January 2023. David Ikumi, for the Source 1 July 2023, reports on the following challenges for hybrid modelling outlined : [SOURCE: Page_84]

• Common Application Programming Interfaces [SOURCE: Page_84]

• Development of effective and harmonised scientific terminologies 1 the International Water Association magazine [SOURCE: Page_84]

• Establishment of good modelling practice frameworks for hybrid models [SOURCE: Page_85]

• Improved methods for dealing with uncertainty [SOURCE: Page_85]

• Development of methods to achieve good data quality and metadata [SOURCE: Page_85]

• Continuous refinement of the architecture for machine-learning algorithms. [SOURCE: Page_85]

3.2      Research questions This thesis explores the hybridisation of different representations of treatment wetlands: on one side with a symbolic approach, and on the other with a numerical approach. In Chapter 4, we will be interested in determining whether and if so to what extent we can unify a multidisciplinary knowledge on nature-based solutions with natural language, and propose to develop an ontology with the objective to build a shared representation of water management using Nature-based Solutions, and to facilitate exchanges of knowl- edge and data. [SOURCE: Page_85]

Moving on from the concepts to the characteristics of nature-based solutions and treatment wetlands, we need to operate to some degree a transition from a symbolic to a numerical approach. In Chapter 5, we will study to what extent we can aggregate and compare data from different resources, and we propose a methodology to validate data with the objective to shed light on implicit choices, and homogenise individual validation practices. [SOURCE: Page_85]

Data-driven pre-sizing models for treatment wetlands currently generate unrealistic design estimates. Assuming the collected data to be reliable, this observation leads to the exploration of the existing data- driven model structures and of alternatives, such as mechanistic models. In Chapter 6, the core of this thesis will be to test to what extent hybrid models 2 can improve wetlands representations in the face of ignorance of certain natural processes. The objective is to compensate for the drawbacks of individual approaches to make a more reliable model. [SOURCE: Page_85]

In practice, decision-making may avoid the conservative over-sizing of the systems, because available and affordable land is difficult to obtain. The multiple criteria, even when restricting the scope to the technical dimension, lead to the need to study optimisation options for the pre-sizing of treatment wetlands. So finally in Chapter 7, we will question the applicability of the hybrid models to real cases based on the collected data, and investigate the place of numerical predictions and estimates in decision-making, and to what extent and how trust can be re-established in numbers, with the objective to handle uncertainty and provide more transparency. [SOURCE: Page_85]

2 i.e. combining mechanistic and empirical numerical approaches [SOURCE: Page_85]

62 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_85]

Chapter 4 [SOURCE: Page_86]

Symbolic representation [SOURCE: Page_86]

”What’s in a name? That which we call a rose, by any other name, would smell as sweet.” [SOURCE: Page_86]

William Shakespeare, Romeo and Juliet, 1597 [SOURCE: Page_86]

This work addresses the challenge of improving communication between actors from different disci- plines and the exchange of data. The scope covers global water management and mathematical process modelling, describing technologies, measurements, and mechanisms that occur. In this chapter, the objec- tive is to improve the understanding of treatment wetlands. We first establish a thesaurus and highlight current misunderstandings due to terminology, and in a second step, we develop a symbolic representa- tion of wastewater treatment by treatment wetlands. Several ontologies related to water management have been identified (Oliva-Felipe et al., 2017) and others that target modelling (Elag and Goodall, 2013), but none has been designed to describe a wastewater treatment train that mobilises treatment wetlands. Therefore, we opted for the structure of a food transformation process-oriented ontology and the integration of our ontology into it. Next, we propose an excel data exchange format for the collection of experimental data, based on the vocabulary and relationships identified for treatment wetlands. [SOURCE: Page_86]

4.1      Challenges for projects on wastewater and treatment wetlands MULTISOURCE project addresses the challenge of knowledge exchange, between researchers of different expertise, and from researchers and practitioners to decision-makers. The multiple tasks and activities are divided into thematic work packages that need to interact with each other. Two reasons justify the need for a symbolic approach to knowledge unification: first, even within a given discipline, science is global and international and needs interactions between researchers which are currently done in English. Second, Nature-based Solutions are emerging and interdisciplinary concepts, such that there may not be a stable common representation and understanding across disciplines. Clear definitions of concepts and consensual terms are necessary to prevent misunderstandings and miscommunication, and to a further extent, they help to establish the scope for regulations. Concepts are compiled and characterised under formats of varying complexity: vocabularies, thesaurii, ontologies (see Figure 2.3). However, we observed that missing terms and definitions occur even in official resources such as GEMET which does not list treatment wetlands, or INRAE vocabulary that employs a literal translation of the French filtre planté but does not provide consensual synonyms (treatment wetlands or constructed wetlands). The construction of definitions up to ontologies is well detailed as described in the state of the art (see Section 2.3.3), but methodologies are not always fully followed so that definitions and references to existing resources are lacking. [SOURCE: Page_88]

Anticipating the first Annual Meeting of the MULTISOURCE project 1 in June 2022, we sent two videos explaining what ontologies are 1 . As identified in the state-of-the-art, ontologies can mitigate communi- cation difficulties expected from collaborating in an inter-disciplinary project. Partners around the world are to collaborate with data exchange: those responsible for ENTS 2 pilots sending samples to partners for specific analyses, urban planners responsible for storm events interacting with API developers for decision- making. Furthermore, not all participants were directly familiar with nature-based solutions, but would study them as application objects, for life-cycle and cost assessments, stakeholders engagement and gender studies, urban planning or micropollutant contamination. [SOURCE: Page_88]

Cvitanovic et al. (2025) name this objective of knowledge exchange and associated activities as knowl- edge brokering. They identified critical points to knowledge brokering: practical and process, individual, organisation, financial, social and material. We designed a short survey for the Annual Meeting so that participants could share about encountered difficulties and future issues they expect from the project. They next had to write down those that are in relation with the scope of ontologies. The identified issues, see Figure 4.1, are clearly related to: [SOURCE: Page_88]

communication (social) related to direct exchanges, or article reading: language barrier, synonyms, mis- conceptions, disagreements on the Nature-based Solutions classifications and technologies, [SOURCE: Page_88]

data (practical and process) related to heterogenous methods: data formats, units used, database man- agement, analyse mixed data, data management. [SOURCE: Page_88]

Within the same survey, we also checked the interest of the participants in the development of an ontol- ogy to mitigate the problems; see Figure 4.2. They do expect better communication with a common ground (mean grade 4.3/5 agreement with the utility of the ontology) and facilitated exchanges of knowledge and data (4/5). Less confidence lies in the possibility to understand other disciplines. Finally, we had envisioned specific objectives for the ontology in June 2022 that the stakeholders prioritised in Figure 4.3. The main need is to standardise the vocabulary before structuring a database or describing a treatment train. The merging of knowledge between multiple disciplines was classified as the last, which means that stakehold- ers may not all find use in having actual access to a different domain of knowledge. [SOURCE: Page_88]

We define two objectives: • to develop a thesaurus in order to elucidate the terminology and characterise Nature-based Solutions technological units, which will be of use for the second objective, [SOURCE: Page_88]

• to develop an ontology establishing the important properties of treatment wetlands, and structuring the variables involved in the treatment of domestic wastewater. It will represent treatment steps as transformation processes, which will be of use for modelling. 1 Sophie Hai Yen Guillaume-Ruty, Josep Pueyo-Ros, Joaquim Comas, Nicolas Forquet. Introduction to ontologies for MULTISOURCE project. 2022. 〈hal-04922987〉 2 Enhanced Natural Treatment Systems, the preferred term employed in MULTISOURCE project [SOURCE: Page_88]

4.2      Roadmap for the ontology Multiple online resources as well as the existing ontological resources mentioned in Chapter 2 identified key concepts related to water. Rather than working from scratch and facilitating future interoperability, we consider reusing these resources as advised by Gómez-Pérez and Suárez-Figueroa (2009). Gómez-Pérez and Suárez-Figueroa (2009) presents the NeOn methodology for reuse and re-engineering of knowledge resources. This methodology comprises a basic construction scenario that can be enriched according to specific situations leading to 10 final scenarii. Bellow are detailed the four scenarii that are applicable to our case: [SOURCE: Page_89]

Scenario 2 Reusing and re-engineering non-ontological resources, such as taxonomies and thesaurii (IN- [SOURCE: Page_89]

RAE Voc, GEMET), [SOURCE: Page_90]

Scenario 5 Reusing and merging ontological resources, in particular INWS and WaWO+ concepts, [SOURCE: Page_90]

Scenario 8 Restructuring ontological resources. TransformON ontology is the main ontology that we ex- tend to cover wastewater treatment, [SOURCE: Page_90]

Scenario 9 Localising ontological resources. PO$_2$ Manager requires the translation of concepts in English and French. Ongoing work to include Spanish, German and Italian should facilitate collaborations and usage of the ontology. [SOURCE: Page_90]

We noticed that some concepts do not have definitions. Because the advantage of ontologies over other knowledge representations is the inclusion of relationships between concepts, one might be tempted to directly implement an ontology by relating concepts, bypassing the definition step. We integrated in red elements that we consider essential to a perennial usage of the ontology into the typical methodology for its construction (Noy and McGuinness, 2001; Uschold and Gruninger, 1996): [SOURCE: Page_90]

### 6. Documentation, guidelines

We believe that the integration of the construction of a thesaurus facilitates the construction of an ontology with the selection and definition of important terms and properties. Both tools will further help establish a common data exchange format. [SOURCE: Page_90]

4.3      Thesaurus The first objective of the thesaurus is to improve communication and understanding on wastewater treat- ment, nature-based solutions, and treatment wetlands. The second objective is to facilitate the construction of the ontology. [SOURCE: Page_90]

67 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_90]

4.3.1      Gathering information The construction of the thesaurus consisted in successive construction of the different knowledge represen- tations following a gradual amplification of the complexity of the knowledge representation, as illustrated in Figure 2.3, in a bottom-up approach. We started from gathering the typical terms to categorising the concepts and creating the relationships between them. We held two workshops, one in the context of MUL- TISOURCE involving stakeholders from different backgrounds, and the other in the context of a modelling seminar in INRAE. During the first Annual Meeting of the project MULTISOURCE, we organised our first 40 minute long workshop on the identified terminology and taxonomy related to wastewater treatment and Nature-based Solutions. About 30 participants were dispatched according to the type of expertise: in 2 groups of researchers (ICRA, INRAE REVERSAAL, INSA Deep, Montana University), 1 group of munici- pal agents (Milano, Oslo, Lyon) and 1 group of industrial agents (IRIDRA, Rietland). Our second workshop took place in a later phase in 2024, and lasted 1 hour. It involved three researchers 3 from BOKU Uni- versity and Sylvie Gillot from INRAE REVERSAAL. Participants had to give comments on and suggest changes to: [SOURCE: Page_91]

• The taxonomy and terminology of Nature-based Solutions, see Figure 4.5, the municipality group considered this document only. [SOURCE: Page_91]

• The description of the treatment train (relative to the relations in the thesaurus), see Figure 4.8. [SOURCE: Page_91]

• The vocabulary related to experimental data, see Figure 4.10. [SOURCE: Page_91]

The different steps to the construction of the thesaurus are detailed below: [SOURCE: Page_91]

Folksonomy - From the professional environment and the scientific literature we read, we had a set of typical terms falling under the scope of interest. We followed a bottom-up approach to gather typical terms characterising NBS technological units, that are employed in the scientific literature, in water- related ontologies, thesauri, and experimental data files: [SOURCE: Page_91]

• the material in direct relationship with wastewater (for treatment, transport, and analysis) • the constituents monitored in wastewater and the concepts related to concentration and units • the relevant characteristics relative to treatment wetlands • the operational parameters and influencing factors for treatment • the performance can be deduced from the difference between influent and outflow measure- ments • the relation can be deduced from grouping the designs of treatment wetlands (dimensions and scale) • the mechanisms related to the monitored constituents. [SOURCE: Page_91]

This description sets the basis for costs estimation. Costs are dependent on many factors, but precise estimates can be deduced from the sum of unitary elements composing the object of study (e.g. a treatment wetland, a treatment train). The participants were interested in the costs which are tackled by MULTISOURCE Work Packages 3 and 4 4 . Controlled vocabulary - We restricted the list of terms to scientific and technical ones only. Starting with the holistic work from Castellar et al. (2021), we focused on the Nature-based Solutions technological units, that are further categorised between horizontal and vertical implementations see 4.5. We had additional inputs from the three researchers during the 1 hour long workshop, reviewing the relevant concepts corresponding to parameters that are monitored in treatment wetlands. Glossary - The participants were interested in engaging with stakeholders from water authorities, which is a task handled by MULTISOURCE Work Packages 3 and 6 5 . We opted instead for legal docu- ments and guidelines. We retrieved definitions and the Unique Reference Identifiers (URI) 6 provided online by official institutions (European Commission Directives 2020, 2006 and 1991, US-EPA on- site Wastewater Treatment Systems Manual (USEPA, 2002), the World Health Organisation (WHO, 3 Guenter Langergraber, Bernhardt Pucher, and Alba Canet Marti 4 one of the interests of these work packages is on economic costs and life-cycle assessment 5 they focus on business models for financing ENTS implementations in cities, and on stakeholders engagement 6 URI are sequences of characters which may include the term identified, or not. They have no scientific use but rather operational benefit in computer science and informatics. [SOURCE: Page_91]

68 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_91]

2006), the FAO AGROVOC, (OiEau, 2024), Eionet European Environmental Agengy (EEA) General Multilingual Environmental Thesaurus GEMET). We made a synthesis of the definitions, and when missing, there is ongoing work to provide definitions based on the methodology given by Vezina (2009). Dictionary - The participants showed interest in mapping the different translations in order to work in their native language. We aligned English terms with similar meaning, and gathered translations and their definitions when provided, from EU regulations. Current other translated terms have been generated from DeepL, and corrected by native speakers, young water professionals (predoctoral researchers and technicians) working in ICRA: in French: myself, Spanish: Anna Pico, German: Josephine Vosse, Italian: Massimiliano Riva. Then further corrections were made in French based on Chocat et al. (2022), in Castellano (Salas and Pride e Inmaculada Cuenca, 2007), in German (Hoffmann, 1996), and in English with the senior water modelling professionals during the second workshop. Taxonomy - We labelled Treatment wetlands based on the hierarchical classification made by Fonder and Headley (2013), but did not prioritise any criteria for the categorisation. Water flow direction, hydrology, aeration, degree of technology or type of vegetation are not hierarchically related, so clas- sifications are arbitrary, based on the point of view of the modeller. Thesaurus - The participants were interested in an accessible format of publication, so we will publish the thesaurus and the ontology separately. We highlighted relationships between the different concepts in the framework of a treatment train process. We followed a top-down approach to organise con- cepts based on the core concepts structuring the Process and Observation Ontology (PO$_2$) core model developed by INRAE (Dooley et al., 2022; Weber et al., 2023), see Figure 4.4. [SOURCE: Page_92]

4.3.3      Focus on semantics The different steps to obtain the final set of concepts led us to make choices as to identifying terms that are synonyms and to selecting a preferential term. The taxonomy, dictionary, and thesaurus require properties to characterise and categorise concepts. These three sets can influence and help to determine the concepts in relation to each other or to better define them. For nature-based solutions, the junction between differ- ent disciplines, scientific relevance, and collective symbolic are at stake. More specifically for treatment wetlands, there are also regulatory aspects in the mix. In the following, we delve into the nature of the concepts identified, dealing with categorisation and alignment within PO$_2$ core concepts. [SOURCE: Page_94]

Nature-based Solutions (-) Nature-based solutions is a concept that emerged in 2008 and encompasses many existing approaches and technologies (see Figure 1.2), it is not specific to water-related issues, but to the broader theory of environ- mental/ecological/green economics for sustainability. The definitions given to nature-based solutions reflect a dialogue between technical science and their development at the interface of multiple spheres: [SOURCE: Page_94]

European Commission, 2015 Solutions that are inspired and supported by nature, which are cost-effective, simultaneously provide environmental, social, and economic benefits and help build resilience. Such solutions bring more and more diverse nature and natural features and processes into cities, land- scapes, and seascapes, through locally adapted, resource-efficient, and systemic interventions. [SOURCE: Page_94]

International Union for Conservation of Nature, 2016 Actions to protect, manage, and restore natural or modified ecosystems, which address social challenges, effectively and adaptively, providing human well-being and biodiversity benefits. [SOURCE: Page_94]

UNESCO 2018 Nature-based solutions are inspired and supported by nature and use, or mimic, natural processes to contribute to the improved management of water. An Nature-based Solutions can in- volve conserving or rehabilitating natural ecosystems and/or the enhancement or creation of natural processes in modified or artificial ecosystems. They can be applied at micro- (e.g. a dry toilet) or macro- (e.g. landscape) scales. [SOURCE: Page_94]

Langergraber et al. (2020b) Nature-based Solutions are defined as concepts that bring nature into cities and those that are derived from nature. Nature-based Solutions address societal challenges and enable resource recovery, climate mitigation and adaptation challenges, human well-being, ecosys- tem restoration, and/or improved biodiversity status, within urban ecosystems. As such, within this definition we achieve resource recovery using organisms (e.g., microbes, algae, plants, insects, and worms) as the principal agents. However, physical and chemical processes can be included for recov- ery of resources, as they may be needed to support and enhance the performance of Nature-based Solutions. [SOURCE: Page_94]

The first definition does not mention the nature of the solutions but includes the nature-based aspect and emphasises their role for sustainability, while the second refers to them as actions for nature. All em- phasise how Nature-based Solutions respond or aim to respond to challenges in more than just a technical discipline. Nature-based Solutions are not limited to nature-based technologies and need to be tailored to address social, environmental and economic challenges. This integrated scope presents many variables, so that the outcomes are indeed uncertain, and Nature-based Solutions may not be a solution to all aspects of a problem (water risks, costs, co-benefits) (Le Coent et al., 2023). In the case of treatment wetlands, the societal improvement is not always considered when their implementation is remote, and they may not always participate in climate mitigation, rather, they may transfer pollution from water to air, since they also emit more greenhouse gases such as N2O, compared to activated sludge (Dufossé et al., 2024). The choice of the term Nature-based Solutions presents a subjectively positive metaphor to the concept, similarly to sponge cities 8 . Bridgewater (2018) analyses that the term Nature-based Solutions itself is misleading and ponders what nature and solutions refer to. Solutions in fact inherently presuppose suc- cess, which could lead to interpreting Nature-based Solutions as immediately operational solutions to all identified challenges, neglecting local scope and specific contextual needs. Mestre et al. (2021) suggests that the term Nature-based Solutions participates in flooding science with green rhetoric whose ecological 8 Bachelard had already analysed in La formation de l’esprit, 1934 how the image of the sponge sets preconceived ideas in physics and chemistry, and thus was actually a drawback to characterise the phenomena studied. Here, the image of a sponge is used in the context of a future permeable and buffer city for rainwater, bringing nature back. Argent et al. (2008) also concludes to the same limits of the metaphor. [SOURCE: Page_94]

71 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_94]

performance remains to be assessed. This green rhetoric may be driven consciously chosen as a political greening trend, and approved in science from beliefs in the curing role of nature against human grey in- terventions, which may originate from epistemological obstacles 9 from researchers in biology and ecology initially being sensitive to environmental preservation. Lautensach (2005) nuances saying the scientific literature shows no clear value statements of ecocentrism, and Palmer et al. (2005) notes that ”a focus on ecological sustainability does not mean advocacy” in the urgency of environmental challenges and high- lights the need to inform decision-makers. Nonetheless, this term may help to reconcile the separated concepts of water (dream) and H2O (technical) back to a common imaginary on which Nature-based So- lution perenniality may rely on 10 . As a comparison, a very down-to-earth and anthropocentric definition stands out from economics, describing Nature-based Solutions as investments that preserve and increase natural capital stocks (Loiseau et al., 2016). This economic perspective is also adopted by Maes and Jacobs (2017) in its European policy perspective: ”any transition to a use of ecosystem services with decreased input of non-renewable natural capital and increased investment in renewable natural processes”. [SOURCE: Page_95]

The broad scope of Nature-based solutions has led to a classification and standardisation of the different terms and concepts that fall under the definition of Nature-based solutions: [SOURCE: Page_95]

• Eggermont et al. (2015) divides Nature-based Solutions into three types according to their level of technology and their provision of ecosystem services in relation to urban challenges: 1 - management, better use, 2 - restoration and recovery, multifunctionality, 3 - full recovery and creation, [SOURCE: Page_95]

• Cohen-Shacham et al. (2019) sees Nature-based Solutions as frameworks, and divides Nature-based Solutions for ecosystem-based approaches into five categories: restoration, issue-specific, infrastruc- ture, management and protection, [SOURCE: Page_95]

• Snep et al. (2020) distinguishes Nature-based Solutions according to their level of technology, [SOURCE: Page_95]

• Palomo et al. (2021) clusters Nature-based Solutions into three challenges: 1 - conserving biodiversity, reducing degradation, 2 - local and indigenous people, biodiversity-friendly development, 3 - climate adaptation and disaster risk reduction, [SOURCE: Page_95]

• Castellar et al. (2021) deciphers that Nature-based Solutions correspond either to an action (inter- vention), or to a physical element (spatial and technological units) differentiated according to the purpose, the degree of technology, the vegetation diversity and the implementation, [SOURCE: Page_95]

• Anderson and Gough (2022) highlights the coexistence of two nomenclatures, one descriptive (infrastructure- related, ecosystem-based management and ecosystem protection approaches) and the other aspira- tional (ecosystem restoration, issue-specific ecosystem approaches). [SOURCE: Page_95]

These different classifications tend to favour the environmental and social objectives of Nature-based Solutions as actions, while the technological criteria are less included. In the literature on sustainable de- velopment, many terms are used as synonyms or close equivalents to Nature-based Solutions, with an over- all stronger reference to physical and technological solutions. Preti et al. (2022) traces the evolution and purposes of terminology from technique to nature, and De Oliveira Demarco et al. (2024) shows that ter- minology is not exempt from trends in the scientific literature. An exhaustive literature review on nature- based solutions would require considering all the following keywords: low impact development (1977), best management practices (1980), water-sensitive urban design (1994), green infrastructure (1995) or engi- neering, sustainable urban drainage (2001), ecosystem-based adaptation (2009), ecological systems or en- gineering, engineering with nature, environmental engineering, watershed management, urban forestry, ecosystem-based disaster risk reduction (2010), green/blue infrastructure (2013) and enhanced natural treatment systems 11 . Some extensive work has attempted to compare the concepts behind all these terms: (De Oliveira Demarco et al., 2024; Anderson and Gough, 2022; Babí Almenar et al., 2021; Escobedo et al., 2019), and (Chocat et al., 2022; Fletcher et al., 2015) with the terms related to urban drainage. [SOURCE: Page_95]

Nature-based Solutions are entities with a clear ontological plurality balancing between the challenges of sustainability, and the implementation technicity. Yet, there is a predominance of technique when look- ing at the physical elements, in particular the technological units (Castellar et al., 2021). Technological 9 see Bachelard, Le Rationalisme appliqué, 1949. Bourdieu would rather speak of bias and determinisms, see Science de la science et réflexivité, 2001 10 Stakeholders engagement is paramount, leading to thinking of the multifunctionality of Nature-based Solutions 11 mentioned in several EU-supported CORDIS H2020 projects [SOURCE: Page_95]

units are actually further crystallised as physical elements and easier to understand (as compared to NBS actions) since they are graphically represented, with the illustrations by Lide Jaurrieta in the framework of MULTISOURCE project. We cannot fit this concept into the core structure of PO$_2$, but the NBS techno- logical unit, yes. We will be interested in differentiating treatment wetlands from the other technological units. The taxonomy presented in Figure 4.5 is based on (Castellar et al., 2021) and (Fonder and Headley, 2013), and the current proposal is presented in Figure 4.6. The paper on taxonomy by Fonder and Headley (2013) was both recommended and considered obsolete. It was recommended to reuse other resources such as textbooks and papers. The taxonomy was questioned on the terms chosen, and the criteria retained to organise the concepts (e.g., hydraulics, objectives). The term treatment wetland was not questioned. [SOURCE: Page_96]

The first criterion of differentiation is the orientation of the implementation, either horizontal (e.g. on dedicated field) or vertical (e.g. along a building wall), and to which we added linear (e.g. along a street). Then, the designs and water hydraulics (surface, subsurface, infiltration or evaporation) constitute a sec- ond criterion, which can to some extent be associated to the type of water handled (greywater, rainwater, wastewater). Tree pits, basins, swales, and trenches are associated with rainwater and road run-off, green roofs with buildings and rainwater, green walls, facades with buildings and greywater, hydroponics, and aquaponics with greywater. In urban contexts, these solutions mitigate the pollution and volume of wa- ter entering sewer networks, while treatment wetlands, ponds, and willow systems are associated with wastewater and tend to be employed after sewer networks and before potential discharge or reuse. Ponds and treatment wetland designs are differentiated based on the types of water handled: from highly loaded to lightly, and are positioned within a treatment train accordingly. Hydraulics (surface, point and lin- ear) were recommended to classify sustainable urban drainage systems (SUDS), and material (water, soil, wetland-based) for Nature-based Solutions. For green wall, the terminology of Pearlmutter et al. (2021) was recommended, and instead speaks of vertical greening systems 12 , which are differentiated based on the support of the plant for growth: ground-based green facade, wall-based green facade, pot-based green facade, and vegetated pergola. Green roofs are further differentiated on the basis of their level of technol- ogy: intensive, extensive, and semi-intensive designs. [SOURCE: Page_96]

These technological units are still being developed and assessed, and their definitions will probably evolve with implementations over time. The current classification in Figure 4.6 shows the preferential terms determined from the exchanges during the workshops. Identified synonyms are the following: [SOURCE: Page_96]

• Evaporative system: zero-discharge system and willow system [SOURCE: Page_96]

• Reciprocating treatment wetland: tidal treatment wetland [SOURCE: Page_96]

• Surface flow wetlands: lagoons, ponds [SOURCE: Page_96]

• Swale: bioswale and retention swale [SOURCE: Page_96]

• Treatment marshes: free water surface treatment wetland and natural wetland [SOURCE: Page_96]

• Vertical Greening System: green wall and green facade [SOURCE: Page_96]

• Wall-based green facade: planter green wall [SOURCE: Page_96]

nota bene 4. The language barrier still constitutes an important challenge. We noticed that no native-English speaker was involved in (Castellar et al., 2021) which may explain the validation and misuse of the term vegetated grid pave 13 , that we changed to vegetated grid pavement. [SOURCE: Page_96]

Treatment wetlands (material) Treatment wetlands and other vegetated technologies have recently been integrated in a broader concept of Nature-based Solutions, which promotes a sustainable development vision for water management 14 . Some definitions of treatment wetlands are given below: 12 they are defined as: ”vegetated surfaces on the building envelope, which include the spread of plants that may or may not be attached to the façade, and can either be rooted into the ground or in pots” 13 to pave is a verb, not a noun 14 Practitioners on treatment wetland or other NBS technical units may find interest in branding their object of study under the name Nature-based Solution, with all the symbolic values it holds. [SOURCE: Page_96]

Fonder and Headley (2013) Two characteristics are issued from natural wetlands’ definition which are: 1. The presence of macrophytic vegetation, and 2. The existence of water-logged or saturated substrate conditions for at least part of the time. The third additional one, specific to treatment wetlands is: 3. The inflow of contaminated waters with constituents that are to be removed. [SOURCE: Page_99]

Asano (2007) An artificial wetland system design used for water quality improvement, for example, sec- ondary wastewater treatment. Constructed wetland systems require more space than mechanized treatment processes, but use little or no energy for operation. / Wetlands intentionally developed in nonwetland areas to duplicate the processes occurring in natural wetlands, but generally for the purpose of improving water quality and with more control. [SOURCE: Page_99]

Salas and Pride e Inmaculada Cuenca (2007) Tecnología de tratamiento de las aguas residuales que imita los procesos que se dan en los humedales naturales. [SOURCE: Page_99]

[SOURCE: Page_99]

These definitions illustrate that although all agree on the objective of ’cleaning’ and ’treating’ wastew- ater, defining a term does not lead to a unique definition. The definitions of Fonder and Headley (2013), Asano (2007) and Salas and Pride e Inmaculada Cuenca (2007) compare treatment wetlands with natural wetlands. Chocat et al. (2022) describes the plants used. WHO (2006) and Asano (2007) mention that they are artificial, and USEPA (2002) mentions the treatment mechanisms used. Unlike Nature-based Solu- tions, treatment wetlands have more down-to-earth technical definitions, probably due to the engineering background of the authors. We could expect that our different technical or social perspectives, depending on our professional backgrounds, may lead us to define concepts based on different properties and cause difficulties in understanding each other. Interestingly, OI-EAU is a non-governmental association, it may target the interest of a non expert audience and OiEau (2024) stands out by providing a very metaphorical definition with the terms purification and power. The term phytopurification has actually been criticised due to potential misunderstanding of the role of plants in treatment wetlands (EPNAC, 2014), but seems to be more appealing. Bachelard distinguished two levels of understanding 15 to objects: • The designated object: it results from perception and common understanding, it is not informative. Stakeholders that do not study treatment wetlands may project an idealised (or inversely a pes- simistic) vision of Nature-based Solutions. [SOURCE: Page_99]

• The instructive object: it results from a rational construction. Practitioners gather an expert under- standing through scientific studies. Interestingly, neither the EU nor France have provided a legal definition of the concept, despite the implementation of more than 5000 treatment wetlands in France. In particular in France, the EPUR NATURE AUTOEPURE designs have been certified in 2012, with 5 different models 16 . Their technical sheet NOR : DEVL1226767V does not have any definition, but a detailed technical description of the design. The technology may have come too late to be considered by the regulations, and the uncertainty associated with the treatment by nature may create a reluctance to rely on it. Similarly to the analysis of Mestre et al. (2021), it can be observed that the integration in the definition of the treatment objective, the improvement of wastewater quality or the UN Sustainable Development Goals, creates uncertainty: [SOURCE: Page_99]

• In the context of water reuse, not all pollutants are to be removed, since some of them are in fact nutrients that can be valorised, in particular in agricultural irrigation 17 . Our perception of ’waste’ and ’pollution’ therefore depends on the context. [SOURCE: Page_99]

• Treatment wetlands are a solution for wastewater treatment, although they (i.e. the treatment prop- erty attributed to them) may not fulfill their purpose. 15 two instances of objectification, see his essay Le rationalisme appliqué, 1949 16 the models are based on the size, or number of population equivalent served: 3000 (5PE), 4000 (8PE), 5000 (10PE), 7000 (15PE), and 9000 (20PE) 17 see chapter 1, with historical practices and fertigation. Nonetheless, this valorisation perspective remains deeply rooted in a com- mercial vision of wastewater, where anthropocentric interests take over. [SOURCE: Page_99]
