Figure 4.7: Example of confusion due to synonyms for the term filter, illustrated by Cled’12. [SOURCE: Page_100]

• On the socio-economic dynamics, the greening of urban landscape with wetlands may inversely lead to gentrification (Fernandez et al., 2024; Sanchez et al., 2024). [SOURCE: Page_100]

The term treatment wetland is used by renowned researchers and practitioners: Dotro et al. (2017), Fonder and Headley (2013) and Kadlec and Wallace (2009). However, it is not mentioned in two recent classifications of solutions/actions, which tend to use the terms: [SOURCE: Page_100]

• Constructed wetland, classified as a Nature-based Solution Technological Horizontal Unit for wastew- ater treatment by Castellar et al. (2021), [SOURCE: Page_100]

• Engineered wetland, fitting in Ecosystem-based Disaster Risk Management, Green Infrastructure, and Integrated Water Resources Management categories according to Anderson and Gough (2022), [SOURCE: Page_100]

• other terms referring to treatment wetlands are artificial wetland (humedal artificial), vegetated filter, planted reed bed (notably used in the French translation: filtre planté de roseaux), marais filtrant, marais artificiel, or terre humide construite in Quebec, but rarely employed in France (they would correspond to an inadequate literal translation), [SOURCE: Page_100]

• Anderson and Gough (2022) also identified the following aspirational nomenclatures for treatment wetlands : Biophilic design, Low-impact design, Regenerative urban design, Resilient infrastructure, Sustainable urban drainage systems. [SOURCE: Page_100]

Constructed and artificial have been less employed because of their reference to technical and human- made aspects, while treatment refers instead to their objective, which is more positive. The term reed bed is also inadequate because the plants used may not always be reeds. When speaking about an individual reed bed, the term filter is also used. Cled’12 illustrated the issue of synonyms in Figure 4.7, in which multiple concepts are represented by the same term. And inversely, the nomenclature is subject to changes and treatment wetlands present many synonyms. In the literature the term subsurface is removed from the subclasses names falling in the subsurface flow category. Acronyms have also evolved, such as the case of horizontal flow treatment wetlands: from HSSF CW or HSSF TW, to HFTW and HF wetlands (Kadlec and Wallace, 2009; Dotro et al., 2017; Zidan and Hady, 2018). [SOURCE: Page_100]

Treatment wetlands are generally named on the basis of water saturation conditions and hydraulic flow direction, which influence the performance in pollutant removal, (Fonder and Headley, 2013). The presence and type of plants, the type of substrate, if reactive, and the type of inflow may also be used in treatment wetlands names. Fonder and Headley (2013) classified treatment wetlands into subcategories based on hydrology and vegetation. The classification also becomes more arduous as innovations and in- tensification on treatment wetlands are made, such as the addition of artificial aeration or reactive media. Aeration, reactive media and flow direction create conditions for specific phenomena to occur, so we con- sidered them essential and differentiating properties to treatment wetlands rather than simple attributes. We therefore kept these properties, from the nomenclature of Fonder and Headley (2013). We chose to keep aerated treatment wetlands on the same level as non aerated treatment wetlands rather than hierarchi- cally organised based on the hydraulics. French systems and treatment wetlands for CSO were discarded from this taxonomy because one is a specific implementation of vertical flow wetlands that can handle raw wastewater, and the other only specifies the target. We chose to not integrate the names of species used as treatment wetlands vegetation (plant), but we integrated the types of substrates. Treatment Wetlands [SOURCE: Page_100]

fall under the material core concept, which comprises reactors and equipment in TransformON. • Aerated Horizontal Subsurface Flow Treatment Wetland • Aerated Vertical Subsurface Flow Treatment Wetland • Free Water Surface Flow Treatment Wetland: [SOURCE: Page_101]

• Horizontal Subsurface Flow Treatment Wetland • Partially Saturated Vertical Flow Treatment Wetland • Reciprocating Vertical Subsurface Flow Treatment Wetland • Treatment Wetland for Combined Sewer Overflow • Treatment Wetland with Reactive Media • Vertical Subsurface Flow Treatment Wetland • Partially saturated TW (hydraulic) • French VF system [SOURCE: Page_101]

Wastewater treatment plants (process) [SOURCE: Page_101]

Conventional wastewater treatment in Europe is centralised 18 and consists of a treatment train divided into treatment steps, such that for each step usually coincide a treatment objective and a technological unit designed specifically. Their efficiencies depend on the previous steps. These steps are defined in the following: [SOURCE: Page_101]

Pre-treatment This step is based on physical mechanisms, it targets the removal of voluminous elements (rags, sticks, floatables) and grease with the use of a grit or a trap. [SOURCE: Page_101]

Primary Treatment Primary treatment involves physical and/or chemical processes, and removes parti- cles (suspended solids, colloids) and organic matter. It involves the sedimentation of solids and the flocculation of less dense particles (scum), or other processes targeting BOD$_5$, and can be enhanced with the use of chemicals or anaerobic conditions. Biosolids (preferred term unlike sludge which presents a pejorative meaning) form at the bottom. (Asano (2007); WHO (2006), GEMET) The Euro- pean Directives specify treatment objectives with a reduction of BOD$_5$ ”by at least 20 % and the total suspended solids of the incoming waste water are reduced by at least 50 %”. [SOURCE: Page_101]

Secondary Treatment Secondary treatment involves a biological treatment to remove dissolved and col- loidal biodegradable organic matter. It often consists in an aerobic process (eg. activated sludge, la- goon, trickling filters) followed by a secondary sedimentation that generates biosolids. (WHO (2006); Asano (2007), GEMET) [SOURCE: Page_101]

Tertiary Treatment Tertiary treatment improves the removal of nitrogen and/or phosphorus and residual suspended solids, as well as pathogens. Technologies mobilised are usually depth and surface filtra- tion (ie. on sand or with a membrane).(Asano (2007), GEMET) [SOURCE: Page_101]

Quaternary Treatment This type of treatment will be introduced in the upcoming revision of the European Directive on urban residual wastewater. It takes place after the steps mentioned above and targets the removal of a broad spectrum of micro-pollutants. 18 centralisation refers to the connection of individual wastewater discharges into an underground network of sewer pipelines, also referred to as grid-based system in Hoffmann et al. (2020) [SOURCE: Page_101]

78 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_101]

Disinfection Disinfection is sometimes associated with tertiary treatment. It targets the removal of pathogens 19 . They originate mainly from faecal contamination which is monitored with the bac- terial indicator E. coli. Depending on the mechanism mobilised by the technology, pathogens are filtered (e.g. membranes), inactivated or destroyed by oxidation (eg. from UV lights, or from chem- icals such as chlorine or ozone) or by heat. (WHO (2006); USEPA (2002); Asano (2007), Glossaire OiEau, GEMET) [SOURCE: Page_102]

Similarly to wastewater, conventional treatment plants are well defined by authorities such as the US EPA and the EU in its directives. The definitions on which the regulations are based even mobilise a very technical vocabulary (BOD$_5$, nitrogen, phosphorus, flocculation, population equivalent), demonstrating the difficulty of legislating on technical concepts. Primary treatment is linked to treatment objectives for BOD$_5$ and TSS, which correspond both to an observed treatment performance guaranteed by existing technolo- gies and to an objective (or requirement) to be considered as primary treatment. [SOURCE: Page_102]

Figure 4.8: Treatment train with Treatment Wetlands, working document for the workshop [SOURCE: Page_102]

We nested wastewater treatment process under biowaste treatment. As mentioned previously, the treat- ment steps are not only employed for designing WWTP systems, but also for establishing regulations on their performances. We therefore chose to keep these pivotal concepts, notably in order to facilitate the possible integration of ontologies for conventional WWTP. These steps are associated with the concepts of pre-treated, primary treated, secondary treated wastewater (etc.). Aligning with TransformON which em- ploys step to define specific phenomena (or mechanisms), we nested the nomenclature for treatment steps under the process class. Disinfection is a treatment step that is involved in both Surface Water Treatment and Wastewater Treatment, sometimes considered part of Tertiary treatments. In TransformON, this pro- cess is a type of cleaning, which we kept as is. [SOURCE: Page_102]

In practice, treatment steps, composing a treatment train, have blurry boundaries. A technology might be designed as a primary treatment, but operates in practice like a secondary treatment as well, ie. a technological unit may not solely target the constituents defined for the step it was built for. In the case of treatment wetlands, this notion of steps can hardly be employed. Treatment wetlands do not fit into this stepwise approach because they present less controlled operational conditions, leading to the occur- rence of concomitant phenomena compared to those from conventional technologies. They are however still put in these categories based on the previous step in the treatment train. They rather participate in an appropriate treatment which is defined by the Directive 91/271 as ”a treatment of urban waste water by any process and/or disposal system which after discharge allows the receiving waters to meet the rel- evant quality objectives and the relevant provisions of this and other Community Directives”. Treatment wetlands can effectively remove TSS, carbonaceous constituents, as well as nutrients (Meuleman et al., 2002; Gholizadeh et al., 2015; Zhai et al., 2016; Han et al., 2017), although the literature also reported nutrient removals to be mitigated Mekonnen et al. (2015) notably for phosphorus removal. They also re- move pathogens (Shingare et al., 2019; López et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2016; Smith, 2005; García et al., 2013; 19 infectious (micro)organisms that can cause diseases, among the following types: bacteria, viruses, protozoa, and helminths [SOURCE: Page_102]

79 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_102]

Headley et al., 2013) and micro-pollutants (Tondera et al., 2013; Scheurer et al., 2015; Pálfy et al., 2017; Sossalla et al., 2022). [SOURCE: Page_103]

Wastewater (component) A recent publication by Messager et al. (2024) has shown that definitions are key elements of regulations, using the example of French watercourses, officially defined in 2015, and explaining that a quarter of mapped hydrographic segments do not fall within the objects of legal protection established by the French Water Act, in particular 28% of headwater and perennial segments, which represent 67% of watercourses. Similarly, the categorisation and definition of anthropogenic water discharges and types of pollution is a cornerstone for the establishment of pollution control regulations. The definition of sanitation proposed by an independent expert, C. de Albuquerque, was re-used by the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (E/C.12/2010/1), although it only covers human excreta and not grey water, sewage or wastewater (de l’eau, 2011). The generic term wastewater is defined as follows by different institutions: [SOURCE: Page_103]

Water Science Glossary, 2018, usgs.gov water that has been used in homes, industries, and businesses that is not for reuse unless it is treated. [SOURCE: Page_103]

General Multilingual Environmental Thesaurus, GEMET Used water, or water that is not needed, which is permitted to escape, or unavoidably escapes from canals, ditches, reservoirs or other bodies of water, for which the owners of these structures are legally responsible. [SOURCE: Page_103]

EU regulation n.166/2006 urban, domestic and industrial waste water, as defined in Article 2 (1), (2) and (3) of Council Directive 91/271/EEC of 21 May 1991 concerning urban waste water treatment (9), and any other used water which is subject, because of the substances or objects it contains, to regulation by Community law. [SOURCE: Page_103]

WHO (2006) Liquid waste discharged from homes, commercial premises and similar sources to individual disposal systems or to municipal sewer pipes, and which contains mainly human excreta and used water. [SOURCE: Page_103]

Asano (2007) Used water discharged from homes, business, cities, industry, and agriculture. Various synonymous uses such as municipal wastewater (sewage), industrial wastewater, and stormwater. [SOURCE: Page_103]

OiEau (2024) Water that has been used by man. We usually distinguish wastewater from domestic, in- dustrial or agricultural origin. These waters are discharged into the natural environment directly or through collecting systems with or without treatment. We also talk of sewage or effluent. [SOURCE: Page_103]

All definitions converge in saying that it is water used for anthropogenic activities, that finds no further use. Wastewater is subject to a variety of management approaches and scales, from household to urban, from individual discharges to collectors and treatment. Wastewater is differentiated by its producers, who determine the composition and amount of nutrients, pathogens, heavy metals, etc. in the effluent. If it is mainly produced by household and commercial activities, it is called domestic or municipal wastewater or domestic sewage. Typical domestic wastewater can be further distinguished based on the type and diver- sity of water sources, each of which contributes a specific proportion of the pollutant load, see Figure 4.9. In this context, domestic wastewater does not contain industrial effluents in quantities that could endan- ger the functioning of the sewerage system, the treatment plant, public health or the environment (WHO, 2006). Industrial wastewater comes from food processing, textiles, mining, oil extraction, etc. Due of com- bined sewer systems 20 , rainwater that seeps over impervious surfaces (urban run-off) ends up mixed with wastewater. Thus, urban wastewater is composed of domestic wastewater and urban run-off in varying proportions depending on rainfall events and/or commercial and industrial wastewater. [SOURCE: Page_103]

The different types of wastewater have been added without hierarchy. We added a general class treated water only to avoid creating too many types of treated water based on their quality along the treatment train. The quality could be added later on based on the classification established for water reuse. Wastew- ater does not belong to the class biowaste from the definition provided by the Directive 2008/98/EC 21 , nor to the class bioliquids defined in the Directive (EU) 2018/2001 22 . Domestic wastewater originates mainly 20 combined sewer systems receive both wastewater and rain run-off, it is also known as unitary sewer system, Directive 2024/3019 21 ”bio-waste means biodegradable garden and park waste, food and kitchen waste from households, restaurants, caterers and retail premises and comparable waste from food processing plants.” 22 ”bioliquids means liquid fuel for energy purposes other than for transport, including electricity and heating and cooling, produced from biomass.” [SOURCE: Page_103]

from human metabolism and household activities, from residential settlements, institutions, commercial buildings and services. In a context of water reuse, wastewater eventually still requires specific treatment but may rather be seen as a resource. With the current paradigm shift from WWTP to WRP to WRRF to biorefineries 23 , the anthropocentric status of wastewater is elevated to that of a resource, such that wastewater treatment should not only purify water, but also preserve nutrients, aggregate metals, and provide energy 24 and materials. [SOURCE: Page_104]

Human practices and rainfall events are uncontrolled factors influencing the composition of wastewa- ter, leading to large variability over time and resulting in variability in wastewater treatment performance. Water management may seem neutral, in particular when we see how technical terms and numbers rule in regulations, but wastewater is subjective and anthropic concept which cannot be dissociated from social and cultural practices. An example to the limits of categorisation, or to the broad set covered by the term wastewater in terms of volume, wastewater production and management varies greatly across continents with the highest production corresponding to 20 times the lowest, with different agricultural, industrial or recreational uses, see their volumes in Table 4.2. Strande et al. (2023) illustrate how categories and terminology affect how we perceive and understand reality, and in particular, they impose a certain rep- resentation that we may clumsily project on other realities. They explain that the current categories and terminology do not correspond to the situation of many regions, and note how the elucidation of terminology and proper categorisation of actual practices and situations can inform for better assessment and manage- ment of sanitation worldwide. They show that septic tanks and pit latrines actually cover a wide range of techniques and practices over different contexts, and present different risks. Similarly, faecal sludge from on-site storage does not solely cover dry faeces but also wastewater flowing in a sewer network, with great variations in concentration, and not solely from households but also from offices, restaurants etc. [SOURCE: Page_104]

Substances and pollutants (component) [SOURCE: Page_105]

The EC directive No 155/2006 defines pollutant as ”a substance or a group of substances that may be harmful to the environment or to human health on account of its properties and of its introduction into the environment”. The concept of pollutant is defined relative to its properties and human activities. Similarly to wastewater that can be treated and reused, pollutants are not systematically pollutants. For the receiv- ing water body with a certain sensitivity, nitrogen and phosphorus are elements that, if introduced in a certain bioavailable form and concentration, can cause eutrophication (Preisner et al., 2020) and destroy its ecosystem. If we speak of nutrients, pharmaceuticals or cosmetics, we instead perceive value in these pollutants that have been used, but are not needed. Douglas (1966) actually defines pollution as matter out of place and constituting a source of danger, and analyses how pollution is a social and symbolic concept that characterises societies sense of order in what they value and what they consider taboos. In the biore- finery perspective, nitrogen and phosphorus may be extracted, and have value as nutrients in agriculture. Although present in other ontologies, we decided to align with the valorisation vision and did not place the main monitored substances (nutrients) under the class pollutant. Inversely, substances that have a high use value turn out to generate pollutants on the long term (Villarín and Merel, 2020). Known as contami- nants of emerging concern (USEPA, 2002; Asano, 2007), these substances have recently been identified in water and are considered for regulatory action. The risk to human health and environment associated with their presence, frequency of occurrence and source is however still uncertain and pends further assessment. [SOURCE: Page_105]

We added the CAS number to the definition of constituents that are registered in the Chemical Ab- stracts Service: [SOURCE: Page_105]

With the amended European Directive 91/271/EEC, micro-pollutants must also be monitored. They are contaminants of emerging concern, sometimes clumsily named emerging contaminants, and are better characterised as sophisticated chemical analytical tools have emerged from science and technology, such as High-performance liquid chromatograph with tandem mass spectrometry (HPLC-MSMS). To avoid confu- sion, micro-pollutants are referred to organic micro-pollutants (OMP), micro referring to the concentration levels, and microplastics (MP), micro referring to the size of the particles. The OMP can be categorised based on their use/function, as well as their chemical structure (functional groups). The nomenclatures de- scribing specifically the chemical composition and characteristics of pollutants reveal the ambivalent status of pollutants. Treatment wetlands have been studied for the removal of classical pollutants (C, N, P based substances and solids) as well as contaminants of emerging concern (Ávila et al., 2015; Hijosa-Valsero et al., 2011). In particular, this terminology has been employed in regulations, and the new Directive 2024/3019 considers monitoring these pollutants and treating them in a quaternary treatment. INWS ontology con- siders the concept of pollutant (Ahmedi et al., 2013), while WaWO+ (Oliva-Felipe et al., 2017) imbricates pollutants under the class water features, divided into biological, chemical, and microbiological features, as well as indicator parameter. [SOURCE: Page_105]

Practitioners specified that observations can also concern components such as air, soil, plants and sed- iments. [SOURCE: Page_105]

82 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_105]

Concentrations (attribute) Although treated like molecules, some measured concentrations correspond to the results of calculations for given parameters. The following parameters cannot be considered as components 25 : • COD: chemical oxygen demand, which is a measure of the oxygen consumed in the oxidation of organic and inorganic matter. • BOD: biological oxygen demand, which is a measure of the biodegradable organic matter converted to inert compounds by bacteria under aerobic conditions, typically over a five-day period. • TKN: Total Kjeldahl nitrogen, which includes organic nitrogen and ammonia-N NH$_3$-N, which also includes ammonium-N NH$_4$-N. • TN: Total nitrogen, which includes the nitrogen molecules nitrite NO$_2$- and nitrate NO$_3$-, as well as total Kjeldahl nitrogen. • TP: total phosphorus, which includes phosphorus-based molecules, in particular orthophosphate PO43-. • TSS: Total Suspended Solids, corresponding to the particulate elements. Regarding attributes, practitioners noted that they are monitoring more operational conditions than only temperature: loading rate and flow, plant growth, plant harvesting, mass balance (N, P, C) and gas emission sampling. They emphasized the multi-dimensional aspect of studies: over time with dynamic processes measured with hydraulic tracer tests or gas balances, and over space with multiple points of measurement of the concentrations or flowrates, at the inlet and outlet and within the wetlands. Finally, they reminded that they report separately the values, the units of measurement, the number of replicates and the associated sampler or sensor. [SOURCE: Page_106]

Infrastructures and measuring devices (material) We made a graph in Figure 4.10 based on how practitioners take experimental measurements, represent- ing the features measured, the sampling point, and the measuring device. Practitioners advised to include much more material: overflow, tank, valves, pumps, aeration, substrate, plant types. They recommended to opt for a wider view, including the sewer network beforehand, source of water matrix, end user for reuse. This may prove useful notably for the economic costs evaluation and the life-cycle analysis. We included the classes 26 from WaWO+ concerning Water Transport Infrastructure and Sewerage System, but followed TransformON hierarchy, because the material in itself is not specific to water (eg. pump, pipeline). In TransformON, corresponding steps exist in the form of verbs/actions such as pumping. We noticed INWS and WaWO+ ontologies reused sensor and sensing device from SSN ontology, but classified them hierarchically in different orders. We reused the sensor sub-classes defined in INWS 27 . [SOURCE: Page_106]

Mechanisms (step) The mechanisms occurring along a treatment train, or within treatment wetlands and other NBS techno- logical units are very similar to the steps occurring in product transformation described in TransformON. Steps include transport, piping, pumping, and the more abstract transformation step that includes biolog- ical, chemical, physical, or a combination of processing. Some technologies in food processing are designed to isolate certain mechanisms undergone by the products (filtration, pasteurisation, grinding, extrusion). However, Treatment wetlands involve multiple mechanisms for the treatment of wastewater (targeting organic matter, nutrients, pathogens, micro-pollutants), that can occur in series and in parallel, and can hardly be differentiated. As examples of steps already present in TransformON: adsorption, absorption, biodegradation, digestion, mineralisation, nitrification, denitrification, and oxidation. We considered that these mechanisms can be represented as substeps of treatment wetlands. [SOURCE: Page_106]

We noted that there exist a cleaning step, but in comparison to wastewater treatment, the focus is not restrained to cleaning the product (water). Cleaning steps may be more general categories than the processing steps. 25 their definitions are provided in Appendix B.1 26 the classes xxx in WaWO+ are referenced with the URI https://kemlg.upc.edu/wawo-core-tbox#xxx 27 the sub-classes xxx in INWS are referenced with the URI http://inwatersense.uni-pr.eud/ontologies/inws-core.owl#xxx [SOURCE: Page_106]

Methods (method) [SOURCE: Page_107]

Methods refer to the sampling, extraction and analysis methods used to characterise components. Report- ing the methods used is essential to determining whether different sets of measures can be compared or not. Sampling can be done punctually by hand leading to grab samples, or continuously with autosamplers leading to composite samples. Standardised methods have been developed on the national, European and international 28 levels, showing the great interconnection between science and technique, and a participa- tion in a globalisation of scientific practices and knowledge. Obtaining the ISO certification is voluntary and allows industries and research institutes to have access to and align with standards such as the ISO 14 000 series on environmental standards. However, they come with fees and also set prerequisites that low-income countries may not be able to keep up with, notably in terms of administration, technical skills, and technologies. [SOURCE: Page_107]

The methods used by INRAE LAMA 29 chemical analysis laboratory 30 , and Suez 31 are indicated below. [SOURCE: Page_107]

28 on the national level in France: NF, delivered by AFNOR; on the European level: EN, delivered by CEN; and on the international level: ISO standards, delivered by ISO 29 Laboratoire de chimie des milieux aquatiques 30 methods used in the framework of the experiments led for MULTISOURCE project on treatment wetlands in the research platform REFLET of REVERSAAL, based in Craponne 31 from Suez Water Handbook [SOURCE: Page_107]

To filter the samples a preliminary step: [SOURCE: Page_108]

• Total Suspended Solids (TSS): glass fiber filter of 0.7 µ m, which also allows the extraction of the dissolved fraction for filtered COD analysis • Main cations 32 and anions 33 : filtration < 0.45µ m to avoid clogging of the ionic chromatography [SOURCE: Page_108]

To measure concentrations 34 the measuring step: [SOURCE: Page_108]

• Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD): dilution method NF EN 1899-1, manometric methods • Chemical oxygen demand (COD): potentiometric titration NF T 90.101 on raw and filtered sam- ples • carbonates: potentiometric titration NF EN 9963-1 • Total organic carbon (TOC) and dissolved organic carbon (DOC): catalytic combustion NF EN 1484 • NK: mineralisation with selenium, followed by sulphuric acid titration, NF EN 25663 • Main cations and anions: ionic chromatography, according to norms NF ISO 10304-1 and NF EN ISO 14911 • Total Suspended Solids (TSS): NF EN 872, centrifugation method NF T 90.105-2 • Total phosphorus (TP): mineralisation with aqua regia in microwave, followed by ICP-OES, according to NF EN ISO 11885 and ISO 15587-1 • hydrocarbons: NF T 90.202 [SOURCE: Page_108]

Process scale (scale) In TransformON, it is possible to indicate a scale for the process and for the measurements. Regarding the latter, the scale refers to the compound size or type: atomic, cellular, molecular, organ, organism, particle, population. Regarding process scale, the scale of wastewater treatment systems is expressed in legisla- tions and technical guidelines as a number of population or people equivalent (PE). This metric is not always consensual because of the people equivalent possible variability as seen in the part on wastewater: wastewater loads and volumes vary based on cultural and industrial practices. The number of population equivalent corresponds to inflowing volume or BOD loads, where 1 PE corresponds to 0.2 m^3 /d, or to 60g BOD in Europe (from Directive 91/271/EEC, (Henze et al., 2008)), and 80g BOD in the USA in 1995 (from (Rowe and Abdel-Magid, 1995)). The USA then aligned with 60g in its (EPA Act, 1992, (Urban Waste Water Treatment Regulations, 1994)). The scale can also be considered with categories, which is the case in TransformON. We added the household scale which is specific to certain individual installations, to the laboratory, pilot, and industrial scales. The thresholds between the categories is however not so clear, and may not depend on the size (a household scale may be smaller or larger than a pilot scale, but we could also consider it to be an industrial scale). The scale may be associated with the degree of technology or rather the technology readiness level. Indeed, the degree of technology may not be relevant in the case of low tech innovations. [SOURCE: Page_108]

4.4      Identification We now move on to the development of the ontology. The large catchment-scope of water management has been tackled by Oliva-Felipe et al. (2017) but lacks the inclusion of Nature-based Solutions. We realised that an ontology on Nature-based Solutions and water management would be too large, notably given the project duration. We focus on the scope of treatment trains with treatment wetlands which are widely employed and whose discharges are subject to regulations. The objective is to describe a wastewater treat- ment plant consisting of treatment wetlands in series, and describe treatment wetlands composition and functioning, such that users can visualise where and how the data was obtained. The final scope is thus process-oriented, on domestic wastewater and treatment wetlands, for pilot to full scale applications and field experiments. However, this ontology should be open to being completed to include all types of Nature- based Solutions, and to being merged with ontologies developed for conventional WWTP. [SOURCE: Page_108]

32 Na+, K+, Mg++, Ca++, N-NHA+ 33 Cl-, SO$_4$-, N-NO$_3$, N-NO$_2$, P-PO$_4$ [SOURCE: Page_108]

85 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_108]

We chose to integrate the ontology into TransformON because it is process-oriented - with current ap- plications on food transformation process and biorefinery - rather than developing one separately reusing water-related ontologies that have either too large or too narrow scopes. This choice is also motivated by the intuitive interface that allows the upload of excel-based data, as well as by our maintenance strategy. A wastewater treatment plant can be seen as a biorefinery 35 , where the treatment process is similar, the effluent and by-products can be reused and valorised. By choosing to develop the ontology within Trans- formON, we follow the envisioned future of WWTP as biorefineries. TransformON is also in phase with economic cost and life-cycle assessments, providing larger scopes (catchment or worldwide) where mate- rials and products can be traced from the site of origin. We believe the PO$_2$ Manager to participate in bridging knowledge and data through the co-construction of ontologies and itineraries, which are struc- tured based on the ontologies, and offer a structure to experimental data. This software to implement food transformation ontologies being under development, we worked together with the developers in order to: [SOURCE: Page_109]

• integrate the ontology into the food transformation ontology TransformON developed for TRANS- FORM department of INRAE, [SOURCE: Page_109]

• ensure a good compatibility between the software and the needs, [SOURCE: Page_109]

• ensure a perennial maintenance in case of semantic or software evolution, [SOURCE: Page_109]

• obtain a common template for data exchange. [SOURCE: Page_109]

Competency questions The ontology structure and scope should be able to answer the following competency questions: [SOURCE: Page_109]

1. Relative to the process: What are the mechanisms involved in a treatment wetland? 2. Relative to the equipment and resources: Which steps compose a treatment train? What is the composition of a treatment wetland? What are the operational conditions set for the treatment train? 3. Relative to the product: What is the composition of wastewater at a given step? [SOURCE: Page_109]

In the future, questions regarding costs, regulations and environmental impacts may be added. [SOURCE: Page_109]

Maintenance strategy The software and ontology TransformON are being developed and maintained by a research team of INRAE TRANSFORM, with corresponding author Magalie Weber, Patrice Buche, and Stéphane Dervaux. The ontology for Treatment Wetlands does not have a referee for maintenance, but will still be functional by being part of TransformON. Upgrades to integrate a complete representation of WWTP is envisaged by researchers from the research unit REVERSAAL. [SOURCE: Page_109]

4.5       Conceptualisation with a thesaurus for wastewater and TW The very first task to any work is to define the key elements involved. In particular, experience can lead experts to neglect this task, leaving collaborators in the fog. We proposed a thesaurus on wastewater treatment and NBS technological units such that we can all start this research on the same page. [SOURCE: Page_109]

4.6       Formalisation 4.6.1      Focus on concepts and alignment Alignment 36 was done based on the compiled information in the thesaurus, with other resources on the concept level, by reporting the synonyms, acronyms and definitions in their URI in PO$_2$ Manager. In Figure 4.11 we show an example with the concept Treatment wetland, which is a type of Technological unit Nature-based Solution, which itself is a type of material. We selected one preferential term and kept the others as synonyms because they provide a historical link to older scientific literature. The objective was to keep only one definition, however this was not always possible. Indeed there exist differences 35 refer to the introduction on future wastewater management evolution, in Chapter 1.1.2 36 the process of establishing the relations between the existing concepts, and of identifying exact and close matches [SOURCE: Page_109]

between languages, and for a given language between organisations. The definition relies on necessary properties to understand the concept, and the level of understanding depends on the person’s knowledge and background. We suggest to keep two types of definitions, one which is closer to the perception of the designated object, and one which is technical for the instructive object. Regarding exact and close matches, they can be put in relation using their URI. If multiple URI existed for the same term in INRAE thesaurus, we favoured the resource that also had a definition. For treatment wetland, there already exist multiple URI notably outside of INRAE’s thesaurus: aims.fao.org/aos/agrovoc/c_331329, id.cabi.org/cabt/ 14210, lod.nal.usda.gov/nalt/12628, opendata.inrae.fr/thesaurusINRAE/c_4602 and opendata. inrae.fr/thesaurusINRAE/c_4501 [SOURCE: Page_110]

4.7       Implementation of the ontology Standardisation with PO$_2$ Manager One of the great assets of implementing the ontology in PO$_2$ Manager and within TransformON was the possibility to update both the software and the ontology together with their developers. The new features in PO$_2$ Manager concern the itinerary module. Classes 37 are organised in an operational structure to represent a transformation process: [SOURCE: Page_111]

• observations are made on itinerary and on steps [SOURCE: Page_111]

• the scale is indicated for observation measurements and for the process [SOURCE: Page_111]

• substeps can be added to represent mechanisms occurring in TW [SOURCE: Page_111]

We followed the naming conventions set by TransformON. The classes in PO$_2$ Manager are all written in singular and in lower case letters (waste water), which is different from the standard used by INWS and WaWO+ in Protege, in PascalCase (where the first letter of each word is in capital letter, and multiple words are concatenated without spaces, eg.WasteWater). Other standards are using kebab-case (dash) or snake_case (underscore) rather than spaces. The relationships in both TransformON and the other ontologies are written in a concatenated way, camelCase: with a lower case for the first letter of the verb, and a capital letter for the first letter of the second and next words hasSubStep. [SOURCE: Page_111]

nota bene 5. Other standards for relationships are using flatcase (lower cases only), and kebab-case or snake_case (has-sub-step). [SOURCE: Page_111]

4.7.1      Itineraries and knowledge graph Based on the thesaurus which models concepts with definitions, and based on experimental practices, we now model interactions between concepts and define relations between concepts that are beyond is a type of or is part of relationships. These are more complex relationships that can be defined in an ontology, and are visually represented in itineraries proposed in PO$_2$, see 4.12. By looking for the meaning of words and the relations between concepts such that the ontology structure overlaps with data, the goal of the ontology is to reliably describe and model wastewater treatment 38 . [SOURCE: Page_111]

Mobilising classes in itineraries PO$_2$ Manager already structures the ontology to relate the upper concepts to the instances that the user can provide in the itinerary module. More information on the relationships defined and concepts reused (from sosa/ssn, time ontology, OBO Foundry) can be found in (Dooley et al., 2022; Weber et al., 2023). On the interface, direct relations are deduced as illustrated in Figure 4.12: a composition (wastewater) or a step (pumping, processing - wetland) has some observations made on a particular scale, that concern a specific attribute of a component or material associated with the composition. This attribute can be charac- terised thanks to specific materials and methods. A treatment train is essentially composed of a succession of steps (eg. treatment wetlands) along which components (product compositions such as wastewater) enter and exit, see Figure 4.12. Concepts can be related to multiple other concepts in one-to-many, many-to-one or many-to-many relationships, which create a network of interactions and is useful in case multiple inputs enter a step or multiple outputs exit a step. We can associate observations to the entire itinerary of a pro- cess (here a biowaste treatment process), a step, and a component. Each observation can concern another component or material contained in the process, step or component. Chains of non hierarchical relations are made, mobilising son concepts from the core father concepts above. [SOURCE: Page_111]

For biowaste treatment process, the observation concerns the air temperature. For the pumping step, the observation concerns the flow rate provided by the pump material, which is measured with a probe. For the processing steps, the observation concerns the description of the treatment wetland material, which 37 concrete representations of the concepts, see the vocabulary in the State of the Art, Chapter 2.3.2 38 Noy and McGuinness (2001) specified: ”Ontology development is different from designing classes and relations in object-oriented programming. Object-oriented programming centres primarily around methods on classes - a programmer makes design decisions based on the operational properties of a class, whereas an ontology designer makes these decisions based on the structural properties of a class. As a result, a class structure and relations among classes in an ontology are different from the structure for a similar domain in an object-oriented program. ” [SOURCE: Page_111]

4.8      Common data exchange format Developing an ontology allowed to better identify key concepts in wastewater management with treatment wetland systems. Nature-based Solutions target different types of water and mobilise different mecha- nisms to handle situations where storage, treatment or reuse are needed. Their designs are also specific such that the scope for experiments or modelling should be at the level of the individual Nature-based Solutions technological units. We saw during the Annual Meeting that exchange knowledge and data, and structuring a database were classified as second in terms of use and interest, see Figures 4.2 and 4.3. [SOURCE: Page_113]

wetland studies, see Table 4.3. We observed in the literature that many descriptions of treatment wetlands are incomplete to allow a comparison of the systems. The file results column in the Table corresponds to another file containing the actual result data for measured parameters, see Table 4.4. Its development was based on MULTISOURCE data exchange file, REVERSAAL data storage file, and PO$_2$ Manager data itinerary file. [SOURCE: Page_115]

The excel format is composed of ten sheets. The parameter sheet provides standard information on the parameters of interest measured in treatment wetlands. The source sheet provides the meta-data that permits the traceability of the data. Then, the other sheets follow a structure from the most general and stable description to the most detailed and punctual: [SOURCE: Page_115]

• the treatment plant sheet provides a description of the context of implementation of the treatment wetland [SOURCE: Page_115]

• the treatment train sheet focuses on the size and number of steps [SOURCE: Page_115]

• the technological unit sheet provides a description of each step in terms of design and technical characteristics [SOURCE: Page_115]

• the operational condition sheet provides information on the context specific to an experimental study [SOURCE: Page_115]

• the sampling sheet provides the values of the grab measurements made during the experimental study, along with the statistical descriptors that may be required, and the information on the mea- suring devices and analytical methods. [SOURCE: Page_115]

• the online measurement (associated with the file results sheet) provides the values of the online measurements made continuously by a probe, and the information on the measuring devices and analytical methods. [SOURCE: Page_115]

4.9      Conclusion In this Chapter, we studied to what extent we could unify knowledge given a context of necessary interac- tions between scientists and stakeholders of a process-engineering oriented approach to wastewater treat- ment. A full integrated appraoch would require much more resources and time. Nature-based Solutions are at the intersection of different disciplines, but even when focusing on technologies and wastewater, consensus may not be found. Among the reasons: different levels of knowledge are conflicting, different expert points of view and objectives, and the globalised adoption of concepts, notably with regulations and standardisations, masquing other realities. Nonetheless, we believe that all these subjectivities lead to better understanding the complexity of the concepts, and even the non expert approaches are ways of get- ting to grips with the concepts 39 . We have created a thesaurus of terms typically used when describing or studying NBS technological units, and the context of wastewater treatment. This thesaurus includes defi- nitions and synonyms in English, and translations in French, Spanish, German and Italian. Anticipating the use of the terms in the development of the ontology, we structured the thesaurus according to the core concepts of the PO$_2$ Manager software. [SOURCE: Page_118]

We developed an ontology in this software as an extension of the TransformOn ontology, which describes product transformation processes. This ontology integration allowed to establish a unification of naming and concepts between food transformation and wastewater treatment. This approach constitutes a pro- posal of differentiation between components, material, and properties. We believe that the great interest of ontologies lies not solely on the resulting map of concepts but mostly on the construction process, which in our case lacked the mobilisation of stakeholder. This process-oriented approach was found to be the most interesting to represent the knowledge about treatment wetlands in particular the processes (mecha- nisms, or towards modelling: sub-models (Dehghani Tafti et al., 2024)) involved, and to keep a broad scope compared to a fully numerical modelling orientation. The ontology reconciles the knowledge about treat- ment wetlands in a structured way and provides the backbone to represent experimental data in process itineraries. We summarise the information on the ontology in Appendix B. [SOURCE: Page_118]

Data can be interpreted and structured through the ontology and the itineraries. It is collected using a specific and standardised data exchange format. This format is at the interface between the ontology and a database. It will help to trace data and improve its interpretation, integration and exchange. For the MULTISOURCE project, it was not possible to create a thesaurus or an ontology in time. However, the dynamics of the project and the opportunity to meet researchers from all over Europe has been beneficial for their development, as translations and synonyms have been agreed with some of them during workshops and meetings. Moreover, life-cycle assessment was difficult to do within the scope of the project because of the lack of information. In the future, with the need to have integrated approaches rather than an isolated treatment wetland, PO$_2$ Manager and TransformON will be interesting for the possibility to move on to smaller scopes (catchment scale, worldwide scale) encompassing more information in time and space on the scenarii studied. Stakeholders and wastewater standards (regulations) may also be included, allowing the reuse of other ontologies. [SOURCE: Page_118]

39 and hopefully in this non expert imaginary, poetics and wonder persist outside the philosophical or technical objectives of qualifying the concept. [SOURCE: Page_118]

Chapter 5 [SOURCE: Page_120]

Data for modelling [SOURCE: Page_120]

”Every utopia faces the same problem: What do you do with the people who don’t fit in?” [SOURCE: Page_120]

Margaret Atwood (2003) [SOURCE: Page_120]

To develop data-driven models, we collected data on HF and VF wetlands from the literature. We con- cluded that very few observations are available and comparable across studies. When large quantities are unavailable, it is crucial for accurate modeling to provide the models with high-quality data and train them accordingly. The objectives of this chapter are to ensure the use of a reliable dataset for modelling and to gain a better understanding of treatment wetlands from the dataset, experimental practices, and reference expert knowledge. In this chapter, we describe the data collection and processing, and present a six-step methodology to assess the reliability and quality of the data. We apply this methodology with a workflow specific to treatment wetland. The innovative aspect lies in the use of quality checks based on a probabilistic approach that relies on specific expert knowledge, limiting the risk of too arbitrary hence het- erogeneous data processing and quality categorisation. This methodology helps to automate these tasks, while ensuring the modeller’s awareness to apply the checks appropriately. In the final step, we examine the dataset and derive valuable insights to create a synthetic dataset. [SOURCE: Page_120]

The content of this chapter has been written together with my supervisors in a first paper Guillaume- Ruty et al. (2024b), entitled A validation workflow for treatment wetland performance data and published in Water Science and Technology in 2024. It is available in open access: https://doi.org/10.2166/wst. 2024.182. [SOURCE: Page_120]

5.1       Challenges for data on Treatment Wetlands Fully automated methodologies for fault management are based on data-driven approaches and large datasets Liu et al. (2023). They are starting to develop on the scale of complete WWTP as reviewed by Liu et al. (2023), focusing on process and instrumentation faults. With more human intervention, two statisti- cal methodologies have been developed specifically for time series data, within the respective frameworks of activated sludge models (Rieger et al., 2010; Rieger, 2012) and metrology in urban water management (?). These methodologies attempt to perform several checks and categorise data quality. Their evaluation of experimental data involves statistical tools and expert knowledge and is based on five criteria, namely: [SOURCE: Page_122]

• Plausibility: Measurements must be consistent with expected results under specified conditions and must be within the principles of physics and instrument ranges. [SOURCE: Page_122]

• Consistency: Repetitive and time-series data must be consistent with each other, and measurements taken by different instruments must be consistent without contradiction. [SOURCE: Page_122]

• Accuracy: Measurements must be close to the expected true value. Accuracy is sometimes assessed in conjunction with precision by assessing the closeness of repeated measurements. [SOURCE: Page_122]

• Auditability: The data collection and reconciliation process must be transparent and traceable. Com- prehensive documentation, including date, place, experimental design, and instrument details, al- lows the study to be reproduced. [SOURCE: Page_122]

• Synchronicity: Measurements taken with different instruments must be coordinated in time. [SOURCE: Page_122]

Given the challenges posed by a small and heterogeneous data set with treatment wetlands, data vali- dation is a critical step in ensuring model reliability. Pilot and full-scale treatment wetlands are operated under real outdoors conditions, with wastewater fluctuations and different monitoring practices and op- erators. In order to be able to establish conclusions on a worldwide scale, we must therefore assess to what extent data can be trusted from such different contexts, and to what extent this data can define a homogeneous and comparable set. [SOURCE: Page_122]

5.2       Roadmap for a data validation workflow Rieger (2012); ? have developed statistical methodologies tailored to the validation of time series data from a single site. These methodologies mobilise historical data and a cumulative understanding of the system being monitored. Consequently, we have adapted these methodologies to validate a dataset 1 obtained from the literature by compiling information from different sources and sites. A methodology has been defined in six steps, each with two actions (Figure 5.1); it is open to both iterations and loops. Our focus was on evaluating the data set against the criteria of plausibility, consistency, and verifiability. [SOURCE: Page_122]

5.3       Dataset for TW 5.3.1 Step 1. Definition of framework Substep a: Scope definition This study focuses on horizontal flow treatment wetlands (HF wetlands) for urban/domestic wastewater on a global scale. Because HF wetlands have sometimes been studied and compared to vertical flow treatment wetlands (VF wetlands), their sufficient number led to include them in the analysis. The scope of this study was limited to experimental data (from pilot to full scale) published in peer-reviewed scientific journals. [SOURCE: Page_122]

Substep b: Definition of objectives The sole objective is to obtain reliable data for future work: identification of explanatory variables for treat- ment processes and performance, and definition of a predictive data-driven model for treatment wetlands design. In particular, we want to assess the reliability of the data in a more automated and systematic approach. 1 we may as well speak of quality or reliability evaluation [SOURCE: Page_122]

Figure 5.1: Data validation methodology in 6 steps, and corresponding tasks to perform for each step (with examples in italics). Loops can be envisaged between the various process tasks [SOURCE: Page_123]

5.3.2      Step 2. Data collection Worldwide coverage is difficult to achieve in an experimental project. Therefore, we collected steady- state data on treatment wetlands from the scientific literature. A bibliographic search was performed on SCOPUS using the query: TITLE-ABS-KEY ((horizontal AND flow OR hssf OR treatment AND wetland OR constructed AND wetland) AND (wastewater OR wastewater AND treatment)) AND (PUBLICATION YEAR > 2000). Both HF and VF wetlands were reported if they were used in multiple stages or studied together for comparative purposes. We then added papers selected by another study (Acuña et al., 2023) from WOS. [SOURCE: Page_123]

The articles were selected using a three-stage process: first, a rough selection based on title/keyword- s/abstract; then, a more detailed selection based on screening for specific terms; and finally, a detailed selection based on a thorough reading of the articles. We used the R language (Team, 2023) to screen all .pdf files, and the data were processed using the pdftools (Ooms, 2023) and tm (Feinerer et al., 2008) packages. [SOURCE: Page_123]

Substep a: Identification of relevant (meta) data Specific terms related to design and pollutants were searched for within the content of the pdf files (exclud- ing the references subsection). The pollutants of interest in this work are the organic matter and nutrients on which the designs of treatment wetlands are based: particulate matter, carbonaceous compounds, nitro- gen and phosphorus compounds. We used the following terminological criteria to pre-select articles for full reading: [SOURCE: Page_123]

• At least one occurrence of a dimensional term from the following: area, length, width, depth [SOURCE: Page_123]

• At least four 2 occurrences of a pollutant term from the following BOD, COD, N H$_4$ , N H$_4$ − N, N H$_3$ , N H$_3$ − N, NO$_3$ , NO$_3$ − N, NO$_2$ , N$_2$ O, TK N, T N, PO$_4$ , PO$_4$ − P, TP, TSS. 2 to limit fortuitous appearances [SOURCE: Page_123]

100 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_123]

The raw data was reported in a relational database structured according to the categories outlined in Table 5.1, with an emphasis on metadata showing the categories source and treatment plant. We defined a set of mandatory and optional fields, targeting elements that are expected to correlate with the mecha- nisms of pollutant removal and performance (Table 2.1). [SOURCE: Page_124]

For the treatment wetlands dataset, we defined an additional set of variables calculated from others, such as contaminant loads and hydraulic and organic loading rates. We also provided units using the R package units by Pebesma et al. (2016), and data for the sites consisting of the average temperature of the four coldest months, the average precipitation from Karger et al. (2017), and the type of climate from Chen and Chen (2013). The correspondence between datasets is achieved through the geographical coordinates of the locations (city or country). We used the N ominatim tool in the G eoP y.geocoders package from Python. The climates are provided in a .csv file from Chen and Chen (2013) in raster format, with coordinates and associated climate reported in increments of 0.5. We assigned them to each case study location tw by taking the shortest distance between the .csv and location coordinates kop pen, correcting the raster format offset by centring: [SOURCE: Page_124]

d(kop pen, tw) = min((Lat kop pen,i − 0.25 − Lat tw )2 + (Lon kop pen,i + 0.25 − Lon tw )2 ) [SOURCE: Page_124]

For elevation, temperature, and precipitation, the data are provided in a .tif file from Karger et al. (2017). The files are read using the rast function from the R package terra and the values corresponding to the location of the case studies tw are extracted using the extract function from the R package raster. [SOURCE: Page_124]

Substep b: Conventions of equivalence, identification of relevant grouping variables and attributes We have obtained the following Figures: [SOURCE: Page_125]

• 507 articles from the initial query (title, keywords, abstract). [SOURCE: Page_125]

• 380 articles from the automatic screening of their abstract, depending on the terms searched. The number of publications increases significantly between 2015 and 2019: the median year of the search period (1995-2022) is 2017 (general description in Figure 5.3). [SOURCE: Page_125]

• 291 articles from an automatic screening of their pdf. The script scans the pdf files and counts the number of defined terms. This resulted in about 100 papers being rejected. This script can lead to false rejections ("false negatives") due to an illegible format for screening or for the Figures. The pa- pers wrongly accepted ("false positives") concerned inadequate systems, specific types of wastewater or pollutants, missing values or absolute values, absence of units or elements that allow a posteriori calculation: dimensions, flow rates, concentrations. [SOURCE: Page_125]

• 68 articles after a complete reading. The final number of studies selected was low compared to the initial number of case studies, due to insufficient information on designs and contexts. Let’s remember that the aim here is to build a dataset for modelling purposes, not just to report on removal performance. Some studies dealt with both types of TW, so we ended up using 54 papers to build the HF wetland dataset and 31 papers for the VF wetland dataset. [SOURCE: Page_125]

To what extent are the case studies comparable? According to which criteria can they be aggregated? The definition of the scope, the collection and the analysis of the data were based on a definition of the enti- ties to be studied by identifying the characteristics that make them similar and different, i.e. the categories of equivalence (Desrosières, 2006, 1992). Categorisation consists of both a taxonomic operation (defining common features) and an identification operation (assigning observations to categories), the latter being the basis for data validation. We have adopted the following conventions, in particular from the work on developing an ontology in the previous chapter: [SOURCE: Page_125]

Wastewater taxonomic operation Wastewater types were differentiated based on the source or treatment step from which the wastewater originated. Water categories were grouped under the following names [SOURCE: Page_125]

• Raw waste water: any type of waste water from household, domestic, residential, pilot or waste water treatment plants without any treatment stage. [SOURCE: Page_125]

• Primary treated waste water: any type of raw waste water that has also undergone a first stage of any type of primary treatment or pre-treatment. Primary treatment includes sedimentation, septic tank, Imhoff tank, upflow anaerobic filter and sludge blanket, and anaerobic pond. [SOURCE: Page_125]

• Secondary treated waste water: no distinction was made between the different secondary treatments. [SOURCE: Page_125]

The data have been homogenised by converting the pollutant concentrations to their N and P equiva- lents where appropriate (Table 5.2). [SOURCE: Page_126]

Wastewater identification operation The conformity of the wastewater composition to the type to which it should belong is assessed by checking the concentrations and typical concentration ratios between pollutants. We have compiled and defined as expert knowledge the concentration intervals of the differ- ent pollutants and their ratio intervals (Figures 5.4 and 5.5) defined by the following authors: Canler and Perret (2007) for secondary wastewater (wastewater treated by activated sludge); Henze et al. (2008) for ur- ban wastewater; Mercoiret (2009) with 10000 observations from WWTPs throughout France; and Hauduc (2011) with 10 observations from WWTPs throughout the world. Interestingly, the COD:BOD ratio is re- ported to be between 0.5 and 3, meaning that BOD can be (up to twice) higher than COD measurements. This contradicts the fact that COD should be higher than BOD and may be due to the imprecision of the BOD measurement method. [SOURCE: Page_126]

Treatment Wetlands From an engineering perspective, treatment wetlands have been divided into vertical and horizontal types based on the direction of water flow within the medium (Fonder and Headley, 2013). We have retained this classification, i.e. HF and VF wetlands differ in the direction of flow, sub- [SOURCE: Page_126]

strate granulometry and number of parallel beds alternately fed. This distinction between HF and VF wetlands is mainly justified by the different processes taking place, which result in different NH$_4$ removal performances, as shown in Table 2.2. The scope was limited to total areas greater than 1 m^2 and included different scales: pilot, household, pilot-household and WWTP. A series of multiple treatment wetlands was sometimes referred to as a single treatment wetland system. However, we considered each stage individu- ally, with reference to its specific position within the treatment train. Treatment wetlands substrates were grouped into more global categories based on the composition of the main layer: [SOURCE: Page_127]

• Sand: any type of sand [SOURCE: Page_127]

• Gravel: any type of gravel, limestone [SOURCE: Page_127]

• Granules: ceramsite, Leca [SOURCE: Page_127]

• Other minerals: tuff, slag, tezontle [SOURCE: Page_127]

• Other organics: sphagnum, soil, mulch [SOURCE: Page_127]

• Unknown: when the substrate was not mentioned. [SOURCE: Page_127]

Variables were grouped according to the common category of reference: [SOURCE: Page_127]

• Scale: length, inflow rate, depth, HLR, HRT, total surface area [SOURCE: Page_127]

• Design: nominal surface area, nominal cross-subsection [SOURCE: Page_127]

• Climate: air temperature, inflow water temperature, precipitation, altitude [SOURCE: Page_127]

• Water: inflow conductivity, inflow pH [SOURCE: Page_127]

• Substrate: porosity, minimum granulometry, delta granulometry [SOURCE: Page_127]

• Inflow concentrations: expressed in mean concentration of the 6 pollutants [SOURCE: Page_127]

• Removal performances: for all 6 pollutants. [SOURCE: Page_128]

Most studies cover a long period of time and only report average values of measured concentrations. The term ’observation’ is used here to refer to the average of the concentration measurements reported for a given pollutant, while ’sampling campaign’ refers to the period covered by a given study. No dis- tinction has been made between grab (punctual) and composite (averaged) samples. Where available, the standard deviation, median, minimum and maximum values were all recorded. After defining the equiva- lence categories, both stored datasets contained a majority of Treatment wetlands used for primary treated wastewater: 62 HF wetlands (with 68 sampling conditions) and 33 VF wetlands (with 37 conditions). 12 HF wetlands (30 sampling events) and 10 VF wetlands (13 sampling events) were for raw sewage treat- ment (Figure 5.6). BOD was reported in 87% and 82% of the sampling reports for HF and VF wetlands respectively, while COD was reported in 86% and 76%, NH$_4$ -N in 49% and 91%, TN in 56% and 69%, TP in 43% and 31% and TSS in 74% and 76% (5.8). NH$_4$ -N is more frequently reported for VF wetlands than HF wetlands, as they are expected to achieve high removals, and TP is less frequently measured overall, as Treatment wetlands are not designed for removal and regulations only consider thresholds for eutrophication sensitive areas. Nevertheless, it may be useful to measure TP from the perspective of reuse of treated wastewater. [SOURCE: Page_128]
