5.4      Data validation Good or bad? Normal or pathological? Categorisation is not always clear-cut, which led Canguilhem (1966) to introduce the idea of a continuum in medical and health assessment. In this vision, setting a threshold between typical and outlier seems arbitrary. The continuum approach is interesting to smoothen thresh- olds beetween quality categories for data quality of water measurements and this will guide the following. Which observations are abnormal? This synonym for outlier is misleading because it could implicitly imply that the observation is outside a norm that would follow a normal distribution 3 . The main characteristic of the concentrations of constituents reported in the case studies was the mean, followed by the standard deviation, and rarely the median, minimum or maximum. In the case of the mean concentrations of pol- lutants measured in waste water, it can be seen that in most cases the mean was higher than the median. Oliveira et al. (2012) actually observed that influent and effluent concentrations for several treatment sys- tems followed a lognormal distribution, although the Treatment wetlands were not investigated. [SOURCE: Page_129]

More than 60 observations were collected for each constituent, except for TP, which consisted of 44 observations. This amount of data was considered sufficient to model a distribution based on the mean concentrations observed in the influent primary treated wastewater. Our analysis revealed a positively skewed distribution, an aspect that could be partly attributed to the inherent constraint that concentra- tions must have positive values. Consequently, this constraint inherently results in a scenario where the median is consistently smaller than the mean concentration (Figure 5.9). This mean-median difference suggests that over 50% of the time the treatment wetlands operate at concentrations below the mean. The Shapiro-Wilk test led to the conclusion that the resulting data set is unlikely to be observed if the parent population is normal with an alpha risk of 5% for all constituents (H$_0$: ”The distribution is not significantly different from a normal distribution”). This observation highlights that the use of statistical tools based on symmetry and normality hypotheses that do not fit the data set reduces their reliability. We graphically conclude the same observation from the distributions of pollutant concentrations from HF and VF wetland effluents, which were not considered by Oliveira et al. (2012). [SOURCE: Page_129]

Conceptually, we can conclude on the lognormal distribution from the principle of proportional effects: the mean concentrations C can be decomposed as C n = X n X n−1 ...X 2 X 1 C 0 , a product of n independent ran- dom events (degradation, dilutions, etc.) with yields X i undergone by an initial concentration C 0 . From the central limit theorem, log(C n ) = log(C 0 ) + Σni=1 log(X i ) follows a normal distribution, and thereby we deduce that C n follows a lognormal distribution. [SOURCE: Page_129]

5.4.1 Step 3. Error detection Especially in the Treatment wetlands field, experimental data are expensive and results vary with the methodology. The risk of heterogeneous and scarce observations hindering proper data analysis requires data quality checks. We have defined data reliability checks by questioning the extent to which the obser- vations meet certain criteria and then assigning quality weights, labels and flags to the observations. 3 A normal distribution is notably assumed on the population when performing a Z-score or a Chauvenet criterion test. [SOURCE: Page_129]

106 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_129]

Figure 5.9: Distribution of mean pollutant concentrations in primary treated wastewater (solid vertical line: mean value, dashed vertical line: median value, dark blue curve: fitted lognormal distribution) [SOURCE: Page_130]

Substep a: Identification of key factors and indicators We identified the following key factors that should be checked for quality: [SOURCE: Page_130]

• Type of inflow wastewater. It seems relevant to check the adequacy between the taxonomic operation (type of wastewater indicated) and the identification operation (composition). We have used the typical concentration and ratio ranges as indicators. [SOURCE: Page_130]

• Concentration measurements. When measuring the concentrations of several organic carbon, nitro- gen or phosphorus constituents, there may be inconsistencies between the results of the measure- ment methods. Based on the constituents physical inequalities, their concentrations should be used as indicators. [SOURCE: Page_130]

• Water composition. The case studies are considered together as a global population of regionally and spatially distinct and independent subpopulations. Because humans have similar metabolic and domestic activities, the water characteristics are assumed to follow similar patterns (presence of constituents). Concentration has been chosen as the indicator. [SOURCE: Page_130]

Substep b: Construction of checks and metrics We decided to base our distinction of outliers and faults from good values on the following three checks, opting for a continuous representation of values. Two types of output were derived: the probability of ob- taining such a value, and an associated label for better visualisation. [SOURCE: Page_130]

Accuracy Check - inflow Water Type and Concentration Two checks have been defined. For each pollutant and ratio of pollutants, the values were compared with the typical concentration and ratio ranges defined by the experts in (5.4) and (5.5). The closeness to the expected true values could thus be assessed for each type of wastewater, with outliers being furthest from the reference values. [SOURCE: Page_130]

• To fit a law, we assumed that the expert min-max intervals comprised 90% of the distribution. [SOURCE: Page_130]

• The probability thresholds for quality labelling were defined so that the tolerant range covered 95% of the distribution [0.025, 0.975], while the stringent range covered 90% of the distribution [0.05, 0.95]. [SOURCE: Page_130]

Concentrations [SOURCE: Page_130]

• We fitted a lognormal distribution LogN (µ, σ2 ) to the expert data (5.4) for each pollutant to represent the concentration distribution. [SOURCE: Page_130]

107 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_130]

• We optimised σ so that P[C < min] ∼ 0.05 and 1 − P[C < max] ∼ 0.05, i.e. using R, the value that minimises the distance: abs(plnorm(min, µ, σ) − 0.05) + abs(1 − plnorm(max, µ, σ) − 0.05), where µ = 2 log(median), otherwise log(mean) − σ2 , or if none is available, log( min+2 max ). [SOURCE: Page_131]

• We computed the probability of getting each observation value or higher according to the fitted dis- tribution. [SOURCE: Page_131]

• We labelled cases as unlikely if they were outside the tolerant range, or unusual if they were outside the stringent range. The output was called quality concentration. [SOURCE: Page_131]

Ratios [SOURCE: Page_131]

• A normal distribution N (µ, σ2 ) was fitted to the expert data (5.5) for each ratio to represent the ratio distribution. [SOURCE: Page_131]

• We optimised σ so that P[ratio < min] ∼ 0.05 and 1 − P[ratio < max] ∼ 0.05, i.e. using R, the value that minimises the distance: abs(pnorm(min, µ, σ) − 0.05) + abs(1 − pnorm(max, µ, σ) − 0.05), where µ = mean, otherwise median or, if none exists, min+2 max . [SOURCE: Page_131]

• We have calculated the probability of obtaining the ratio value or higher according to the fitted dis- tribution. [SOURCE: Page_131]

• For each pollutant, we calculated the proportion of checks that were in both the tolerant and stringent ranges from the ratios that applied specifically to it. [SOURCE: Page_131]

• We labelled cases unlikely if more than half of the tolerant checks or more than 0.8 of the stringent checks were not validated, or unusual if more than 0.2 of the tolerant checks or more than half of the stringent checks were invalidated. The output was called quality water type. [SOURCE: Page_131]

Consistency Check - Quality Measure (in/out) We checked that the measured concentrations satisfied the following physical inequalities of the form C tot > ΣC i . We then weakened the checks to simpler ones (by removing pollutants, replacing TKN by TN which is more global) to keep the checks working in case not all pollutants were measured: [SOURCE: Page_131]

• Organic carbonaceous components: [COD] > [BOD] [SOURCE: Page_131]

• Reduced nitrogen components: [TK N] > [N H$_4$ − N] + [N H$_3$ − N] and [T N] > [N H$_4$ − N] + [N H$_3$ − N], [T N] > [N H$_4$ − N], [T N] > [N H$_3$ − N] [SOURCE: Page_131]

• Oxidised nitrogen components: [T N] ∼ [TK N] + [NO$_3$ − N] + [NO$_2$ − N] and [T N] > [NO$_3$ − N] + [NO$_2$ − N], [T N] > [NO$_3$ − N], [T N] > [NO$_2$ − N] [SOURCE: Page_131]

• Phosphorus components: [TP] > [PO$_4$ − P] [SOURCE: Page_131]

To fit a law, we considered a one-sided test that identifies when C tot < ΣC i and assumed that 90% of unverified inequalities should be contained in the interval of differences [0, gap], setting gap = 0.1C tot . [SOURCE: Page_131]

We defined the probability thresholds for the quality labels so that the tolerant threshold included 95% of the values and the stringent threshold included 90% of the values. [SOURCE: Page_131]

• We fitted an exponential distribution Exp(λ) for each pollutant C tot to represent the distribution of unverified inequalities. [SOURCE: Page_131]

• We optimised λ so that P[di f f erence < gap] ∼ 0.9, i.e. using R, the value that minimises the dis- tance: abs(pexp(gap, λ) − 0.9). [SOURCE: Page_131]

• We computed the probability of obtaining each difference or higher according to the fitted distribu- tion. The verified inequalities reach P = 1. [SOURCE: Page_131]

• For each component, from the inequalities that apply specifically to it, we calculated the number of checks that meet both the tolerant and the stringent ranges. [SOURCE: Page_131]

• We labelled cases as unlikely if at least one tolerant check was not validated and as unusual if at least one stringent check was not validated. These cases may be evidence of a faulty measurement method or choice of equipment. The outputs were called quality measure in and quality measure out. [SOURCE: Page_131]

108 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_131]

Plausibility Check - Chauvenet (in/out) We statistically assessed whether a given concentration value, taken from the set of all inlet or out- let concentrations, was likely to be erroneous. This check is similar to the concentration accuracy check, except that no external expert knowledge is introduced. In particular, we used this check to compensate for the lack of expert data for primary treated effluent. We used the Chauvenet criterion, initially defined for an assumed normal distribution. This assumption could not be made for the chemical concentrations in the effluent. After plotting the distribution of cases for each constituent, we observed a positive skew- ness, the output of the normality test, and the range of definition with positive values. It was decided to fit a lognormal distribution LogN (µ, σ2 ) to the data (Oliveira et al., 2012; Von Sperling et al., 2020). Therefore, for a given component at concentration C i in the dataset, the associated probability PC i is PC i = 1 − P logN [C < C i ]. The limited number of observations does not provide a statistical basis for the raw sewage study. However, we can derive a similar conclusion from the theoretical approach of the principle of proportional effects, as based on the central limit theorem. [SOURCE: Page_132]

Unusual values were defined only on the right tail of the distributions, with: • a stringent threshold at 0.1 probability of occurrence, • a tolerant threshold at 0.05 probability of occurrence. We labelled cases unusual if their probability PC i was less than 0.1 and unlikely if their probability was less than 0.05. The outputs were called Chauvenet compliance and Chauvenet out compliance. [SOURCE: Page_132]

We additionally applied this check to the operating condition scale to assess the homogeneity of the surface HLR values by fitting a lognormal distribution to the data. The output was called Compliance Chauvenet HLR surface. [SOURCE: Page_132]

5.4.2 Step 4. Data quality categorisation and concatenation The data validation methodology is linear. In practice, iterations and jumps back into the workflow have been necessary to adjust the choice of equivalence categories or the definition of checks. We defined cat- egories to facilitate the visualisation of the results, but the probabilities obtained for each check serve as a quantitative measure of trustworthiness that is easier to use as a weight for subsequent data quality weighted modelling. This quantification also avoids discarding too many or too few data points due to dichotomous labelling. [SOURCE: Page_132]

Substep a: Construction of label categories For the quality flag, the number of labels was kept to three, with a terminology related to the modelling perspective found in (?), plus a fourth if the checks could not be applied: • good (fit for use) when observations complied with stringent checks, else • doubtful (questionable) when observations complied with tolerant checks, else • unsuitable (unfit for use) and • unchecked when the checks could not be applied. [SOURCE: Page_132]

Substep b: Concatenation of checks The existence of multiple outputs for a given check and observation, and of multiple checks for each obser- vation leads to the need to concatenate them. We chose the following rules to move on to the categorical approach: • Per observation: the results of the different checks were concatenated into a quality flag by taking the worst result per observation: unlikely yielded unsuitable, unusual yielded doubtful, probable yielded good. The label unchecked was not considered in the concatenation. [SOURCE: Page_132]

• The flags of the different observations were further concatenated into a single flag per sampling campaign. We calculated the proportion of unsuitable and doubtful flags and labelled the sampling campaign as unsuitable if more than half of the flags were unsuitable or more than 0.8 of the flags were doubtful, otherwise as doubtful if more than 0.2 of the flags were unsuitable or more than half of the flags were doubtful. [SOURCE: Page_132]

109 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_132]

At the observation level, we have chosen to concatenate with the most conservative label. However, this doesn’t lead to a fine discrimination, as two observations can get the same flag despite having different proportions of this worst label. Other possibilities are to take the mean, the weighted sum or the median of the checks. The weighted sum is interesting when special indicators or key factors are to be prioritised. [SOURCE: Page_133]

5.4.3      Step 5. Data reconciliation Data reconciliation, in particular the treatment of missing data, is an optional step in data processing. [SOURCE: Page_133]

Substep a: Handling of missing data - Data imputation The main variables with missing data concern the sampling conditions and the substrate layers of the TW (missing more than half of the time), followed to a much lesser extent by width and length (missing about 20% of the time), see Figure 5.10. Nutrients are also less frequently investigated in this dataset. [SOURCE: Page_133]

Figure 5.10: Proportion of missing data per variable and per sampling campaign. [SOURCE: Page_133]

Missing data were handled for clustering and multivariate analysis, and ideally not for models, as such handling steps lead to higher artificial correlations between variables. For a small, non-time series and heterogeneous dataset, we considered imputation of missing data rather than other methods (interpola- tion, removal, replacement), which could lead to biased estimates and underestimation of uncertainty. We considered data to be missing at random (MAR), as missing data are not randomly distributed across vari- ables, but are randomly distributed for each variable across case studies. More specifically, we assumed that there is no explanatory factor for the occurrence of missing data for a given variable, and that the full imputed dataset would follow similar observed distributions. We used the predictive mean matching method from the MICE package (Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011; van Buuren, 2018). This method randomly draws a value from the distribution of observed values for each missing data, as determined by an adjustable set of predictor variables (Figure 5.11). [SOURCE: Page_133]

We have generated an imputed dataset with additional constraints to ensure that plausible values are imputed. [SOURCE: Page_133]

• For clustering: we considered a subset of the common datasets of HF and VF wetlands as primary and secondary treatment. It consists of the influent concentrations of BOD, COD, NH$_4$ -N, TN, TP and TSS. We imputed the unmeasured influent concentrations per sampling campaign and iterated the process on the imputed values that yielded unsuitable labels during the consistency/accuracy check. [SOURCE: Page_133]

• For multivariate analyses, we imputed the full datasets separately for HF and VF wetlands as sec- ondary treatment. Predictor variables were chosen to either precede them chronologically or to be considered constant with respect to the predicted variables (Figure 5.11). [SOURCE: Page_133]

For variables with few observations, there is considerable variability between imputed datasets in terms of sampling conditions. The imputation method leads to higher correlations between certain vari- ables, but we considered this approach more realistic than others (van Buuren, 2018). In particular, the generation of multiple imputed datasets (see densities of imputed concentrations in Figure 5.12) allows the handling of uncertainty and its incorporation into modelling. [SOURCE: Page_133]

Figure 5.12: Density distributions of MICE concentration datasets after imputation (n=5, red lines) and before imputation, with observed values (blue line), units: mg/L [SOURCE: Page_135]

Substep b: Handling of faulty values and outliers We assessed the information, proportion and leverage of the data marked as unsuitable. We did not modify or remove incorrect values or outliers, as it has been highlighted that process-based corrections can also introduce bias, as described by Villez (2017). However, for better visualisation, the unsuitable values were removed from the dataset. For modelling purposes, we chose to discard values that were considered isolated for the inflow rate and surface area variables, i.e. when there was a gap of the order of magnitude between the values and the rest of the data. We excluded an accuracy check for the identification of the scale categories based on inflow rates and surface areas, but performed a plausibility check on the HLR. Given a sufficiently large and homogeneous dataset, ’outliers’ could be identified using the Chauvenet criterion. The outliers should be discarded, as they can have a high leverage on the fitting of a statistical model and greatly alter its domain of definition, but the very low values of the quality weights would avoid the need to remove them. [SOURCE: Page_135]

5.5      Knowledge extraction 5.5.1      Step 6. Data description and multivariate analysis Substep a: Impact of quality categories [SOURCE: Page_136]

Expert knowledge The expert knowledge gathered for the wastewater type identification operation presents overlapping criteria between the defined equivalence categories (5.4 and 5.5). These blurred boundaries for the con- centration and ratio criteria indicate a potential use in the detection of unrealistic values, but remain insufficient for the identification of a wastewater type a posteriori. We then assessed the correspondence between the water types and the clusters obtained with imputed data by performing bottom-up hierarchical clustering, from the factoextra package, (Kassambara and Mundt, 2020). We compared the use of a Eu- clidean metric (usual) and a Pearson metric (similarity between observations) on influent wastewater, with k = 2 clusters, on the sampling campaign dataset composed of influent raw and primary treated concen- trations (5.13). The taxonomic operation also shows an overlap between raw and primary treated effluent (4 th graph). The method with the Euclidean metric discriminated mainly between low and high concentra- tion values, whereas the method with the Pearson metric differentiated the dataset into clusters showing greater similarity to the classification between raw and primary treated wastewater. The correspondence between Pearson and the real classifications suggests that the relationships between pollutants are in- volved in the discrimination of wastewater types. The algorithm assigned 30 out of 42 raw wastewater sampling campaigns to cluster 1, but only 49 out of 103 primary treated wastewater campaigns to cluster 2. The taxonomic and identification definitions of the wastewater types allow only weak discrimination. The equivalence categories for the scale do not correspond to the clusters and also overlap, indicating that the composition of the effluents did not vary between the scales. However, the pilot scale showed only lower concentrations. [SOURCE: Page_136]

Figure 5.13: Clusters obtained and real labels for one imputed concentration dataset for inflow raw and primary-treated wastewater samplings, with k = 2 clusters. The identified Pearson cluster 1 seems to cor- respond to the primary wastewater group, while the identified Pearson cluster 2 seems to correspond to the raw wastewater group. The Euclidean and Pearson metrics were compared to define the distances for the clustering method, both with and without additional variables corresponding to the ratios. The concentrations have been scaled. [SOURCE: Page_136]

It was difficult to obtain expert knowledge to use as a reference. In particular, the concentration range check could not be performed for primary treated effluent due to a lack of expert knowledge. Our accuracy and consistency checks were also based on weak assumptions regarding the choice of thresholds and dis- tributions of concentrations, ratios and measurement gaps. The expert knowledge used was mainly based on European practices. The composition, volume and concentrations of wastewater can vary considerably depending on the water use. Indeed, water production varies between regions: for example, 209.5 m^3 .yr −1 per capita in North America vs. 67.6 in Latin America and the Caribbean (Jones et al., 2021). The typical values and ranges used to compare case studies may be irrelevant. The scope and thresholds determined from the expert knowledge may influence the categorisation of the data quality. In particular, some very [SOURCE: Page_136]

113 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_136]

high mean influent concentrations (BOD, COD, TN) corresponded to a snowy, humid, warm summer cli- mate (Dfb) and were also labelled doubtful or unsuitable during the plausibility check using the Chauvenet criterion. These may not be outliers, but rather typical cases in the corresponding regions (India, Nepal and Poland), where lower water use and volume lead to higher concentrations. The performance in iden- tifying ’outliers’ for the expert checks thus increases both with the homogeneity of the dataset and with the closeness to the domain of expert knowledge. In other words, the power of our checks increases when applied to sub-populations. When applied to a context larger than the reference, the reliability of the tests decreases. A single statistic applied to a large scope is not as efficient at detecting outliers. [SOURCE: Page_137]

The following discussion only presents results for the second imputed dataset from the application of the MICE method. For HF wetlands, our imputation using the modified predictor matrix showed fewer changes in the initial correlation matrix (presence of correlations and value) compared to the standard pre- dictor matrix. The removal of inappropriate values resulted in a reduction of some of the weaker correla- tions (Figure C.2). For VF wetlands, the modified matrix also resulted in fewer changes, namely weakened strong correlations and strengthened weak correlations. The removal of inappropriate values weakened strong correlations for the original non-imputed dataset. [SOURCE: Page_137]

Quality categories We found that primary treatment wetlands have a higher proportion of unsuitable flags than secondary treatment wetlands due to the possibility of performing an additional check on inflow concentrations. For the water type check, half of the ratios are unsuitable for HF wetlands, while almost a third of the ra- tios and concentrations are unsuitable for VF wetlands. As water uses and compositions and treatment technologies vary around the world, the water categories (or their boundaries) established from a given reference may become obsolete, i.e. their use would be inappropriate to extrapolate to a different context. [SOURCE: Page_137]

The categorisation process resulted in 33% of HF as primary treatment and 21% of HF as secondary treatment being labelled as unsuitable, together with 35% of VF as primary treatment and 19% of VF as secondary treatment, as shown in 5.14. The final quality indicator, i.e. the flag, is highly dependent on the elements and the method used for concatenation. The data validation methodology resulted in the poten- tial rejection of up to one third of the observations (unsuitable, in red) for some of the constituents (5.8). The accuracy check on the water type (ratios) resulted in most of the unsuitable flags, in particular more than half for TSS in HF wetlands, which could be due to the single tested ratio COD:TSS with a narrow expert range, followed by the plausibility check using the Chauvenet criterion. The studies do not always monitor the full set of constituents or pollutants of the same family; therefore, in most cases, checks on the measurement quality could not be performed (see checks in Figures 5.14 and 5.15 for details per pollutant and label). Meanwhile, the consistency check of the measurements was hardly limiting (Figures 5.14 and for details 5.15). For the water type, NH$_4$ -N was almost never checked, while for the measurements, the main relationship checked was BOD < COD. We did not find any expert knowledge for the check of the quality concentration for primary treated wastewater, which could mean that there is no agreed standard because "primary treated wastewater" covers too many cases (variability in the composition of the raw wastewater, variability in the process used for primary treatment). Let’s also note that for the quality control of the water type, the references and the distribution chosen may not be adequate, since they lead to the classification of more than half of our observations as "doubtful" for COD and "unsuitable" for TSS. The correspondence between scores and flags is not so obvious from Figure 5.16. [SOURCE: Page_137]

nota bene 6. Comparison of Chauvenet criterion and Z-score, which is more often employed, is available in the Appendix C.3. [SOURCE: Page_137]

Treatment performances Figure 5.18 shows a plot of removal performance against climate type, according to the usual removal performance (Table 2.2). Climates, differentiated and correlated with precipitation and air temperature (see Figure in Appendix C.2, C.2), can directly influence the natural processes occurring in TW. We have also observed lower or extreme removal performance in HF wetlands associated with unsuitable labels for the following climates: [SOURCE: Page_137]

• Aw : Tropical savanna with dry winter, for cases in the USA (25°C), [SOURCE: Page_137]

We performed a multivariate exploratory analysis of the dataset to identify pairwise correlations and potential causality. We included removal performance and Flag as supplemen- tary variables. To facilitate data visualisation and interpretation, we used two methods from the Fac- toMineR package (Lê et al., 2008): [SOURCE: Page_139]

• MFA (Multiple Factor Analysis): We grouped the variables from the correlation plots under a common reference (climate, design, inflow concentrations, scale, water). MFA weights the variables within each group. [SOURCE: Page_140]

• PCA (Principal Component Analysis): We used the variables from the correlation plots, removing one of the pairwise highly correlated variables to avoid multicollinearity. PCA gives the amount of variance explained for numerical variables. [SOURCE: Page_140]

Using MFA, 36% and 40% of the variance in the datasets can be explained by the first two principal components (Figure 5.19). Variables within a common group are generally correlated. Removal perfor- mance tends to follow inflow concentrations. For HF wetlands, the variables that mainly contributed to PC$_1$ are related to climate, design and inflow concentrations, while those that mainly contributed to PC$_2$ are related to scale, substrate and water characteristics (pH and conductivity). PC$_3$ contains 12% of the variance explained by substrate, water and scale, and PC$_4$ contains 11%, mainly explained by water. For VF wetlands, climate, design and inflow concentrations mainly contribute to PC$_1$, while design and scale mainly contribute to PC$_2$. Interestingly, the corresponding quantitative variables used for substrate and scale did not discriminate between the different categories (Figure C.2). PC$_3$ accounts for 11% of the vari- ance explained by substrate and climate, and PC$_4$ accounts for 10%, mainly explained by substrate. [SOURCE: Page_140]

The removal performances (red) are generally correlated with each other and with the influent concen- trations. In the case of the HF wetland, the N-k-C model, a simplified representation of hydraulics and pollutant kinetics, already includes this correlation, with the presence of a residual background concentra- ∗ tion C ∗ such that it increases with inflow concentration, while the fraction CC decreases with increasing in inflow concentration (Kadlec and Wallace, 2009). The short length of the red arrows for NH$_4$ and TP in 5.20 indicates low correlations with the principal components and corresponding variables. For HF wetlands, the removal performances are aligned along PC$_1$, to which the design variables contribute most. Thus, the greater the nominal surface area and cross-sectional area (i.e., the greater the area per unit inflow volume), the greater the removal performance. For VF wetlands, depth and nominal cross-sectional area contribute most to PC$_2$. Air temperature and precipitation are negatively correlated and uncorrelated with removal perfor- mance. Conversely, it is well known that air temperature is positively correlated with and enhances the reaction kinetics, as reflected in particular in the kinetic removal rate k as a simplified expression of the Arrhenius law in (Von Sperling et al., 2023; von Sperling et al., 2023; Kadlec and Wallace, 2009). [SOURCE: Page_142]

Confounding factor The nominal surface area (divided by the inflow rate) is negatively correlated with air temperature (as well as with water temperature): from -0.51 with to -0.46 without any unsuitable sampling campaigns for HF wetlands. This correlation with temperature is also visible in the hydraulic retention time: from -0.42 to -0.48 (Figure C.2). We consider that the removal of unsuitable sampling campaigns hardly mod- ifies this correlation. Apart from temperature, larger nominal surface areas (especially long and narrow [SOURCE: Page_142]

119 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_142]

TW) and long HRT improve contaminant removal (Nan et al., 2023). Higher temperature usually improves removal kinetic rates and treatment performance, so the correlation with surface area rather than treat- ment performance suggests a causal relationship: knowing that higher temperature improves treatment performance, the Treatment wetlands design is adjusted accordingly. Aiming for ’standard’ performance, it is possible to under-design the Treatment wetlands in warmer climates, while it is necessary to over-design the Treatment wetlands to compensate for colder climates. Therefore, as the temperature increases, the surface area decreases. However in the data, the fact that the removal performance decreases with higher temperature suggests that the hypothesis does not hold or that the consideration of temperature in the designs was inadequate. For example, the Polish case study has a much higher ratio of surface area to flow rate than other case studies. In this case, the temperature effect is already mitigated by the surface area, which could explain the lack of a clear trend in removal performance by climate type. Air temperature is therefore a confounding factor in the causal relationship between surface area and removal performance. Therefore, the effect of air temperature may have been mitigated (masked) by this design adjustment. [SOURCE: Page_143]

The assumption that the compiled set of treatment wetlands is truly representative may prove to be op- timistic, as many factors actually influence the functioning of treatment wetlands. For modelling purposes, the use of all existing variables would result in an inadequate SFR (or number of degrees of freedom). Further work is required to identify all the characteristics relevant to Treatment wetlands removal perfor- mance. [SOURCE: Page_143]

5.5.2      Data reliability towards data exchange format The data validation applied to Treatment wetlands allowed to consider which elements are critical for the collection, description and comparison of TW. In the context of limited data production and open data visions, the development of a data exchange format is interesting but needs precautions in order not to become unusable. [SOURCE: Page_143]

The importance of metadata To ensure reliability, we only considered peer-reviewed publications, although even then datasets are rarely directly checked. Their DOI, authors and date are available in the supplementary material of the corresponding published paper and in a column of the datasets provided in the R package tw.dataset. The location of the study is also important, especially in uncontrolled conditions such as TW. It may not corre- spond to the location of the corresponding author. National databases and operational reports could also be included to increase the size of our dataset. The quality framework by Gootzen et al. (2023) provides valuable insights for both assessing the quality of data sources and combining datasets for a given context (as defined by a target variable, target population and level of aggregation). This framework considers the following dimensions that would prove useful in our steps 1 and 2: Relevance, Population coverage, Pop- ulation representativeness, Variable validity, Concept stability, Correctability, Recentness, Process timing, Accessibility, Meta-data, and Comparability. [SOURCE: Page_143]

Statistical operations We suggest reporting statistical operations and calibration corrections that occur during raw data pre- processing. In particular, it may be more interesting to present the data in graphs (scatter plots, his- tograms) than to summarise them with the typical metrics (mean, median). As a measure of overall trend, the use of the mean rather than the median or mode has prevailed over time, with a paradigm shift from finding the "true" or "right" value to a more abstract and summary value. In practice, the mean is associ- ated with a normal distribution, i.e. it is interpreted as the most common or normal value assigned to a variable. However, the norm associated with a variable may not actually be a normal distribution; it may be skewed, and the mean may not correspond to a real case. The mean remains interesting as a barycentre for non-normal distributions. When reporting a summary of a dataset, Von Sperling et al. (2020) recommends reporting the standard deviation in parentheses after the mean to avoid implying symmetric dispersion. We also suggest adding the skewness and the number of observations. [SOURCE: Page_143]

Standardised measurements Surface areas were sometimes reported as that of the whole treatment train (consisting of several treat- ment wetlands in series) rather than separately for each stage. As a result, when recalculating the HLR for the operation of first stage HF wetlands, almost all HLR based on surface area with a median of 0.10 m^3 .m−2 .d −1 are above the usual range reported by Cross et al. (2021): 0.02-0.05 m^3 .m−2 .d −1 . The ob- [SOURCE: Page_143]

served median for the HLR based on the cross-sectional area is 1.36 m^3 .m−2 .d −1 . The median OLR based on surface area is 14.24 .m−2 .d −1 for BOD, 31.29 for COD, and many observations are above the typical operating conditions reported by Cross et al. (2021): 8 g BOD .m−2 .d −1 and 20 g COD .m−2 .d −1 . The observed median OLR for TSS is 7.22 .m−2 .d −1 , which is slightly below the typical HF wetland value of 10 g TSS .m−2 .d −1 . The observed median OLR based on cross-sectional area is 169.15 for BOD, which is below the threshold of 250 g BOD .m−2 .d −1 . A few observations rose to 4-10 times the threshold. Conversely, for VF wetlands almost all HLR based on surface area are below the typical value of 0.1 m^3 .m−2 .d −1 , with a median of 0.04. The median area-based OLR for COD is 16.13, which is slightly less than the typical value for VF wetlands of 20 g COD .m−2 .d −1 . [SOURCE: Page_144]

We propose to provide all key elements that allow the calculation of other variables from which they are derived (treatment performance and concentrations, total HLR or HRT and number of beds). We have observed that hydraulic loading rate (HLR) and hydraulic retention time (HRT) are reported in different ways; in most cases the value is divided by the surface area, which suggests (in the case of HF wetlands) its use as a proxy for Treatment wetlands volume to dimension the metric. For HF wetlands, we suggest reporting the HLR calculated for both the surface area and cross-sectional area of each TW, or in the case of multi-stage TW, each first stage, to provide an additional indication of flow rate and tendency to clog. Pucher and Langergraber (2019b) found that HLR was correlated with clogging in the case of VF wetlands. [SOURCE: Page_144]

5.6      Conclusion This work aimed at determining to what extent literature-based data can be aggregated and compared. We have collected and analysed data on the design and treatment performance of HF and VF wetlands for wastewater, using a literature-based approach and a global scope. This literature-based approach as- sumed the consistency across the studies in sampling, extracting and analysing measurements. It also assumed that the variability of measurements over different time periods was of lesser importance than other factors (mean value of concentrations, mean temperatures and location). The size of the dataset ob- tained for this study demonstrated that more information and data should be reported in published results to facilitate interpretation and re-use. With a data-driven modelling perspective, we developed a general 6-step methodology for data quality validation and further illustrated the process on a dataset of HF and VF wetlands. [SOURCE: Page_145]

The assumption of continuity between ’outlier’, ’faulty’ and ’good’ data is a cornerstone of the reasoning process and allows us to better understand the complexity of data validation. The output of the quality assessment is less categorical than the typical good, doubtful and bad labels. The quality output can be directly considered and used as an importance weight for each observation to improve the reliability of data-driven models. In line with this approach, we have analysed some common data handling practices and proposed appropriate indicators, metrics and outputs for greater clarity, comparability and auditabil- ity. The ’automation’ of data validation and quality labelling should not be seen as a way of removing experts from the decision-making process. On the contrary, expert input is needed in the proposed itera- tive data validation workflow. Expert knowledge is needed to identify variables and key factors, to define equivalence categories, to select reference knowledge and thresholds, and to select construct checks and quality categories. Moreover, it should be emphasised that the diversity of case studies limits the power of the quality checks, in particular the scope of the expert knowledge chosen to check a global population of Treatment wetlands may not be as relevant as finer and more localised checks. A better characterisation of subpopulations of Treatment wetlands can contribute to the definition of more reliable quality checks and models. [SOURCE: Page_145]

Despite oversimplified (e.g. rule of thumb) guidelines for Treatment wetlands design, we observed that temperature was already a key factor considered in Treatment wetlands designs to achieve adequate pollution treatment. The correlation-based MFA and PCA visually showed that the removal performance of each pollutant depended on different variables, not only related to the design, but also to climate, system scale, initial wastewater composition and substrate. Finally, we believe that incorporating this quality methodology into research practice will allow for more efficient production and (re)use of experimental data, in addition to more reliable data-driven models and a common data exchange format. [SOURCE: Page_145]

Numerical representation [SOURCE: Page_146]

”Grown-ups love numbers. When you talk to them about a new friend, they never ask you about the essential things. They never say: ’What does his voice sound like? What games does he like best? Does he collect butterflies?’ Instead, they ask: ’How old is he? How much does he weigh? How much does his father earn?’ Only then do they think they know him.” [SOURCE: Page_146]

Antoine de Saint Exupéry, The little prince, 1943 [SOURCE: Page_146]

In the context of the MULTISOURCE project, which proposes to pre-design Nature-based Solutions for new projects, we want to determine to what extent hybrid modelling can reliably improve pre-design predictions. This chapter aims to improve the prediction of individual mechanistic and learning models for steady-state contexts by developing two hybridisation methods: in parallel and in series. In a context of limited available knowledge and data, we test the hypothesis that the hybridisation of mechanistic and learning models provides the best reliability compared to the individual approaches, by relying on both knowledge and data. We first generate synthetic data based on the knowledge obtained on real case-studies, with the objective to equally represent all possible values and combinations of the variables. We identify the conditions for this proof of concept by testing different levels of noise and numbers of observations. We secondly evaluate the individual mechanistic and learning models on the context of horizontal flow treatment wetlands, as a reference to compare the performance of the hybridisation methods. We then determine a weighted sum of the two models which obtains the closest fit with the data. [SOURCE: Page_146]

6.1      Challenges for modelling Model hybridisation has been shown to improve predictions by mobilising multiple mechanistic models, multiple learning models or models of both types. It has been successfully developed based on time se- ries data and for the description of wastewater treatment plants, contaminant concentration predictions (Borzooei et al., 2019; De Jaegher et al., 2021, 2020; Mašić et al., 2017; Quaghebeur et al., 2021, 2020; Ver- haeghe et al., 2024). In the context of treatment wetlands, in the previous Chapter we collected steady state data, and observed that data is scarce and heterogeneous. We are interested in determining to what extent model hybridisation can be applied to our situation and improve treatment wetlands design models. We want to show that combining less complex mechanistic models to data-driven models helps capturing the predictions made by a complex model. The heterogeneity of the dataset in terms of number of observations and parameters available per pollutant, and in terms of dispersion of values may hinder the visualisation of the contribution of a hybrid modelling approach. We therefore propose in this Chapter to first develop and assess hybrid models using a synthetic data set. [SOURCE: Page_148]

6.2      Roadmap Within this chapter, we outlined a workflow designed to integrate mechanistic models with machine learn- ing models that have been trained on synthetic data, as illustrated in Figure 6.1. The creation of the synthetic dataset of inlet concentrations was carefully considered: (i) values were chosen to match the range of those documented in the literature (see Chapter 5), and (ii) the correlation between pollutant concentrations was handled by sampling their ratios instead of sampling each value independently. After generating the dataset of inlet concentrations, it served as input to the reference model developed from the BIO_PORE model (Samsó and Garcia, 2013). It simulates a treatment wetland to predict outflow con- centrations, for all the case studies determined in the synthetic data set. This new data set is used as the reference data, assuming that the complex model can reproduce the data complexity observed in a real dataset. Subsequently, a straightforward mechanistic model, characterised by fewer reactions and less inter-variable interaction, is employed to simulate an incomplete mechanistic estimations. Conversely, a machine learning model is trained for predicting outflow concentrations. The two models are then com- bined with a weight depending on the reliability attributed to the machine learning model. [SOURCE: Page_148]

6.3      Synthetic dataset The collected and validated dataset in Chapter 5 provides information such as the interval range of a variable, its distribution and its correlation with other variables. This served as a foundation for creating a synthetic dataset containing a greater number of samples, thereby avoiding the limitations discussed in Chapter 5. The synthetic dataset regarding treatment wetlands focuses on examining horizontal flow wetlands for wastewater that has undergone primary treatment, encompassing only the concentrations of COD and nitrogenous compounds, as well as the dimensions of length and width, and the rate of inflow. From R package MASS (Ripley and Venables, 2009), we used Latin Hypercube Sampling to generate 200 values so that each range for each variable is sampled equally and the space of combinations is sampled equally overall. To do so, each dimension was divided into 200 intervals in the range [0,1] from which a value (probability) was randomly drawn, see case 2 in Figure 6.2. [SOURCE: Page_148]

6.3.1 Relations Pollutant concentrations are linearly positively correlated with each other and with the design variables. These relationships are quantified by the ratios r i j as seen in Figure 5.5 for the concentrations of X i and X j , such that X i = r i j X j , and r i j tend to follow a normal distribution. From the original data set, which defines the ratios for surface area to inflow rate and width to length, they appear to follow a lognormal distribution. These distributions are fitted to the data and their parameters are stored. We generated a LHS sample (values comprised in [0, 1]) of 10 dimensions corresponding to: COD, COD:BOD, COD:TN, COD:TP, COD:TSS, BOD:NH$_4$, length, nominal surface area (S:Q), and width:length. Then each dimension was transformed to fit to the stored range and density distribution of the corresponding variable, using the LHS values as quantiles: [SOURCE: Page_148]

COD ∼ logN (µ cod , σ cod ) [SOURCE: Page_148]

We used the truncated nor- mal distribution qtruncnorm() function with the boundaries determined using the expert knowledge, see Table 6.1. This avoids too large intervals of values, and allows to indicate that values must not be negative. To ensure the physical consistency that COD > BOD and TN > NH$_4$, we have modified the lower bound of the ratio COD:BOD from 0.5 to 1, and instead of using the ratio BOD:NH$_4$ to deduce NH$_4$, we have used the expert knowledge on the lower and upper bound from NH$_4$:TKN and used them for NH$_4$:TN. 6.4      The mechanistic model: BIO_PORE The BIO_PORE has been developed by Roger Samso within the framework of his PhD thesis (Samsó and Garcia, 2013). It aims at implementing the CWM$_1$ biokinetic model (Langergraber et al., 2009) into COM- SOL Multiphysics®. It solves time-dependent partial differential equations in a 2D domain. The physics taken into account are: (1) the water flow and (2) the transport of solute species which source/sink terms are estimated using the CWM$_1$ biokinetic model. BIO_PORE distinguishes itself from comparable models, such as the HYDRUS Wetland Module (Langergraber and Šimůnek, 2012), by utilising a logistic limita- tion term that restricts bacterial growth according to the available pore space. This feature is especially important for long-term simulation (Samsó and García, 2014). Subsequent advancements have resulted in substituting this logistic constraint with the full integration of the biokinetic and hydraulic models: as bacterial concentration rises in the pore space, the pore radius diminishes, consequently influencing the hydraulic characteristics (Samsó et al., 2016). The current complete BIO_PORE model represents 17 bio- logical processes. [SOURCE: Page_152]

In this study, we focused on major processes involving carbonaceous and nitrogenous fractions, to avoid long simulation runtime. Two simplified versions of the BIO_PORE model are used: [SOURCE: Page_152]

• Model A is the reference model to generate the dataset of observations, [SOURCE: Page_152]

• Model B acts as the oversimplified mechanistic model, which will be completed by the machine learn- ing model to figure out the observations from model A. [SOURCE: Page_152]

Common features to Model A and B are: [SOURCE: Page_152]

hydraulics Richards’ equation: ∂∂t (²P ρ ) + ∇ · (ρ u) = Q m and u = − µκ (∇ p − ρ g), where: ²P is the porosity, ρ the fluid density, µ the dynamic viscosity, κ, and g the gravity constant. ∂ρ c     ∂(ρ c p,i ) transport An equation describing the transport of diluted species in porous media: ²P ∂ tP,i +                         ∂t +∇· Ji + u · ∇ c i = R i + S i and Ji = −(D D,i + D e,i )∇ c i , where: R i is the reaction rate, S i and Ji . [SOURCE: Page_152]

However they vary in their implementation of the CWM$_1$ model used to evaluate the reaction rate R i . [SOURCE: Page_152]

In model A, out of the 17 processes of the CWM$_1$ model we kept 6 of them, namely: (1) hydrolysis, (2) aerobic growth of X H on S F , (3) anoxic growth of X H on S F , (4) lysis of X H , (5) aerobic growth of X A on S N H and (6) lysis of X A , see Figure 6.5. 6.5      Learning models We saw above that there is dispersion between model A outputs and model B outputs. Using the synthetic dataset from model A, we proceed to train and assess machine learning models that offer various meth- ods for identifying relationships among variables, aiming to determine if they improve the explanation of variance using the same features employed by model B. [SOURCE: Page_153]

130 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_153]

6.5.1      Domain of definition Model B presents causal relationships between the output variable and independent variables. Machine learning models identify correlations and patterns within data. However, these differ from causal relation- ships or physical mechanisms. Their structure can be developed to predict surface area directly, although it would not be a dependent variable in terms of chronology and causality. However, to be able to compare and hybridise them with model B and in order to provide some interpretability, we take a causal approach (chronologically, design S causes outflow concentration C and not the reverse). The machine learning mod- els are developed to predict the effluent concentrations. The machine learning models are not inherently designed to predict or infer new cases, but to estimate cases that would fit within the domain of training of these models, i.e. their domain of validity. The domain of validity is shown in Table 6.3. We assume that within this domain, the correlations and patterns will behave similarly for all unmeasured cases. Conse- quently, after developing machine learning models and assuming high-quality data, if the test set produces inaccurate predictions, it may indicate that the models have overfitted the training data or that the new samples fall outside the training framework. [SOURCE: Page_154]

The final dataset with mechanistic results contains 193 observations due to the abortion of some simu- lations in model B. We will provide graphical examples with COD and SNH-N only. [SOURCE: Page_154]

6.5.2      Machine learning models We follow a typical machine learning model development workflow, see Figure 6.7, which corresponds to the definition of machine learning models in the dashed box ”test models” of the general workflow 6.1. We first perform a stratification of the data based on the inflow rate to obtain similar distribution of cases between the training and test sets 3 . These sets represent 80% and 20% of the dataset respectively. The machine learning models are trained on the 80% set in order to determine the optimal combination of hyper-parameters based on the RMSE metric. This tuning step, i.e. the selection of the optimal combina- tion, and the determination of the variability of the model error are achieved using cross validation. The training set is divided into k = 10 folds such that the model is trained on 9 folds, and validated on the last fold, and the process is iterated for each individual fold to be used as the validation set. Then the full process is repeated 5 times. The model selected is the one with the lowest mean RMSE calculated over the test folds, i.e. the one which is most capable to be generalised. A final test of the model is done on the 20% set. 4 We chose a variety of algorithmic structures: [SOURCE: Page_154]

• Tree-based models (Bayesian additive regression trees, eXtreme Gradient Boosting using decision trees, and random forest), which are ensemble models, i.e. they are characterised by the ability to find specific relationships in subsets of data and still propose a global model by aggregating the results, [SOURCE: Page_154]

• k Nearest Neighbours, which is a local method, 3 in practice the range of values is divided into 3 or 4 intervals 4 We set a seed (1000) to control randomness in order to reproduce the results. We implemented functions from the caret R package (Kuhn, 2007, 2008). [SOURCE: Page_154]

The hyperparameters values are given per machine learning model, for COD and SNH-N. [SOURCE: Page_155]

Bayesian additive regression trees The BART model is based on the sum of trees, prior regularisation and Monte Carlo Markov chains, and predicts yi as yi = Σ j g(x i , T j , M j ) + ² i [SOURCE: Page_155]

where Σ is the sum of the regression trees g, the tree models T j are assumed to be independent (for the selection of the splitting variables), and M j is the set of terminal nodes of the tree j, and the residual ² i follows a normal distribution N (0, σ2 ). The prior determines the probability α(1 − d)−β that a node is split for a given tree depth d, with parameters α and β, the distribution on the variable at non-terminal nodes, and the distribution on the rule for node splitting. [SOURCE: Page_155]

The method 5 used is bartMachine. The data are normalised (centred and scaled). The results show a low variance for both training and testing, see Figure 6.8. The hyperparameters and their final values are indicated below (Hyper-parameter: value for COD, value for SNH-N, description, and default value), and we indicated when tuning was performed: [SOURCE: Page_155]

• num trees : 240 (COD), and 160 (SNH-N), tuned between 160 and 240, by 20. The number of trees (weak learners), default : 200. [SOURCE: Page_155]

• k : 2, and 2. The prior boundary, shrinkage, scaling the variance of the terminal node values and controlling the contribution of each tree. [SOURCE: Page_155]

• alpha : 0.95, and 0.95. The base for the prior. Between 0 and 1. [SOURCE: Page_155]

• beta : 2, and 2. The power for the prior. Positive. [SOURCE: Page_155]

• nu : 2, and 4, tuned between 1 and 5 by 1. The number of degrees of freedom, controlling the residual variance. [SOURCE: Page_155]

eXtreme Gradient Boosting using decision trees XGBOOST is an ensemble method based on the aggregation of multiple trees (weak learners), adding trees to improve predictions. The algorithm must minimise the distance between yi and ŷi based on the loss function: L = Σ i l(yi , ŷi ) + Σk Ω( f k ) where L is the loss function, which is the MSE in the case of regression, and Ω is a regularisation term on the complexity of the tree f k and acts as a penalty. Iteratively, L is minimised for f k at the kth iteration. The hyperparameters involved in XGBOOST are associated with 1 Ω( f k ) = γT + λΣ j w^2j 2 where γ and λ (typically not tuned) penalise the complexity and the number of leaves, w j is the weight of the j leaf, and T is the number of leaf nodes in f k . [SOURCE: Page_156]

The method used is xgbTree. Low effluent concentrations are well predicted, but higher values are off and underestimated for both training and test sets, see Figure 6.9. As we can see, the model did not work for S N H , the hyperparameter values are not relevant but may indicate that there has been an issue. The final set of hyperparameters is the following: [SOURCE: Page_156]

• nrounds : 10 (COD), and 10 (S N H ), tuned between 2 and 10 by 2. The number of boosting iterations, default : 6. [SOURCE: Page_156]

• max depth : 10, and 2, tuned between 2 and 10 by 2. The maximum tree depth, default : 6. [SOURCE: Page_156]

• eta : 0.3, and 0.3. The shrinkage (learning rate) of the feature weights (contribution), default : 0.3. Between 0 and 1. [SOURCE: Page_156]

• gamma : 0, and 1. The minimum loss reduction determining the addition of more leaves to trees, default : 0. Positive. [SOURCE: Page_156]

• colsample bytree : 1, and 1. The subsample ratio of features selected to build the trees, default : 1. [SOURCE: Page_156]

• min child weight : 1, and 1. The minimum sum of instance weight, default : 1. [SOURCE: Page_156]

• subsample : 1, and 1. The data subsample percentage selected to build the trees, default : 1. [SOURCE: Page_156]

Random forest Random forest is an ensemble method that aggregates the results of T individual trees f t trained on a subset of features to partition the data, repeatedly for a given depth or minimum node size: 1 ŷi =     Σ t f t (x i ) T The method used is Ranger. The results for COD, see Figure 6.10, are similar to XGBOOST. We used the following hyperparameters: [SOURCE: Page_156]

• mtry : 7 (COD), and 7 (SNH-N), tuned between 3 and 6 by 1. The number of randomly selected predictors at each split in a tree, default : 12. From this default value, we can see that our dataset is too small and does not really correspond to the typical set to model. 5 term used for R package caret, otherwise it is called ’engine’ in tidymodels [SOURCE: Page_156]

Elastic Net This method is based on LASSO (based on the L$_1$ norm) and Ridge (based on the L$_2$ norm) penalised regressions. The algorithm minimises not only the residual squared error (RSS) between the predictions ŷi and the observations yi , but also the RSS summed with an L$_1$ penalty and an L$_2$ penalty on the regression coefficients β i : ¡1−α (βˆ0 , β̂) = ar gmin Σ( yi − ŷi )2 + λ     kβk^22 + αkβk^1 £                                     ¢¤ i                  2 where α is the mixture of L$_1$ and L$_2$ penalties (taking values between 0 and 1), and λ is the proportion of the penalty, divided by 2 for optimisation convenience. [SOURCE: Page_157]

The method used is glmnet. The data are normalised. The fit and predictions are quite poor, with a large residual variance pattern in both cases, see Figure 6.11. The hyperparameters are set as follows: [SOURCE: Page_157]

• alpha : 1, and 0.2, tuned between 0.2 and 1 by 0.2. The mixing percentage, where 1 corresponds to LASSO regression. [SOURCE: Page_157]

• lambda : 0.18, and 0.02, tuned between 0.02 and 1 by 0.02. The regularisation parameter. If this parameter is too great, the model predicts the mean value because all coefficients are shrunk to zero. [SOURCE: Page_157]

k-nearest-neighbours This method aggregates the values of the k nearest neighbours of the new x i : [SOURCE: Page_157]

1 ŷi =     Σ i ynn,i k and the nearest neighbours are determined using the Euclidean distance metric. [SOURCE: Page_157]

The method used is knn. The data are normalised. Both the fit and the predictions are off, see Figure 6.12. Only one hyperparameter is considered: [SOURCE: Page_157]

• k : 7, and 6, tuned between 3 and 9 by 1. The number of neighbours, default : 5. [SOURCE: Page_157]

Figure 6.12: COD and S N H predictions with KNN model [SOURCE: Page_158]

Radial basis function Support Vector Regression SVM handles non-linear relationships when it is based on the Radial Basis Function. This function is a kernel function that measures the similarity between observations x i : [SOURCE: Page_158]

¡ || x^1 − x^2 ||2 ¢ K(x^1 , x^2 ) = exp − 2σ2 where σ is a hyperparameter. [SOURCE: Page_158]

The method used is svmRadial. The data are normalised. The Figure 6.13 shows that the model tends to overfit, with a very good fit for training but a large variance in the prediction of the test set, and in both cases the model tends to drift at higher effluent concentrations, probably due to fewer points to train on. The hyperparameters used are the following: [SOURCE: Page_158]

• sigma : 2, and 2, tuned between 2 and 10 by 2. [SOURCE: Page_158]

• cost : 1, and 1. The cost determines the number of observations that are included in the margin for the contribution to the error, the lower the value, the less penalised the observations. [SOURCE: Page_158]

6.5.3 Selection of best model From the training and test scatter plots in Figures 6.8, 6.9, 6.11, 6.12, 6.10, and 6.13, we observe a good fit for BART and RF models, heteroscedasticity in the predictions for KNN models, GLMNET and SVM models show patterns in the residuals distribution, while XGBOOST presented issues with the data for [SOURCE: Page_158]

135 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_158]

S N H , and overfitting for COD. From the engineering point of view, it may be frustrating that no equation results from these models, but only the hyperparameters and metrics are accessible. Regarding the metrics, only RMSE, MAE and RSQ are computed by the cross validation algorithm, such that there is no standard deviation for MAPE. We computed RMSE, MAPE and RSQ a posteriori for C out predictions, each expressed in a different unit. The metrics take into account the score for both the training and test sets. q RMSE The root mean square error, expressed in mg/L: RMSE = n^1 Σni=1 (yi − ŷi )2 . Its value will be overly influenced by outliers. The lower the better. Pn ¯¯ yi − ŷi ¯¯ MAPE The mean absolute percentage error, expressed in %: M APE = 100         n   i =1 ¯ yi ¯. It is asymmetric, the normalisation avoids the over-influence of high values, but if the data is too close to zero, these values will lead to extremely high MAPE values. Otherwise, values above 100 % indicate that the model is performing poorly. The lower the better. Pn (yi − ŷi )2 RSQ The proportion of variance explained, without units: RSQ = 1 − Pni=1 (y − ȳ )2 . Negative values indicate i =1     i     i that the model performs poorly, worse than a mean-based prediction. The closer to 1 the better. [SOURCE: Page_159]

The metrics are reported for the models applied to the training set, and their standard deviations are reported from the preliminary cross validation step, calculated from the training on the different folds. The results for COD and S N H metrics on the training and test sets are shown in Table 6.4. The differ- ent units and scales lead to difficulties in determining the optimal model. RMSE values seem pretty low, while in truth RMSE values have the same order of magnitude as the mean outflow concentrations of COD (C̄ COD,out = 34.3 mg/L) and S N H (C̄ SN H,out = 0.075 mg/L). The high values of MAPE for GLMNET, SVM and KNN reflect the great residual dispersion along the best fit line in the scatter plots. Overfitting of KNN and SVM is visualised from the RSQ difference between the training set value and the test set value. [SOURCE: Page_159]

Similarly to voting systems, we may not select the same model depending on the method chosen, or even fall into Condorcet paradoxes 6 . Considering COD and S N H results 7 : [SOURCE: Page_159]

• If we consider only the best performing model per metric (see the values in bold), and that training and testing are chronological stages, for COD, BART would be selected by two of the training metrics, although RF predicts better in the test according to the MAPE of the test set. For S N H , either BART or RF models would be selected from the training based on the RMSE, but only BART for the test. [SOURCE: Page_159]

• If we now take the training and test metrics together, we conclude that BART is the optimal model. [SOURCE: Page_159]

• If we look at the first three models, they may not follow the same order depending on the metric chosen. [SOURCE: Page_159]

• We could also set thresholds to discard models: RSQ < 0.4, MAPE > 50 % or RMSE > C out    ¯ . The case where all models are discarded is possible, implying that based on this metric it is not worth using a data-driven approach. [SOURCE: Page_159]

• We could argue that the metrics themselves provide more information than the classification. How- ever, unlike the data quality scores from Chapter 5, which were all probabilities, the metrics here are quantities with different scales and units. The metrics are transformed arbitrarily to have ideal values between 0 and 1, which must be the smallest: RMSE divided by the absolute mean C out , MAPE divided by 100, and 1 minus RSQ. We obtain the ranks by summing the values over the two sets. We obtain BART > RF > GLMNET for COD, and BART > RF > SV M for S N H . Compared to the separate rankings where RF and GLMNET only appeared for one set, they are now part of the final ranking. The scaled metrics from the best tuning can then be compared in Table 6.5 and in Figures 6.14 and 6.15, where standard deviations from the folds are represented as symmetrical bars 8 . Nevertheless, the aggregation of the metrics runs the risk of having compensations between them, similar to the KGE metric 9 . 6 Condorcet paradoxes or Condorcet cycles correspond to situations where there is no transitivity in the preference ordering, for example the models are compared based on three criteria, but each favours a different model, such that the results do not show any favoured model (Gehrlein, 1983) 7 we had different rankings that did not converge unanimously towards a given model for 100 observations, illustrating that the number of observations is a key to the identification of the most adequate model 8 the computation was automatic, variation symmetry may not be the case 9 see Chapter 2 on metrics [SOURCE: Page_159]

We deduce from this example that if the training is not conclusive (e.g. RMSE greater than the order of magnitude of the observations, MAPE close to 100 %, or a negative RSQ), it is not worth considering the results of the test set as they can be misleading. For example, good RSQs have been observed for GLMNET models for COD but they are fortuitous. In our case, the BART and RF models exhibit the best performance. These are ensemble tree-based algorithms, recognized for their ability to effectively capture variance within a dataset. [SOURCE: Page_160]

6.6      Hybridisation of models We notice some remaining variance between the observations (model A) and the forecasts produced by both the mechanistic (model B) and machine learning models. We attribute this variance to insufficient knowledge and data. Therefore, we investigate the combinations of these models to benefit from both modelling approaches. Specifically, we apply parallelisation and serialisation of models, methods commonly described in the state of the art 2. [SOURCE: Page_161]

6.6.1 Models in parallel Parallel hybridisation (Figure 6.16) consists of summing and averaging the predictions of each model. As an evolution, we added a weight or penalty α taking values between 0 and 1, which takes into account the reliability of the machine learning model based on the number of observations used for training and the number of features. [SOURCE: Page_161]

C h ybrid = αC out,ML + (1 − α)C out,mech [SOURCE: Page_161]

C out = αĈ out,ML + (1 − α)C out,mech + ε [SOURCE: Page_161]

α is a weight that corresponds to the reliability of the learning model. However, since the value of α is arbitrary, we investigated how it could be calculated from the available information.ε is the residual variance between the observations C out from model A, and the hybrid model prediction. [SOURCE: Page_161]

mechanistic model,                  ym BIOPORE B [SOURCE: Page_162]

aggregation x^1 , x^2 , ...                                              (weighted    ŷh average) [SOURCE: Page_162]

ML model, BART ŷe [SOURCE: Page_162]

y [SOURCE: Page_162]

Figure 6.16: Representation of a parallel hybridisation for training on (x^1 , x^2 , ..., y) [SOURCE: Page_162]

Optimal α weight [SOURCE: Page_162]

Assuming the training data are reliable, we want the final prediction to be closest to the data. We now optimise α to find the hybrid model with the best fit, measured by RSQ and penalised by the number of degrees of freedom. We want to get the hybrid model that gives the best fit based on least squares, that is find the best weight α to optimise the metric: Σ (C   −Ĉ      )2 ³                        ´ • Nash-Sutcliffe determination coefficient RSQ: max(RSQ) = max 1 − Σi (Cout,i −C̄out,i)2 i   out,i   out [SOURCE: Page_162]

• Mean Squared Error MSE: min(MSE) = n^1 Σni (C out,i − Ĉ out,i )2 . [SOURCE: Page_162]

This is equivalent to looking for α that minimises: Σ i (C out,i − Ĉ out,i )2 [SOURCE: Page_162]

Σ i (C out,i − Ĉ out,i )2 = Σ i (C out,i − αĈ out,ML,i − (1 − α)Ĉ out,mech,i )2 = Σ i (C out,i − Ĉ out,mech,i − α(Ĉ out,ML,i − Ĉ out,mech,i ))2 [SOURCE: Page_162]

Simplifying the notations we set: Σ i (yi )2 = Σ i (z i − α x i )2 [SOURCE: Page_162]

Then, based on the Euclidean norm for vectors, we write the sums in vectorial forms: [SOURCE: Page_162]

Y T Y = (Z − α X )2 = (Z − α X )T (Z − α X ) [SOURCE: Page_162]

Now using vectors, we find α that minimises the term by differentiating it with respect to α and finding α such that the derivative is null: f (α) = (Z − α X )T (Z − α X ) [SOURCE: Page_162]

f 0 (α) = 0 = 2X T (Z − α X ) = 2X T Z − 2α X T X [SOURCE: Page_162]

Hence, [SOURCE: Page_162]

XTZ α= XTX (Ĉ out,ML − Ĉ out,mech )T (C out − Ĉ out,mech ) = (Ĉ out,ML − Ĉ out,mech )T (Ĉ out,ML − Ĉ out,mech ) Σ i (Ĉ out,ML,i − Ĉ out,mech,i )(C out,i − Ĉ out,mech,i ) = Σ i (Ĉ out,ML,i − Ĉ out,mech,i )2 [SOURCE: Page_162]

Scaling the metric [SOURCE: Page_162]

If there is heteroscedasticity (e.g. in the case of predicting outflow loads) such that the residual variance is proportional to the square root of the variable, the influence of high values can be mitigated by scaling, i.e. dividing by the square root of the variable, in a similar way to weighted least squares. [SOURCE: Page_162]

α is defined in such a way that it becomes higher the more data (and therefore degrees of freedom) are available to the learning model and the smaller the distance between predictions and observations (i.e. for the least squares metric: the smaller the (R)MSE or the higher the RSQ). Based on the mechanistic (model B) and ML predictions, we can distinguish the following cases: • If one tends to overpredict and the other tends to underpredict C out , α ∈ [0, 1], • If both tend to either under or over predict C out and model B performs better, α < 0, • If both tend to either under- or over-predict C out , and machine learning performs better, α > 1. nota bene 8. With this expression, α is not restricted to take the values ∈ [0, 1], but we can set it so that if α ≤ 0 we set α = 0 (only the mechanistic model is used) and if α ≥ 1 we set α = 1 (only the learning model is used). [SOURCE: Page_163]

Adjusting with degree of freedom Then we add the same adjustment term as for RSQ ad j to adjust the goodness of fit RSQ, with the number of degrees of freedom (i.e. the amount of data used minus the number of explanatory variables used by the ML models) n − p. If α is constrained ∈ [0, 1], we can use the same expression as for RSQ ad j : n−1 αad j = 1 − (1 − α) n− p−1 else: n− p−1 αad j = α.ad justment = α n−1 Now, the smaller the number of degrees of freedom, the more the adjustment degrades α, hence the smaller the weight given to the learning model. 6.6.2      Model comparison Now, the parallel hybridisation is done between model B and RF, using the adjusted values of α computed above. The results are shown in Figure 6.17. We can visually assess that the ML model does not perform as well as model B for S NO in the test set, which can be explained by the fact that the RF model is not predicting on its domain of training, and is thus extrapolating. The inflow rate is the third smallest of the range, and as seen in Figure 6.6, the outflow concentration of S NO is outside of the prediction range of the training set. The systematic overestimation by model B for COD and underestimation for S NO are compensated by the RF model. For S N H , the ML model is closer to the perfect fit, and the hybrid model avoids the high variation of model B. By focusing on the higher values with S N H , we can observe the clear improvement brought by the addition of the machine learning model. The parallel hybrid model provides a good compromise in both the training and test phases. However, with the current fitted weight, the parallel method may entirely rely on either of the models depending on the reliability attributed to the machine learning model. The difficulty in assessing the performance for S NO lies in the fact that the outflow concentration range covered by both is much larger than for S N H , with fewer high values. For S NO the systematic underfitting of model B is corrected by the hybrid model for the lower values in the test set. The highest value in the test set outflow concentration of S NO appears to be a situation of extrapolation since no value in the CV-training exceeds 60 mg/L. [SOURCE: Page_164]

The efficiency criteria are shown in Table 6.6, and transformed in Figures 6.25 and 6.26. The low values of the residuals lead to difficulties in visualising the low differences between models based on RMSE. BART and RF models best perform for COD and S N H on both the training and the test sets, but with a standard deviation for RMSE which is of similar order of magnitude. The MAPE metric is in relative units and is usually not very relevant when dealing with residuals, because the difference with the predictions (RMSE) can be of a larger order than the residuals, as shown by the extremely high MAPE values all above 100%. Here however, residuals are even larger than the initial observations. For the training set, the Table 6.6 shows that the models perform well on RSQ, but poorly on MAPE, notably for S N H . XGBOOST and GLMNET models did not work for neither COD nor S N H . XGBOOST being based on residual variance, the values for SNH-N may have been too low, and there may have been too many predictors for the LASSO regression. [SOURCE: Page_168]

6.6.4      Model comparison After calculating the serial hybrid model predictions, we observe from the training and test results in Fig- ure 6.27 that for the ML model, reusing the same features as model B to explain the residual variance does improve the predictions of outflow concentrations in the case of S N H . In particular, the underesti- mation tail of model B is compensated by the RF model. Compared to parallel hybridisation, the serial hybridisation relies first on the mechanistic model, whose prediction is then adjusted with the fitted ma- chine learning model on the residuals. This method may thus better ensure the reliability from the point of view of causality from a predictive model to a corrective one. Similarly to the parallel hybridisation, the systematic overestimation of COD and the underestimation of S NO are compensated by the RF model. A slight improvement is observed for S NO , but the initial mechanistic fit from model B was already good. We do not observe any extrapolation shift unlike the parallel hybridisation, because the residual of the isolated and extreme outflow concentration of S NO is still in the training range. [SOURCE: Page_169]

6.7      Influence of data quality and quantity We then trained the data-driven models on altered data with 200, 100 and 50 observations, and with different levels of noise with a standard deviation increasing with the initial observation values by 20, 10 and 5 %. The new observations ynoise are drawn from truncated normal distributions: [SOURCE: Page_170]

C out,noise = C out + ² + ε [SOURCE: Page_170]

ε ∼ N (0, ² yi ) [SOURCE: Page_170]

From the results shown in Figure 6.28 representing the extreme cases of the study, we determine when serial hybrid models are relevant to use: 50 observations are not enough for the model to perform correctly for neither COD (prediction shift) nor S N H (inadequate trend fitted), and 20% of noise in the data leads to the impossibility for the hybrid model to predict S N H precisely. [SOURCE: Page_170]
