6.8      Conclusion In this Chapter, we proposed a theoretical approach to hybrid modelling in the context of treatment wet- lands by generating a synthetic dataset covering equally a set of reduced value ranges observed in the real dataset of the previous chapter. The dataset contained 193 observations and 7 features, and concerned inflow concentrations of COD and nitrogenous fractions. We developed a mechanistic model: model B, as an oversimplified version of the BIO_PORE mechanistic model, and a data-driven model. The random for- est model was selected among multiple machine learning algorithms. Clear residuals patterns show that [SOURCE: Page_171]

148 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_171]

GLMNET models did not provide an adequate relationship for the variables, and KNN and SVM showed a slight overfitting and residuals patterns that may suggest a change of behaviour between low and high outflow concentrations. The results illustrate the observation that tree-based models are generally good structures for modelling due to their ensemble approach. [SOURCE: Page_172]

The selection of the machine learning models was based on the metric RMSE, but multiple metrics are needed to characterise the goodness of the predictions. In particular, the models performance should be assessed based on both the training and the test phases, to avoid overfitting and incorrect variable corre- lations. We saw that the metrics are very sensitive to the data sample, and depending on how they relate predictions and observations, they do not amplify the same residuals. We saw that the standard deviation calculated on the validation folds during cross-validation provides information on the potential variability and future robustness of the model for real predictions. [SOURCE: Page_172]

We developed two types of hybrid models: one which uses the mechanistic and data-driven models in- dependently in parallel, and an other which uses them in series such that the data-driven model is trained on the residual variance between the mechanistic predictions and the observations. From this assumption, we improved the combinations by adding a weight to account for the degree of freedom of the dataset 10 that sets the conditions for a reliable training of machine learning models. We proposed a weighted sum of the individual models results based on the fitting to the training data in the case of parallel models. It implies that if enough quantity and good quality data is gathered, the machine learning model could potentially take over the prediction, such that the hybrid model only relies on a data-driven approach with no causality. This is not the case for the serial model because the hybrid model starts from the prediction of the mechanistic model and modulates it subsequently based on the reliability of the machine learning model. We saw that the domain of training of the models is important: the presence of isolated and ex- treme values in the dataset can lead to overfitting, and the use of a test set that presents values outside of the domain of training leads to extrapolation, which machine learning models are not developed for. From the results, we show that the hybrid models, both the parallel and serial methods, improve the outflow concentration predictions as a regulator of either the mechanistic or the data-driven model. This is a proof of concept with a synthetic dataset, however the values do not correspond to true observations. [SOURCE: Page_172]

10 i.e. the number of observations minus the number of explanatory variables (features) [SOURCE: Page_172]

Chapter 7 [SOURCE: Page_174]

Application of hybrid modelling [SOURCE: Page_174]

”Thoughts without content are empty; intuitions without concepts are blind.” [SOURCE: Page_174]

Immanuel Kant, Critique of Pure Reason, 1781 [SOURCE: Page_174]

The context of treatment wetlands is a typical case of both limited knowledge and data available. We saw previously that hybrid models successfully improve outflow concentration predictions based on syn- thetic data. We now propose an application case using NkC* model (see the State of the art, Chapter 2) as the mechanistic part, and study statistical and machine learning models as the data-driven part. Sta- tistical models are envisaged because machine learning models may be too complex given the number of observations for the phosphorus and nitrogenous compounds. We use the validated dataset from Chapter 5 and include when possible, the information gained from the quality weights in the training of the machine learning models. The global scope and the need to incorporate elements characterising each treatment wetland, wastewater and site, previously obtained from the literature, led us to a different type of dataset than those typically used for wastewater treatment plants. This chapter seeks to investigate the added benefits of model hybridisation by examining the role of additional features in predicting outflow concen- trations. Initially, we assess the standalone mechanistic and learning models applicable to horizontal flow treatment wetlands to serve as a benchmark for evaluating the efficiency of the hybridisation techniques. Then, we use a greater set of features for more complex data-driven models. In a causal approach, the individual models are developed to predict the effluent concentrations. Finally, we propose to estimate the area of treatment wetlands based on treatment objectives and costs, and to consider the uncertainties associated with the models. [SOURCE: Page_174]

7.1      Mechanistic model: NkC* model We saw that the BIO_PORE models provided outflow concentrations that do not correspond to typical values observed. With a more practical approach, we now consider a typical model used for horizontal flow treatment wetland design: the NkC* model, described in Chapter 2. Compared to the model B of Chapter 6.3, the model is less complex and does not require as much time for its simulations. It does not apply to fractions, but to the pollutants identified in Chapter 5: BOD, COD, NH$_4$-N, TN, TP. As TSS is particulate, it does not undergo the same processes and is filtered rather than biodegraded. So it will not be studied for hybridisation, but only with the data-driven approach. [SOURCE: Page_176]

7.1.1 Parametrisation In this work, we examine the selection of NkC* parameters and have compiled expert insights from the literature (Table 7.1) to establish empirical values for the model parameters: [SOURCE: Page_176]

• The hydrodynamics are approached using tanks-in-series and are represented by the parameter N, the number of tanks in series. We calculate it from an empirical relationship, determined by the recent work of von Sperling et al. (2023), from the length L and the water depth h of the wetlands: L N = 0.686( )0.671 h [SOURCE: Page_176]

• The biodegradation is approached using a first order kinetic rate k assumed to be constant across all reactors (tanks). It may include interactions such as limitation between pollutants. From the Table 7.1, we can see that the range of values for k is spread over different orders of magnitude and we use the one from the 50th percentile (as many k are smaller and larger than k 50th ). Moreover, the kinetic rate can be adjusted for temperature using a simplified version of the Arrhenius law for BOD, NH$_4$-N and TN, for which we have the parameter θ . Except for BOD, for which different k values have been determined for different concentration ranges, the kinetic rates of the pollutants are assumed to be constant, following a first order. If the water temperature is not given (more than half the time for BOD), the typical kinetic rate k 20 is used, otherwise: [SOURCE: Page_176]

k T = k 20 θ (T −20) [SOURCE: Page_176]

• The residual background concentration C ∗. [SOURCE: Page_176]

We implemented the NkC* model and predicted the effluent concentrations of HF wetlands for primary and secondary treatments, see Figure 7.1. It is noted that the model frequently overpredicts the measured concentrations for BOD and COD. However, the R-squared (RSQ) statistics reveal that the model fails to adequately account for all the observed variance, with some RSQ values even being negative. This implies that a model providing simply the mean would yield better results, as shown in Table 7.2. And when pre- dicting outflow loads, the model underestimates the pollutant load removed per unit area, Figure 7.2, with a poor RSQ as well. The residual for small nominal surface cases is amplified in the calculation of the RSQ metric. [SOURCE: Page_176]

We then use the information from Chapter 5, with the quality scores and flags associated with the data, to adjust the metrics and give more weight to more reliable observations. Given the inadequate alignment of the model with our data, we opted to calibrate the kinetic rate parameter k on our dataset, even though there were few observations. The assumption is that k includes all processes impacting pollutant removal, notably the limitations from other compounds as described in model A from Chapter 6. Results from calibration attempt are shown in the Appendix E.1. Regrettably, the calibration did not yield conclusive results, so we utilised the k values from the literature, which are derived from a larger dataset. [SOURCE: Page_177]

About 40% of the total variance in the dataset can be projected along the first two principal components. The residuals from the NkC* predictions are still globally correlated with inflow concentrations, pH and conductivity, and negatively correlated with porosity, granulometry and environmental information. It is difficult to assess the correlation with the design of the TW. Looking at the Focused PCA 2 on the residuals in Figure 7.5, we can see that most variables actually have more than 30% missing data, so if we remove these variables, only 4 are left: depth and length are not part of the additional variables, altitude is a global variable and precipitation is entirely imputed. If we consider the variables with more than 30% missing data, between 3 and 5 variables have a correlation with the residuals above 0.4. Porosity and granulometry vary little between case studies, so it may be difficult to draw conclusions. 7.2      Learning models We saw above that the variance in the dataset is not completely explained by the NkC* model. Using the dataset validated in Chapter 5, we now compare statistical and learning models that provide multiple ways to extract relationships between variables, to see if they can better explain the variance using the same features as those used by the NkC* model. Moreover, we saw that there are several additional variables that could be used to explain the variance among those collected for the dataset. We thus train the data- driven models with this greater set of features and assess whether their addition improves the predictions. [SOURCE: Page_179]

7.2.1      Domain of definition Data-driven models learn correlations and patterns from data, but these are different from causalities or physical processes. Learning models are inherently designed not to predict or infer new cases, but to esti- mate cases that would fit within the domain of training of these models, i.e. their domain of validity. We assume that within this domain, the correlations and patterns will behave similarly for all unmeasured cases. Therefore, after training data-driven models and assuming that the data is of good quality, if poor predictions occur for the test set, it may be that the models have overfitted the training data, that they are not appropriate, or that the new cases are outside the training domain. [SOURCE: Page_179]

1 the PCA projects individuals and variables along two principal components which are the two linear combinations of the variables that capture most of the variance in the dataset 2 Focused PCA works similarly to the typical PCA, but instead of projecting individuals and variables along two principal components, it projects them around a target variable (Falissard, 1999). [SOURCE: Page_179]

A limitation of the dataset is that the values are mean concentrations and variability is a source of un- certainty in the correspondence between individual inflow and outflow concentrations. Unlike mechanistic models, the present data-driven models are trained on mean effluent concentrations and therefore predict mean effluent concentrations rather than point effluent concentrations. By design, the models cannot pre- dict extreme cases. The mean inflow and outflow concentrations have been reported with their standard deviation. Although we usually assume a correlation between the actual inflow and outflow concentra- tions, the format of the collected data does not allow one to conclude on their correlation. I.e., we assume [SOURCE: Page_180]

7.2.2      Statistical models with the same features as NkC* To make the individual machine learning models comparable to NkC*, we use the same set of 6 features as for the mechanistic model to define reference models (Q, C in , S T , l ength, de pth, T p air ). Model devel- opment is carried out together with model validation, see workflow in Figure 7.7. The objective for a model is to estimate unseen data, so we divide the data sets per pollutant into a training and a test set. Unfortu- nately, the models require a complete dataset (no missing values) such that we chose to discard incomplete samples from the study. Statistical models are indeed usable for small datasets, but this may induce a bias if the missing data was actually not randomly missing, but we wanted to avoid drawing conclusions from imputed data. For each pollutant, the numbers of observations used for the training and test sets are as follows: [SOURCE: Page_182]

P ollutant                 BOD           COD             N H$_4$               TN        TP              TSS N b observations                 56              85              33             39         33                  54 T raining                   33              58              22             20         14                  31 T est               10              17                6             5           4                  9 [SOURCE: Page_182]

We perform cross-validation with k = 10 folds on the training set, and proportionally stratify each divi- sion (see Chapter 2.6.2 for a full description of the methodology) based on scale (household, pilot, full scale) so that all categories are present in the training. Cross-validation of statistical models provides uncertain- ties in the model parameters, which give an idea of the influence of the training sets on the stability of the model, as well as an idea of the error when attempting to extrapolate to new cases. We use the train function from the caret R package (Kuhn, 2007, 2008). The quality flags (weights) are used in training so that less reliable observations have less influence on the parameters of the models. The final values of the parameters are those obtained by fitting the model to the entire initial dataset, and their associated uncertainties are those obtained by cross-validation. To compare them a posteriori, we check the RMSE, MAPE and RSQ metrics on the training and test sets, see Table 7.4. [SOURCE: Page_182]

determined from linear, power and exponential regression models (shape assumptions) relating surface area S to inflow and outflow pollutant loads L: [SOURCE: Page_183]

L out = L in − bS −→ L in − L out = bS [SOURCE: Page_183]

L out = L in − aS b −→ ln(L in − L out ) = ln(a) + b ln(S) [SOURCE: Page_183]

L out L out = L in e−bS −→ ln(             ) = bS L in [SOURCE: Page_183]

With the right hand-side of the arrows pointing to how these expressions are implemented in the pro- gramming language R using lm(). The power model requires the log-transformation of the features. By including L in in the transformed dependent variable, L in has no removal coefficient itself, but is reduced by subtracting the effect of surface. In a multivariate context with the features x i , the equations become: [SOURCE: Page_183]

L out = L in − (Σ i b i x i ) b L out = L in − aΠ i x i i [SOURCE: Page_183]

L out = L in Π i e−b i x i [SOURCE: Page_183]

In the NkC* model the output is the effluent concentration, whereas in the SANNAT-SNAPP model the output is the effluent load. It seemed interesting to follow the NkC* model and somehow normalise by dividing the loads L = CQ and the area S = S nom Q by the flow Q. However, it seemed that the residual error would increase at large scales (multiplying a posteriori by Q) when converting from concentration to load. Let r be the residual error to be minimised and ² the standard residual error. [SOURCE: Page_183]

Multi-variate linear regressions [SOURCE: Page_183]

• for concentrations C out = Ĉ out + ²C : r C = Σ i (C i,in − C i,out − (C i,in − Ĉ i,out ))2 = Σ i (C i,out − Ĉ i,out )2 [SOURCE: Page_183]

• for loads L out = L̂ out + ²L : r L = Σ i (L i,out − L̂ i,out )2 = Σ i Q 2i (C i,out − Ĉ i,out )2 . [SOURCE: Page_183]

The model predictions are shown in Figure 7.8. It can be interpreted that for the load prediction model, the squared difference between predicted and observed concentrations is weighted by the squared inflow rate, so that the model is fitted at higher values of Q (i.e. larger scale). Therefore, the model predicting loads would perform better at large flow rates. The model predicting concentrations would perform better for small flow rates because the error in multiplying the concentration by the inflow rate increases with flow rate, but the squared error can also be fitted to higher values of C out . [SOURCE: Page_183]

Figure 7.8: Linear model coefficients and their confidence interval, fitting on the train set and prediction of the test set. [SOURCE: Page_183]

Looking at the whole dataset, the coefficients and variability across the cross-validation folds are as follows: [SOURCE: Page_183]

Q             C in            S area       T p in,water         Length             de pth Mean coeff            0.0033            0.9002           −0.0023          −0.9021            0.4733         −12.3751 Std dev           0.0026            0.0097            0.0023            0.1092           0.0716            2.9037 [SOURCE: Page_184]

The inflow rate Q and surface area S area show a great standard deviation associated with their coeffi- cient, and depth shows the highest coefficient. Due to the large discrepancy in the dataset, we investigate ways to compromise predictions of low and high effluent concentrations. [SOURCE: Page_184]

Weighted Least Squares Heteroscedasticity in the dependent variable (C or L) can be mitigated by the weighted least squares method (Wooldridge, 2016), which simply consists of scaling all the variables by the square root of C or L and running the regression without intercept but with p 1 : (var) [SOURCE: Page_184]

C out         1          S           Q         Length       de pth      T p air       C in p      = β0 p      + β1 p      + β2 p      + β3 p      + β4 p      + β5 p       + β6 p      + r corr C in        C in        C in        C in        C in        C in        C in         C in [SOURCE: Page_184]

The coefficients β i are then used to predict the usual variables: [SOURCE: Page_184]

Ĉ out = β̂0 + β̂1 S + β̂2 Q + β̂3 Length + β̂4 de pth + βˆ5 T p air + β̂6 C in [SOURCE: Page_184]

The results for the training/test are shown in Figure 7.9. Looking at the whole dataset, the coeffi- cients and variability across the cross-validation folds are as follows: [SOURCE: Page_184]

i                 Q             C in        S area       T p in,water        Length           de pth M ean(β i )          −0.0006          0.8784         0.0016            −0.9127           0.3533        −7.6836 Sd(β i )           0.0056         0.0081         0.0046              0.0623          0.0628          2.1919 [SOURCE: Page_184]

Depth is given the greatest weight and only inflow concentration, water temperature and length have a standard deviation of a lower order than the mean coefficient value. [SOURCE: Page_184]

Piecewise linear Another method is to split the data set and define a piecewise linear regression. However, we do not use the dependent variable to split. We define two subsets based on the median of the inflow concentration. The small values are used for the linear small model and the higher values for the linear large model. This method may not always be relevant, as each regression is then defined with the same explanatory variables but on fewer observations, with the risk of overfitting. So now, based on (Wooldridge, 2016), we test whether two regressions are statistically better than one, i.e. we check whether the probability of improving the residual variance by as much with two regressions by chance is small. The relative change in the sums of squared residuals (SSR) moving from the full to the piecewise model can be measured by the F-ratio. With n = 51, n lar ge = 59 and n small = 16 observations, k = 6 features, and one intercept, the F-ratio (≥ 0) of the SSR is written: (SSR l inear − SSR piecewise )/(d f − (d f ,small + d f ,bi g )) F= SSR l inear /d f (SSR l inear − SSR piecewise )/(n − k − 1 − (n small − k − 1 + n bi g − k − 1)) = SSR l inear /(n − k − 1) (SSR l inear − SSR piecewise )/(k + 1) = SSR l inear /(n − k − 1) (SSR l inear − SSR l inear,small − SSR l inear,bi g )/(k + 1) = SSR l inear /(n − k − 1) [SOURCE: Page_184]

Taking a risk of α = 0.05, and having a numerator degree of freedom of 7 and a denominator degree of freedom of 51, the critical F value is F c ∈ (2.17, 2.25) (from the appendix in (Wooldridge, 2016)). So we get: F = (139967 −95880−3573)/7 139967/(58−7)     = 1.82 and thus F < F c , so we conclude that piecewise linear regression does not improve the linear model, see Figure 7.10 and coefficients in Figure 7.11. [SOURCE: Page_184]

In the following two cases, the optimisation of the parameters with the squared error is not done directly on the final dependent variable (C out or L out ), but on the transformed ones (ln(L in − L out ) and ln( LLout )). It in is possible to redefine the calculations ourselves, but the power and exponential-based expressions to be minimised are interesting as they are. [SOURCE: Page_185]

Power based model This type of model is not applicable to the TN, NH$_4$ and TP cases as the outflow concentration can be higher than the inflow, so the implementation requiring ln (L in − L out ) is not defined. Considering the power model: C in −C out 2 • for concentrations: r C = Σ i (ln(C in − C out ) − ln(C in − Ĉ out ))2 = Σ i (ln(                )) C in −Ĉ out [SOURCE: Page_185]

L in −L out 2 • for loads: r L = Σ i (ln(L in − L out ) − ln(L in − L̂ out ))2 = Σ i ln(                  ) = rC . L in −L̂ out [SOURCE: Page_186]

The concentration and load cases compute the same residuals based on log-transformed concentrations, so the gap between observed and predicted higher concentrations is underestimated. The weight of the un- derestimations of C out is high (the square logarithm of the ratio ¿ 1 is large), so the model can tend to overestimate C out . The main problem with this model is that it cannot handle the TN, NH$_4$ and TP that may be produced within the treatment wetlands and that it may predict negative concentrations, see Fig- ure 7.12. The model is therefore rejected. [SOURCE: Page_186]

Towards selection of best model The outcomes of these models are fairly moderate, particularly the power model which forecasts negative effluent levels. The piecewise regression, on the other hand, poses an elevated risk of overfitting, demon- strated by a negative RSQ in one of the smaller test sets. Overall, depth was given most weight. Depth is known to play a great role in vertical flow wetlands, but not as much for horizontal flow wetlands. The low weights of inflow rate, surface area and length may be due to their correlations (see Chapter 5), meaning that the associated variance is divided between their three coefficients. As a conclusion, we draw from the results that the models do not have an adequate structure to handle the dataset. [SOURCE: Page_187]

7.2.3      Data-driven models: machine learning models The results with these regressions are not satisfactory, so we tested machine learning models that can find more complex relationships. We used implemented functions from the caret R package (Kuhn, 2007, 2008). We chose tree-based models (Bayesian additive regression trees, eXtreme Gradient Boosting using decision trees, and random forest), which are ensemble models, i.e. they are characterised by the ability to find specific relationships in subsets of data and still propose a global model by aggregating the results. We tested k Nearest Neighbours, which is a local method, Elastic Net, which is a regularised regression that handles multicollinearity and is based on the L$_1$-norm and L$_2$-norm penalties of LASSO and Ridge regression methods, and Support Vector Regression, which can handle non-linear relationships in certain algorithms. [SOURCE: Page_187]

To make the models comparable to NkC* and regression models in this individual assessment, we used outflow concentration as the dependent variable and inflow rate, length, nominal surface, nominal cross- section, depth, total surface, and inflow water temperature as features. We follow the workflow described in Figure 7.14. 3 The dataset is imputed using the Mice predictive mean matching method because machine learning models require complete datasets and removing missing data would result in a size too small for the models to handle. Influx loads are used as a stratification variable to proportionally split the data 3 We set a seed (1000) to control randomness generated in R functions, in order to reproduce the results. [SOURCE: Page_187]

between the training and test sets. For the tuning of the machine learning models (see chapter 2.5.4) we use cross-validation with k = 10 folds, repeating the process 5 times, and again we use the inflow loads as a stratification variable (in practice the range of values is divided into 3 or 4 intervals). The selection of the best tune is based on the RMSE. RMSE, MAPE and RSQ are calculated on the training and test sets. In the caret package, only random forest and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBOOST) handle case weights, so we use the weighted RMSE, weighted MAPE and weighted RSQ as performance metrics to evaluate these models on the training and test sets, using the functions provided by the yardstick R package (Kuhn et al., 2024) and the scores computed in chapter 5. Unchecked observations are given the arbitrary score of 0.2. [SOURCE: Page_188]

and XGBOOST. Among them, KNN has the worst RSQ, RMSE and MAPE, and BART and SVM perform well in training based on RSQ, but poorly in testing for all metrics, indicating overfitting in the training phase. Similarly to voting systems, we may not select the same model depending on the method chosen, or even fall into Condorcet paradoxes 4 . Considering COD results only: [SOURCE: Page_191]

• If we consider only the best performing model per metric, and that training and testing are chrono- logical stages, SVM would be selected by two of the training metrics, although XGBOOST and RF predict better in the test (selected by two of the test metrics, see bold values). [SOURCE: Page_191]

• If we now take the training and test metrics together, we conclude that RF is the best performer (selected three times, against twice for XGBOOST and SVM). [SOURCE: Page_191]

• If we look at the first three models, they are not in the same order depending on the metric chosen: [SOURCE: Page_191]

M etric                                    train                                        test RMSE                   SV M > RF > BOOST                          RF > BOOST > SV M M APE                  BOOST = RF > SV M                          BOOST > RF > SV M RSQ                  SV M > RF > BOOST                        RF > BOOST > BART [SOURCE: Page_191]

As we do not select BART in the first phase, we have to replace it in the test set RSQ: RF > BOOST > SVM. Taking into account the additional information from the ranking, in training we conclude to SVM > RF > BOOST, taking the model in majority, but in testing we conclude to RF > BOOST > SVM. However, this ranking will change if we assign scores (weights) to each rank. [SOURCE: Page_191]

• We could also set thresholds to discard models: RSQ < 0.4, MAPE > 50 % or RMSE > C out¯ , see values in red. The case where all models are discarded is possible, implying that based on this metric it is not worth using a data-driven approach. [SOURCE: Page_191]

• We could argue that the metrics themselves provide more information than the classification. How- ever, unlike the data quality scores from the previous chapter, which were all probabilities, the met- rics here are quantities with different scales and units! The metrics are transformed arbitrarily to have ideal values between 0 and 1, which must be as small as possible: RMSE divided by the absolute 4 Condorcet paradoxes or Condorcet cycles correspond to situations where for example the models are compared based on three criteria, but the results do not show any favoured model [SOURCE: Page_191]

Fortunately, more iterations do not seem necessary as this model already outperforms the other types of machine learning models. Similar to the training of the single machine learning models, we train the models on the data to predict the effluent concentrations, the kinetic rates or the residuals from the NkC* model results. The selected features are: inflow rate Q, total surface S, length L, depth d, inflow water temperature T p in , precipitation P reci p, altitude Alt, inflow conductivity Cond in , inflow pH pH in and general porosity ². We then add specific ratios for each contaminant to include information about the relationships between the contaminants: [SOURCE: Page_193]

BOD               COD : BOD                  BOD : T N               BOD : TP               BOD : N H$_4$ COD               COD : BOD                COD : TSS                 COD : T N                 COD : TP N H$_4$             BOD : N H$_4$ TN                COD : T N                BOD : T N TP               COD : TP                 BOD : TP TSS              COD : TSS [SOURCE: Page_193]

The same methodology described in Figure 7.14 is used for the data sampling, cross-validation and pre-processing of the residuals, and the same hyperparameters are tuned as previously for the effluent concentrations. Only the upper bound for the tuning of the mtry hyperparameter 5 of RF is modified, since there are between 12 and 15 features instead of 6. [SOURCE: Page_193]

To wrap up, we studied one typical pre-design model and trained data-driven models on the data. The NkC* model, whose parameters have been calibrated in previous studies, does not predict the data well. For the data-driven approaches trained on 37 observations, XGBOOST, RF and SVM show a good RSQ (above 0.6) and low MAPE (< 20 %) and RMSE (< 20 mg/L) for COD, but perform quite poorly when predicting the test set from 6 features. The data patterns are therefore less clear and do not reflect a mechanistic understanding of the relationships between the variables. [SOURCE: Page_196]

7.3      Hybridisation of models We obtained unsatisfactory results of the single mechanistic and data-driven models due to the lack of both knowledge and data. We now explore the hybridisations of these models in order to rely on both sources of modelling instead of only one. We use the parallelisation and serialisation of models, which are typical methods presented in the state of the art, Chapter 2. [SOURCE: Page_197]

7.3.1 Models in parallel As a reminder from the previous chapter, parallel hybridisation (Figure 7.27) consists of summing and averaging the predictions of each model. As an evolution, we added a weight or penalty α taking values between 0 and 1, which takes into account the reliability of the machine learning model based on the number of observations used for training and the number of features. [SOURCE: Page_197]

C h ybrid = αC ML + (1 − α)C N kC ∗ [SOURCE: Page_197]

C out = (1 − α)Ĉ out,N kC ∗ + αĈ out,ML + r [SOURCE: Page_197]

α is a weight corresponding to the reliability of the learning model. However, as the value of α is arbi- trary, we investigated how it could be calculated from the available information. [SOURCE: Page_197]

NkC* model N kC ∗ (C in ,Q, S, d, L, k,                             Ĉ out,N kC ∗ C ∗, T p) pre- dicts C out [SOURCE: Page_197]

α computed to minimise Ĉ out,ML Full dataset                                                                                  C out − (1 − α)Ĉ out,N kC ∗ − αĈ out,ML [SOURCE: Page_197]

ML(C in ,Q, S, d, L, Cross-validation,                     T p in , P reci p, hyperparam-                        Alt, Cond in , pH in , ², eter tuning                        ratios) predicts C out [SOURCE: Page_197]

Figure 7.27: Methodology for parallel hybridisation of NkC* model and a Machine Learning model for training on one pollutant [SOURCE: Page_197]

Now using vectors, we find α that minimizes the term by differentiating it with respect to α and finding α such that the derivative is null: [SOURCE: Page_197]

XTZ α= XTX (Ĉ out,ML − Ĉ out,N kC ∗ )T (C out − Ĉ out,N kC ∗ ) = (Ĉ out,ML − Ĉ out,N kC ∗ )T (Ĉ out,ML − Ĉ out,N kC ∗ ) Σ i (Ĉ out,ML,i − Ĉ out,N kC ∗,i )(C out,i − Ĉ out,N kC ∗,i ) = Σ i (Ĉ out,ML,i − Ĉ out,N kC ∗,i )2 [SOURCE: Page_197]

Then, similarly to the computation of αad j proposed in the BIO_PORE-machine learning hybrid model, we add the same adjustment term as for RSQ ad j to adjust the goodness of fit RSQ, with the number of degrees of freedom (i.e. the amount of data used minus the number of variables used) n − p. If α is constrained ∈ [0, 1], we can use the same expression as for RSQ ad j : [SOURCE: Page_197]

n−1 αad j = 1 − (1 − α) n− p−1 [SOURCE: Page_197]

Completing the unknown with a data-driven model To reiterate, the method seeks to account for residual variance by considering other possible features. Serial hybridisation is based on fitting the data-driven model to the residuals from the mechanistic model (Figure 2.26), so that the final prediction is, for example, for C out : [SOURCE: Page_199]

C h ybrid = C N kC ∗ + α r ML [SOURCE: Page_199]

C out = Ĉ out,N kC ∗ + α r̂ ML + ε where α is a weight that applies to the learning model only. We define the expression as a function of α and differentiate to find the minimum, leading to: [SOURCE: Page_199]

XTZ α= XTX ( r̂ ML )T (C out − Ĉ out,N kC ∗ ) = ( r̂ ML )T ( r̂ ML ) [SOURCE: Page_199]

Then, setting the adjusted αad j , we obtain for the different pollutant datasets: [SOURCE: Page_199]

The efficiency criteria are shown in Table 7.10. For the training set, the Table shows that the models perform well on RSQ, but poorly on MAPE. However, the MAPE metric is in relative units and is not very relevant when dealing with residuals, because the residuals of the residuals can be of a larger order than the residuals, as shown by the extremely high MAPE values all above 100% for both the training and test sets. The test set has similar RMSE, but extremely poor RSQ values, suggesting that predicting a constant mean would be a better model for the test set. More generally, since overfitting is mitigated by cross-validation, the poor fit to the test set signals a large heterogeneity between the training and test sets, despite all the precautions taken (data validation, stratified sampling, cross-validation). [SOURCE: Page_201]

Calibration of mechanistic parameters with a data-driven model We now introduce another proposal of serial hybridisation, focusing on the improvement of a parameter from the mechanistic model. The objective is to integrate limitations and potential factors influencing the kinetics, in the kinetic rate k in the NkC* model. Global optimisation (calibration) of the kinetic rate k to obtain a unique value best fitting the data was not conclusive. We now have a different approach where k is optimised per case study. We then fit a machine learning model to the optimised k values to see how well the features can explain the kinetics. This model is used to estimate k to run the NkC* model, see Figure 7.37. In the following, the same methodology as described for the training of the previous machine learning models is used for training of this machine learning model, except that the inflow rate Q and the total surface area S are not part of the features. [SOURCE: Page_202]

We use the random forest model and show the results for COD and NH$_4$, with k optimisation and esti- mation, and the resulting C out prediction in Figures 7.38 and 7.39. [SOURCE: Page_202]

We observe that the training and the test show several off-predictions with a greater variance for high values of k and C out . As the metrics also indicate limited performance, we do not investigate this hybridisation method further. The main drawback is that the kinetic values used to train the ML model are calculated based on overfitting, due to the optimisation of k per case study. [SOURCE: Page_202]

7.4       Surface area estimate In developing the models we mentioned that we were actually predicting effluent concentrations. The explanatory variables required to run the models are as follows: [SOURCE: Page_203]

• Environmental conditions: location, altitude, air temperature [SOURCE: Page_203]

• Inflow characteristics: water temperature, inflow concentrations, pH, conductivity, inflow rate [SOURCE: Page_203]

• Design: width, length or depth [SOURCE: Page_203]

Among these features, area, length and depth are used in the models. However, we want to estimate the area, so we may wonder how we can design a wetland if we need its design as an input. We will explain in more detail below how we use optimisation to estimate area, but for now we will focus on an engineering-based approach to determining width and length. [SOURCE: Page_203]

180 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_203]

7.4.1      Physical constraints on treatment wetlands design The operational constraints significantly influence the width, as demonstrated in Figure 7.40. Given spe- cific values for surface area, influent rate, and COD concentration, one can determine the width, which subsequently allows the estimation of the length. Listed below are the design requirements: [SOURCE: Page_204]

Avoid compaction Calculate length L max due to head loss To allow water to flow, a slope is defined at the bottom of the treatment wetland, resulting in an increase in depth and substrate load. In order to maintain a realistic and efficient depth for all beds, a maximum length for the beds is set such that the material added due to the slope s = dh     dl = 0.005 (head loss) of each bed is at most V$_2$ = 0.25V$_1$ of the initial volume without additional slope. We define d 1 the depth and V$_1$ the volume of the wetland without additional slope and V$_2$ the additional volume due to the slope and d 2 the additional depth. [SOURCE: Page_204]

1      1 V$_2$     d^2     L max s = 2    = 2         ≤ 0.25 V$_1$    d^1       d^1 [SOURCE: Page_204]

So L max = 0.25 × 2ds 1 . d 1 is limited to avoid compaction due to weight and overuse of material, and the maximum depth is set to d 1 + d 2 ≤ 1 metres. With an initial depth of d 1 = 0.6 metres, L max = 60 metres and d 2 = 0.3 metres, and with d 1 = 0.3, L max = 30 and d 2 = 0.15. [SOURCE: Page_204]

Avoid dispersion Calculate width wmax to include dispersion phenomenon The maximum width is defined to limit the hydraulic dispersion of the water flow. Due to the influent feed system, and because dispersion decreases as L : w increases, a compartment (bed) ratio of L max : wmax = 2 is set, hence wmax ∈ {15, 30} depending on d 1 . The empirical calculation of N is valid for L/h < 250, so for L max ∈ [75, 150] depending on the value of h. However, it seems that the case L > L max often occurs. Therefore in our dataset, the corresponding N based on the high values of L are outside this empirically found range, and thus are extrapolated. [SOURCE: Page_204]

Avoid overloading and clogging Calculate w from organic loading rate OLR CS and derive L. OLR is often calculated for the surface area of treatment wetlands. However, in practice the inflow in horizontal flow wetlands is loaded along the cross section. The hydraulic loading rate should of course be limited, but so should the organic loading to avoid clogging. The maximum OLR is CQ OLR CS,max = Load A   = wd^1 = 250 gBOD/m^2 .d. Hence, CS [SOURCE: Page_204]

CQ w = kwmax > 250d 1 [SOURCE: Page_204]

where the cross sectional area is divided into k parallel beds based on wmax calculated previously to avoid dispersion. For prediction, the width is therefore calculated as the mean BOD inflow load divided by OLR CS,max de pth. If BOD is not available, it can be estimated from the number of popu- lation equivalents or from known relationships with other pollutants. Consequently, the length can be deduced from the area and width. L Then, L max gives the number of beds in series. [SOURCE: Page_204]

For the example below, we take the maximum cross-sectional organic loading rate to be 250 g BOD/m^2/d and the depth to be 0.6 m. From this, the width and length can be deduced to run the models. Finally, once the surface area has been determined, the number of individual parallel and serial beds and their dimensions can be derived from these rules, e.g. L max ∈ [30, 60] and wmax ∈ [15, 30] depending on the initial depth d 1 ∈ [0.3, 0.6]. [SOURCE: Page_204]

7.4.2 Necessity of optimisation The different models all predict effluent concentrations, so an optimisation function must be used if we are looking for the surface area to achieve given treatment performances. With the original formulation NkC* model, the surface area is derived by transforming the equation to isolate not C out but S. When we consider that N depends on S, the equation requires optimisation of the area per pollutant. The learning models also require optimisation to re-estimate the surface area. [SOURCE: Page_204]

Optimisation consists of looking for an extremum in the domain of definition of an objective function. There exist various optimisation methods, and we can distinguish local and global optimisation. Local optimisation consists in searching for a local extremum, while global looks for the global extremum. For local optimisation, methods rely on the differentiability of the objective function, such as the first-order gradient-based algorithms, or second-order Hessian-based algorithms, or methods that can handle non convex functions. [SOURCE: Page_205]

Optimisation possibilities In the case of the NkC* model, if N is assumed to be independent of S for a given pollutant removal, then S can be determined directly. However, if N depends on the area, then the area is calculated ³           numerically ´ NQ using optimisation. The expression of NkC* can be transformed to compute S = k ( C       o −C ∗ 1/N C i −C ∗ )   − 1 , but in the case where N is determined based on length and depth, then it is actually a function of S, since L varies with S. [SOURCE: Page_205]

The monotonicity of f ensures that there exists a minimum S ob j such that the removal satisfies the regulations/treatment objectives ∀S > S ob j . Consequently, one can employ a local optimisation technique to identify the optimal surface, as there is just one local solution, making it the global one as well. [SOURCE: Page_206]

7.4.3      Asymmetric objective function We propose to study the optimisation of the surface per pollutant, then for multiple pollutants, taking into account the treatment objectives and taking into account the costs. Cled’12 illustrated in Figure 7.41 the difficulties of decision-making due to the multiplicity of dimensions to consider in a given situation. It additionally demonstrates that while science struggles to reach a conclusion on this issue, politics can make decisions. [SOURCE: Page_206]

Treatment-centred objective function The area is optimised per pollutant. If it is mandatory that all C out are less than C ob j , then finding the optimal area that satisfies all is equivalent to finding the optimal area for the limiting pollutant. We are looking for the limiting pollutant for which it is most difficult to get an effluent concentration less than its target, so we are looking for the largest area required to remove all pollutants as required. [SOURCE: Page_206]

If N is independent of S, the constraint is C ob j,i ≥ C out,i i.e. S ob j,i ≤ S out,i , so the minimum area that satisfies these constraints is the maximum S ob j,i , i.e. S optim = max(S ob j,i ). S ob j can be calculated directly from C in and C ob j for all pollutants: [SOURCE: Page_206]

365QN ³³ C in,i − C ∗ ´1/N   ´ S ob j,i =                        ∗ −1 k    C ob j,i − C However, considering the case where N depends on S, it is not possible to isolate S in the equation where N depends on S. Therefore, optimisation is used, see workflow 7.42: S is set as a variable, and due to monotonicity there exists a unique S ob j,i such that ∀S > S ob j,i the removal satisfies the objective. This optimal minimum S ob j,i is computed for all pollutants and the largest area among them is selected. [SOURCE: Page_206]

Optimisation NkC*                         Objective                   function model N kC ∗                        function              newton(S, f ob j ) (C in ,Q, S, d, k, C ∗)        f ob j (C out , C ob j )        computes predicts C out              returns a MSRE                  the optimal surface area S [SOURCE: Page_207]

Figure 7.42: Optimisation workflow to determine the surface area using NkC* model [SOURCE: Page_207]

We define the objective function (i.e. the function to be optimised) to be the squared relative error (SRE, no units) which, for each pollutant i, computes the squared relative distance between C ob j,i and C out,i for a given area S: ³ C ob j,i − C out,i ´2 SRE = C ob j,i The square distance avoids negative values and ensures the existence of a minimum. [SOURCE: Page_207]

Cost-centred penalised objective function [SOURCE: Page_207]

The choice of the limiting pollutant for the design may be too conservative and expensive, so it may be interesting to calculate an area that is a compromise of all the pollutant removal objectives, and rely on an additional treatment, or intensification to reach the objective. The resulting objective function is calculated by aggregating the different SRE. Thus, for all i pollutants considered and a given area S, the mean squared relative error is given: [SOURCE: Page_207]

n ³C 1X      ob j,i − C out,i 2 ´ MSRE = n i=1      C ob j,i [SOURCE: Page_207]

The square then also avoids compensation between pollutant removal when summing distances, and assigns symmetrical costs to targets when the outflow is further away (greater or smaller). The division by C ob j standardises the differences in pollutant concentrations. [SOURCE: Page_207]

If we now consider the area as a compromise between all the pollutant treatment objectives and the costs, the notion of weight or penalty arises. In particular, in terms of treatment, it is better to treat more than the target than to treat less. However, the SRE used above for optimisation is a symmetric expression, so the SRE is the same whether the predicted effluent concentration is 10 mg/L higher or lower than the target. [SOURCE: Page_207]

Starting with the expression above, we see that the SRE removes the scale effect of concentrations by calculating relative quantities. Subsequently, recognising that certain pollutants might require more prioritisation for removal than others, a weight related to the specific pollutant can be introduced. The justification and significance of this weight stem from the impacts of each pollutant, and the sensitivity of receiving bodies to eutrophication, with phosphorus or nitrogen as limiting factors. Unfortunately, similar to the aggregation of data validation checks into a unique flag, a unique optimal area prediction varies with the importance (weight) assigned to each pollutant. Multiple criteria for determining the importance of pollutants can be translated into economic quantities that depend on the location of the treatment wetlands to be implemented: [SOURCE: Page_207]

• The cost of construction, maintenance of the treatment plant and the cost of land. Reaching a con- centration below the target indicates that the removal of the pollutant satisfies the regulatory or treatment goals. However, this might also suggest a need for more land, thereby increasing the ex- pense. The deliverable MULTISOURCE (2023) 6 determined a median construction cost of 14 eper m^3 .yr −1 and a median maintenance cost of 0.13 eper m^3 .yr −1 for HF wetlands, and a median size to flow of 0.07 m^2 .m−3 .yr. Thus, each additional m^2 of surface area (i.e. such that C ob j > C out ) cor- responds to an additional cost of (14 + 0.13)/0.07 ≃ 202 e/m^2 . These summary values are given as an example, but are not very meaningful in practice, as the costs of land, labour, materials, maintenance, etc. can vary considerably around the world. 6 Deliverable 3.2 The Economics of Nature-based Solutions of the MULTISOURCE project [SOURCE: Page_207]

• The environmental impact. Non-compliance with the treatment objective, i.e. achieving a concen- tration greater than the objective C out > C ob j , may have consequences depending on the destination: river, sea, wetland, reuse. The environmental damage caused by untreated discharges has been quantified by Hernández-Sancho et al. (2010) in euros per kg of pollutant released. It shows that re- gardless the destination for discharge, carbonaceous compounds have a lesser impact than nutrients, see Table 7.12. [SOURCE: Page_208]

Shadow price         River        Sea        Wetlands         Reuse TN             16.353       4.612        65.209          26.182 NH$_4$             16.353       4.612        65.209          26.182 TP             30.944       7.533       103.424          79.268 TSS             0.005        0.001        0.010           0.010 BOD             0.033        0.005        0.117           0.058 COD               0.098       0.010         0.122           0.140 [SOURCE: Page_208]

Table 7.12: Parameter shadow prices in e/k g pollutant per year for discharge in River, Sea, Wetlands, and Reuse, we considered that the cost for NH$_4$ (not determined) is the same as the one for TN, from Hernández- Sancho et al. (2010) [SOURCE: Page_208]

This second environmental problem is considered more important to prevent, so a penalty ρ i is applied to obtain the mean penalised relative error: [SOURCE: Page_208]

1X n                            C ob j,i − C out,i MPRE =           ρ i (C ob j,i − C out,i ) n i=1                                C ob j,i where: [SOURCE: Page_208]

• ρ i equals 1 if C out,i < C ob j,i . [SOURCE: Page_208]

• ρ i equals 1 plus the value of the economic cost from the Table 7.12 if C out,i > C ob j,i . ρ i (C ob j,i − C out,i ) represents a cost proportional to the concentration difference (i.e. a quantity per unit volume of wa- ter), so that the MPRE has a physical meaning, being the cost of exceeding the effluent concentrations expressed in e/L. [SOURCE: Page_208]

Using the same example, the optimal surface area calculated with MPRE is 7946 m^2 . The correspond- ing costs over the years are determined from the shadow costs 7 and the CAPEX and OPEX 8 , and the costs invested for the scenario with treatment wetlands implementation are buffered after 13 years, see Figure 7.43. [SOURCE: Page_208]

7.4.4 Comparison of surface estimates The prediction workflow of machine learning models differs from the training one, it relies on the stored models and parameters. The information from the new case study is given to both individual models, then the length and depth are computed from the physical constraints and given to both the NkC* model and the learning model, and finally the outputs (grey boxes) are combined as shown in the workflows 7.44 and 7.45. [SOURCE: Page_208]

We show in Figures 7.46 and 7.47 the results of training and testing the parallel (green) and serial (blue) models on COD and NH$_4$. For better visibility the observation-prediction pairs per model are linked. Overall, the NkC* model presents more variability in its predictions. High concentrations are poorly pre- dicted for all models, showing in particular that the learning models did not have sufficient data to be trained properly. The calculation of α shows a greater reliance on the mechanistic NkC* model in both cases, which indeed fits better for high concentrations. [SOURCE: Page_208]

Let us take the fictitious example of a project to build a horizontal flow wetland to treat wastewater and discharge it into the different destinations. The water and air temperature is 20 degrees Celsius, the inflow rate is 300 m^3/d, and we consider a BOD of 300 mg/L with a target of 50, NH$_4$-N of 40 mg/L with 7 the shadow costs correspond to the avoided damages quantified as costs when comparing a scenario with and without the ac- tion/technology of interest 8 Capital expenditures and Operating expenses [SOURCE: Page_208]

Uncertainty propagation Current models provide a unique design determined from a given set of initial conditions. However, we know from the dataset that there are uncertainties and variability, in many of the features used to pre- dict outflow concentrations. Uncertainties related to data and models in the training phase are detailed in Appendix E.2. We will consider here the uncertainties related to the context of predictions, following workflow 7.48, and assuming that the uncertainty associated with the model structure is smaller than the input uncertainties. Design and location are not subject to variation, but inflow concentrations, inflow rate, water temperature and biokinetics are. Under normal conditions, treatment wetlands may experi- ence short drought or rainfall events, that can increase pollutant concentrations or increase the hydraulic loads received. By utilising uncertainty propagation, we can assess how dependable the optimised design estimates are in meeting their intended performance goals. [SOURCE: Page_211]

Example of application The following is a fictitious example of a project to construct an horizontal flow wetland to treat and discharge effluent into a river. The water and air temperature is 20 degrees Celsius, the inflow rate is 300 m^3 /d and we consider a BOD of 300 mg/L with a target of 50, NH$_4$-N of 40 mg/L with a target of 20, TN of 42 mg/L with a target of 22 and TP of 20 mg/L with a target of 12. [SOURCE: Page_211]

The predicted area by the NkC* model is then 3820.4 m^2 for BOD, 6849.3 for NH$_4$, 8892.0 for TN and 1056.1 for TP. The limiting pollutant is TN because it requires the largest surface area to achieve the ob- jective. It is clear that the determination of the final area depends on the pollutants chosen for the study. These pollutants are determined by regulations based on the risk of eutrophication of the receiving body or other environmental risks. [SOURCE: Page_211]

As the predicted effluent concentration is only a point or mean value, we propagate uncertainties from the input features (keeping the estimated area constant) to the predictions. To do this, we use the Monte Carlo method in the following way: we randomly draw the altered kinetic rate, inflow concentration, inflow rate and inflow water temperature from the example, assuming a truncated normal distribution N (1, 0.1), between 0.5 and 1.5. We then predict the effluent concentration and repeat the process 1000 times. We ob- tain a histogram of the propagated uncertainties on the effluent concentrations in Figure 7.49, from which we deduce the proportion of times that the effluent concentrations meet the set treatment objectives, see Table 7.13. [SOURCE: Page_211]

Surface area (m^2)         BOD           NH$_4$     TN        TP 8892                       100          94.1    49.4     100 6849                       99.9          49      9.3     100 3820                       52.8          0.5     0.2     100 1056                        0             0       0      56.5 [SOURCE: Page_211]

Table 7.13: Distribution of removal performance in % for the different pollutants, with varying conditions, based on Monte Carlo Simulations with n=1000. [SOURCE: Page_211]

Looking at Table 7.13, for the given area and initial uncertainties, we observe that the related con- taminant achieves the goal C ob j in fifty percent of the cases, which is expected. So, unfortunately, despite selecting the largest area identified for TN, the TN removal target is only met for half of the simulation. [SOURCE: Page_211]

From this result, several visions can lead to a decision. Either that the treatment wetland is too small, or that the treatment wetland is not sufficient and should be combined with another solution for TN, i.e. that TN removal should not be rely entirely on the design of the treatment wetland. Considering the first case, we now look for the surface area that allows to comply with the TN removal target 95% of the time. To do so we set as objective function the squared difference between C ob j,T N and the TN concentration corresponding to the 95th percentile from Monte Carlo Simulations. The resulting surface area required for 95% compliance is in our example of 12302 m^2 (so a 38% increase of the selected 8892 m^2), allowing the following removal performances, also illustrated in Figure 7.50 : [SOURCE: Page_212]

190 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_213]

7.5      Conclusion In this chapter, we have applied the hybrid model approach to steady-state data on a global scale. We first fitted the mechanistic model NkC* and trained the learning models individually. We found that the statis- tical models were insufficient to explain the variance in the dataset, so we investigated machine learning models to account for non-linear relationships with effluent concentrations. [SOURCE: Page_214]

In the context of the NkC* model, while the kinetic rate might be an important parameter, additional experimental research may be necessary to identify more associated features. However, deriving conclu- sions from our study using optimised k values to train the model proved inconclusive. The piecewise statistical model performed well as it artificially creates non-linear fits from linear regressions, but led to overfitting as it did not perform well in the test phase. The tree-based models were found to perform best compared to the others and were used for hybridisation. The hybrid models still lack data to train and test the learning models, so they rely mainly on the mechanistic/empirical NkC* model. However, a major feature of the hybrid models lies in this adaptation of the weight given to each model, in particular the reliance on the learning model based on the quantity and quality of the data through the use of scores. We observed large discrepancies between the surface area estimates of the NkC*, RF, parallel and serial models. [SOURCE: Page_214]

The disadvantages of these hybrid models in the training phase, are that we need to take into account the heterogeneity of sites, operating conditions, and wetland designs. Therefore, in addition to good quality data, a greater amount of data is needed to compensate for the increase in features used in the models. We hope to foster the gathering and exchange of data with the use of the common data exchange format. For the testing phase, we need information from the new case study on effluent and site characteristics. However, unlike models developed for a specific treatment plant, our models do not have access to historical data, so many assumptions have to be made about the value of each new feature. Finally, through the propagation of uncertainty, we could adjust the surface areas according to the number of non compliant samples that we agree to allow. We have found that the largest predicted areas are insufficient to systematically achieve the defined treatment objectives. When we considered an optimisation of treatment wetlands surface areas over multiple pollutants, the estimates were greatly dependent on the set of pollutants chosen, as well as on the destination of the treated water. As a way to vary the scope, we also considered their shadow costs associated with the water destination. This leads to consider scenarii with complete treatment trains rather than individual treatment wetlands. [SOURCE: Page_214]
