192 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_215]

Chapter 8 [SOURCE: Page_216]

Discussion [SOURCE: Page_216]

”One only understands the things that one tames, said the fox. Men have no more time to understand anything. They buy things all ready made at the shops.” [SOURCE: Page_216]

Antoine de Saint Exupéry, The little prince, 1943 [SOURCE: Page_216]

The very applied or practical objectives of this thesis in the framework of the MULTISOURCE project, i.e. the improvement of treatment wetlands for design estimate, showed to be closely linked to the his- torical scientific node of unifying knowledge. We intended to unify symbolic representations on treatment wetlands, and numerical modelling approaches hoping to gain a better understanding, and subsequently to provide a more reliable design estimate. This work is of course open to criticism for further improvements, and we will provide some insights gained along the way. We identified three types of challenges in knowl- edge exchange: between researchers of different expertise, from seniors to juniors, and from researchers to decision-makers. [SOURCE: Page_216]

8.1      Sciences unification and standardisation In Chapter 4, on symbolic representation, we proposed to develop a thesaurus conjointly to the development of an ontology. The method aims to depict and structure the symbolic knowledge within the framework of integrated water management. The diverse perspectives from various disciplines could not be ontologically unified into a single consensus. However, the ontology permitted the co-existence of all views, with the sole condition of establishing a preferred term. The main drawback in the development of the ontology lies in the choice for a literature-based determination of synonyms and definitions of the concepts and the involve- ment of stakeholders that was extremely limited. The two workshops revealed to be insufficient in covering all aspects, and the equal representativeness of all possible stakeholders of an integrated approach was not met. We should have developed an approach with a better balance between the inclusion of previous works and the discussion with peers and stakeholders. Because the use of the concept of Nature-based Solutions is expanding, more exchanges and standardisations are needed to be able to compare and reuse results from other studies. Notably, the approach of Castellar et al. (2021) involving participation of stakeholders is interesting because of the discussions to reach consensus, or at least compromise. Jones et al. (2021); Strande et al. (2023) suggest that due to their inherent specificity, localised studies may face challenges in being generalised or replicated in different settings. This is true especially when considering local cultural practices or terminology, indicating that such studies may not seamlessly apply to other contexts. Indeed, the downside of unifying practices is to overlook and lose the specificities required by certain situations. Standard terminologies establish the conditions for communication, but may hide other realities 1 and hin- der their inclusion and research inovation. [SOURCE: Page_216]

The ontology was developed in the PO$_2$ Manager to follow the structure for the description of food trans- formation. This software allows the mapping of data to the structure of itineraries that relate concepts to 1 for example the differences between urban (and well regulated) and rural water management [SOURCE: Page_216]

193 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_216]

form treatment trains. We focused on establishing the thesaurus, but the great interest of developing an ontology is to establish more relations between concepts. The ontologies discussed in the State of the Art section have not yet been integrated following the NeOn methodology (Gómez-Pérez and Suárez-Figueroa, 2009). This applies to the ontologies related to water management at the catchment level as well as those concerning phenomena and numerical modelling. The format of our ontology is well adapted to current technical data and to future inclusions of costs and life-cycle assessments. Nonetheless, the inclusion of concepts such as resilience, biodiversity preservation or enhancement, social dynamics, etc. seems more delicate. Their inclusion may require a translation of these concepts to a qualitative assessment or quanti- tative metric. Finally, we have proposed a common data exchange format defining key pieces of information to report which seems necessary to communicate and compare data. This proposal aligns with a movement for FAIR data, aiming to facilitate Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reuse of data by com- puters, and humans. However, challenges remain as to how to encourage researchers and practitioners to use it. We saw that unification of knowledge with the development of the ontology, the data exchange format and the data validation methodology led to the need for standardisation that reduces the plurality of realities and excludes contemplation. [SOURCE: Page_217]

8.2      Knowledge transmission and automation In addition to unification, we observed that a vital component for advancing science is the dissemination of knowledge and the preservation of a continually expanding set of tools. Science and technique are closely intertwined such that the increase of knowledge and understanding greatly relies on tools and associated qualifications. The question of the maintenance of the ontology, which can evolve over time with changes of collective representations, was determining in ensuring the transmission of knowledge. Similarly, we were confronted to the retirement of the maintainer of the r gdal R package on which depended many packages for the management of geographical information. The packages terra and raster thus became obsolete and incompatible with new R versions until 2024-2025 thanks to other developers who assumed respon- sibility for the updates. Many statistical tools are developed and available as packages in programming frameworks, such as imputation methods, outlier detectors or modelling workflows. They may facilitate the adoption of new, complex or more reliable practices, and allow researchers and practitioners to gain time. However, overly automatised tasks present the risks for users to not fully master their utilisation 2 , and to remain unaware of the complexity of certain situations, or of critical points 3 . Automation through these media of exteriorisation may dispossess researchers automatic skills that they have not reclaimed nor ac- quired. Bernard Stiegler 4 recalls that knowledge is based on a cycle between its exteriorisation through transmission and its interiorisation through singularisation. In this cycle, technique and tools are media of exteriorisation of knowledge, but they may not help gaining more understanding, and rather short-circuit thinking processes, they even lead to a loss of know-how and create dependencies 5 . Irene Vallejo rightly wrote in El Infinito en un Junco, 2019: [SOURCE: Page_217]

Of course, technology is dazzling and powerful enough to dethrone the old monarchies. How- ever, we all long for things we have lost-photos, files, old work, memories-due to the speed at which its products age and become obsolete. First, it was the songs on our cassettes, then the films recorded on VHS. We devoted frustrating efforts to collecting what technology relentlessly pushed into obsolescence. When DVDs appeared, we were told that our archival problems had finally been solved forever, but soon enough, they were back, tempting us with new, smaller- format discs that inevitably required purchasing new devices. The curious thing is that we can still read a manuscript patiently copied more than ten centuries ago, yet we can no longer watch a video tape or access a floppy disk from just a few years back, unless we have kept all our successive computers and playback devices, turning our storage rooms into museums of obsolescence. [...] 2 as noted by Simone Weil in Gravity and Grace, 1947: ”There is no collective thought. On the other hand our science is collective like our techniques. Specialisation. We inherit not only results but methods which we do not understand.”, we have a illustration with the debates on the misinterpretations of the p-value in statistical tests by biologists (Greenland et al., 2016) 3 unfortunately, I cannot guarantee to be immune to these risks 4 see Do Digital Technologies Kill Thought? (Le numérique empêche-t-il de penser?), Revue Esprit, January 2014 5 This situation of dependence leads Bernard Stiegler to speak of hypomnesic techniques or pharmakôn when referring to these deleterious media of exteriorisation of knowledge replacing the role of human memory. On the other hand, writing is a form of tertiary retention that facilitates the use of understanding and reason. [SOURCE: Page_217]

194 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_217]

It would no longer be a matter of our own knowledge, integrated, and indelible, part of each person’s own intellectual baggage, but rather an external appendage. [...] The Internet is trans- forming the use of memory and the very mechanics of knowledge. [...] We tend to remember better where information is stored than the information itself. It is clear that available knowl- edge is more abundant than ever, but almost everything is stored outside our brains. Worrying questions arise: under this flood of data, what remains of knowledge? [SOURCE: Page_218]

The practical objective of looking for more reliable treatment wetland design estimates led us to choos- ing a numerical model developed for design, NkC*, which is simpler but time-efficient compared to the BIO_PORE model. The use of machine learning models presents two aspects: on one side it replaces knowledge and aligns with the practical objective of prediction rather than understanding, and on the other side, it participates in gaining understanding by extracting unseen information (correlations) from data. Already perceived with the automation of calculations and checks using statistical tools, the automa- tion of the search for information and (cor)relations between variables with machine learning and artificial intelligence in general has greatly transformed research practices. It is interesting how science and the production of knowledge can rely on tools that apply processes which we cannot grasp intellectually. Ar- tificial intelligence forces to an act of humility, which we performed with model hybridisation by relying on machine learning to extract unidentified phenomena captured by data. In terms of knowledge trans- mission however, machine learning models are difficult to interpret, such that the role of researchers lies even more in extracting understanding and setting causal relationships. We realised that over-automated methods may transform research practices to technique applications: before using the caret R package, we had started our modelling approach using the tid ymodels R meta-package 6 which precodes many tools, models, and entire modelling procedures. Many parameters are integrated with default options in the functions, meaning that we may not be aware of nor question the subtleties that may be required for our case. We may need to question to what extent we should rely on these media of exteriorisation, balancing with the time required otherwise. [SOURCE: Page_218]

In Chapter 5, on data validation for modelling, we aimed to standardise and automatise data valida- tion practices. The quality of the data needs to be better included in the training of models. We gathered data from the literature and developed a methodology for data validation with the identification of key factors for data quality/reliability, and the use of several subsequent checks. The checks relied on either the establishment of a dataset of reference (or of expert knowledge), or on the distribution of gathered data. Unfortunately, the expert knowledge was either too restrictive in its scope, or too wide and with few case studies. On the other hand, gathered data was sparse and heterogeneous, with missing data patterns on the variable level. A risk is to forget that the notion of outliers is different from the notion of wrong data, in particular for literature-based steady-state data. Statistical outliers may not correspond to a physically wrong situation. Then, the checks provide a weight which is useful for modelling by avoiding the rejection of too many observations, and mitigate the risk related to statistical approaches by fitting typical laws on either the expert knowledge or the dataset. A limit resides in the quantitative approach rather than the more intuitive and meaningful qualitative categorisation into good, questionable, unsuitable proposed by ?. Researchers and practitioners should not be dispossessed from their knowledge and decision power regarding data validation. [SOURCE: Page_218]

8.3      Uncertainties and decision making In Chapter 6, on numerical representation, we developed two methodologies for model hybridisation. The previous modelling approaches presented in the State of the Art aimed either to describe processes deter- ministically or to support treatment wetland design. We proposed models that rely on both the mechanistic description and the data-driven modelling. The parallel method was developed with the use of a weight that depends on the reliability of the machine learning model and the fitting to the training data. This hybridisation presents a risk of overfitting and overreliance on data because the mechanistic model may have a negligible weight. In the serial approach, the mechanistic model serves as a control mechanism, with the hybrid model’s forecast beginning with the mechanistic prediction and adjusting it using the ma- chine learning model’s weighted prediction on the residuals. We saw that some machine learning models showed a change of fit in predicting outflow concentration between low and high values. Tree-based models 6 see https://www.tidymodels.org/packages/, it compiles the following packages: rsample, parsnip, recipes, workflows, tune, yardstick, broom, dials. [SOURCE: Page_218]

195 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_218]

did not present this issue, however in case it should happen, the current computation of the weight is on the global fit, so a piecewise fit could be envisaged. This hybridisation concerned steady-state data which seemed most appropriate in the context of estimating the design of treatment wetlands. We saw that the individual mechanistic and machine learning models presented unexplained variance, i.e. a difficulty in considering and extracting all phenomena and relationships between features and dependent variables. Steady-state data is interesting in design estimate, however, we discarded the typical case of dealing with dynamic data and of using a system of differential equations. An interesting typical hybridisation ap- proach to test consists in embedding dynamic models. We can also question the choice of the complexity of the BIO_PORE models used for models A and B, since treatment wetlands are designed based on a long term perspective, phenomena such as clogging or plant decay may have been important to include. The high complexity of BIO_PORE models also leads to the possibility of developing surrogate models 7 to sim- plify the process and gain time. [SOURCE: Page_219]

In Chapter 7, on the application of hybrid models, we developed hybrid models based on quantitative variables and the NkC* model which is rather used for design than description purposes. We therefore bypassed the contribution of the categorical knowledge that we had obtained from the literature-based dataset. Types of substrate, climate, and plant are nominal variables and difficult to fully replace by quantitative indicators, so they were not included in the models. On the other hand, their direct use in sta- tistical models, considering the limited number of complete observations, would lead to the use of dummy variables which artificially increase variance, because their categories are not ordered. With more data, machine learning models would be interesting, as already done by Nguyen et al. (2022) to compare and select the types of treatment wetlands. They rely on machine learning for the selection of the type of treat- ment wetland while in our approach, the selection is expert-based. The type of treatment wetland is not part of our numerical model, which leads to question to what extent decisions should rely on algorithms. An area of modelling development that remains unexplored in our work is the integration of symbolic and numerical models. This technique involves explicitly defining certain concepts, which can be achieved by referencing the symbolic identification of mechanistic phenomena within a knowledge graph grounded in ontology. This process involves combining relevant sub-models to form a complete model, as outlined by Dehghani Tafti et al. (2024). Alternatively, genetic programming can be used to optimally organise these sub-models, as demonstrated by Gaudesi et al. (2013) in the realm of designing treatment wetlands. With the optimisation section, we showed that hybrid modelling is necessary but insufficient in determining the final best design. Indeed, design estimates are done for each pollutant of interest, and there exist multiple optimisation options. [SOURCE: Page_219]

We saw overall that metrics, i.e. the means we choose to measure and quantify, have impacts on our conclusions, notably with the MAPE, RMSE and RSQ that did not rank the machine learning models in the same order. Uncertainties lie within data and model structures, and we found through uncertainty propagation that treatment objectives may not be achieved half of the time by the design for the limit- ing pollutant. We used uncertainty propagation which concerns input to output uncertainties, but did not consider model parameters uncertainties, which are assessed using sensitivity analysis 8 . By rendering uncertainties explicit, we can provide more information to support an informed decision-making, and at the same time improve reliability by revealing the actual difficulty to grasp, and complexity of reality. How- ever, all sources of uncertainties put light on ignorance, and may actually overwhelm the apparent clarity of initial results, and thus hinder decision-making. Therefore, although we have developed reliable models with a strict methodology starting with data validation, improved robustness using cross-validation, there remains a long way before the determination of the best treatment wetland design. [SOURCE: Page_219]

Overall in this thesis, we targeted the unification of knowledge without deeply involving dialectics, i.e. a confrontation of representations. More research could be done on methodologies that can guide dialectics and thinking into facing complexity and dealing with uncertainties. We found that the data validation, numerical models and programming choices made, partially stem from (time) efficiency requirements. To counter balance the risks to overlook the specificities of situations, researchers may need to dig further into how to create the conditions of wonder and questioning, and enable an informed decision rather than an imposed one. [SOURCE: Page_219]

7 A surrogate model aims to simplify the calculations when a mechanistic model is too complex to run casually. 8 for example, Sobol indexes [SOURCE: Page_219]

196 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_219]

Chapter 9 [SOURCE: Page_220]

General conclusions [SOURCE: Page_220]

”Effort without finality. It is terrible — or the most beautiful thing of all — if it is finality without an end. The beautiful alone enables us to be satisfied by that which is.” [SOURCE: Page_220]

Simone Weil, Gravity and Grace, 1947 [SOURCE: Page_220]

This thesis aimed at improving modelling of knowledge for better decision-making in the context water management with Nature-based Solutions. This improvement focused on wastewater treatment by treat- ment wetlands, and concerned both the symbolic and the numerical representation of treatment wetlands, through the exchange of knowledge between experts and the hybridisation of mechanistic and data-driven modelling approaches for treatment wetlands designs. This thesis proposed methodological improvements for the representation of knowledge with the joint development of a thesaurus and an ontology, the de- velopment and aggregation of fitted statistical tests for data validation, the development of hybrid models based on the reliability of machine learning models, and the development of adapted objective functions to estimate the design of treatment wetlands. [SOURCE: Page_220]

9.1      Main findings In the State of the Art constituting Chapter 2, we saw that unifying knowledge across different disciplines has been a key objective in science throughout history. From a physical encyclopedia, a more sophisticated symbolic representation is now widely used with computers: ontologies. Ontologies can handle multiple scopes and types of relationships between concepts, and overcome the language barrier by mapping con- cepts in different languages. However so far, no ontology developed for water management has considered Nature-based Solutions. We saw that symbolic representations and many concepts can rely on prior and a posteriori quantifications through the use of metrics. Physics-based representations may be the easiest ap- proach to describing reality. Technique through numbers is found in the definition of concepts, the writing of regulations, and decision-making in urban planning. However, the different numerical representations each have drawbacks. Mechanistic models tend to target the description of key processes, but at the cost of a high mathematical complexity. Empirical models simplify the relationships by posing more assump- tions or by fitting pre-defined laws to the phenomena described. Finally, data-driven approaches which are developed in numerous disciplines, manage to handle complex systems but rely on a high quantity of data, and establish relations between all the variables based on correlations and not causality. Numerical modelling overall relies on a methodology from data management to model validation, whose steps are not systematically followed by researchers. We saw that a new modelling approach, hybrid models, is getting interest in the water management community, but their application to treatment wetlands had not been made yet. [SOURCE: Page_220]

In Chapter 4, on symbolic representation, we used a semantic approach to describe key concepts. We gathered concepts following the gradual complexity of various symbolic representations. The concept of Nature-based Solutions is at the intersection of several disciplines while the concepts of technological units, among which treatment wetlands, hold a rather technical essence, making them easier to study [SOURCE: Page_220]

197 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_220]

scientifically. We found that the different perspectives borne in different disciplines lead to defining con- cepts differently, by highlighting certain properties rather than others. We also saw that regulations use definitions to set the framework on which they apply, and tend to use very technical definitions. Conversely, we observed that the subjective nature of definitions and terminology selection can lead to a biased view of reality that may not apply universally. There exist multiple synonyms and representations of concepts, which are dependent on the disciplines and level of understanding. The initial symbolic of concepts is nowadays rather encountered in definitions that target a non expert audience. We aimed at defining the concepts, setting translations and categorising them in a thesaurus. By passing consensus, we put together the different definitions, as well as the multiple terminologies. We then followed a methodology for the con- struction of an ontology, opting for the structure of TransformON food transformation ontology, developed in the Process-oriented Ontology Manager (INRAE). A key element in developing the ontology was that the confrontation and aggregation of the different sources of knowledge, i.e. the process of creation itself rather than the result, led to gaining more understanding. The choice of the PO$_2$ Manager software allows the mapping of data to corresponding concepts and in the future, ensures maintenance and the integration of concepts related to life-cycle assessment or social-sciences in a future step. This ontology allowed the proposal of a common data exchange format to facilitate communication and reuse of data. [SOURCE: Page_221]

In Chapter 5, on data validation for modelling, we carried out a literature-based search for data on subsurface flow treatment wetlands. The data of interest was determined from the concepts and categories defined in the previous Chapter. We were interested in forming a dataset of steady-state data on pollutant removals, treatment wetlands designs, and additional contextual information. The dataset obtained was limited and heterogeneous, with missing data. In the absence of a sufficiently reliable quantity of data, we needed to ensure a reliable quality. We developed a methodology to validate the data, assessing its relia- bility in a standardised and traceable way. We targeted the accuracy, the consistency, and the plausibility of the data, based on either existing reference knowledge, or on a comparison within the gathered data. The methodology produces quality categories and weights to be used for modelling. Regarding the data, treatment performances were associated not solely with designs and materials, but also to climate, scales, and water composition. The downside of automation and standardisation lies in hiding complexity and specificities of certain situations. The drawbacks of the method in identifying outliers and faulty values are that expert-based checks rely on a dataset of reference which may not correspond to the new data, and that dataset-based checks rely on a high quantity of data. [SOURCE: Page_221]

In Chapter 6, on numerical representation, we followed a theoretical approach to apply the concept of model hybridisation to subsurface flow treatment wetlands. We used the data ranges from the previous dataset to generate a synthetic dataset that describes the entire domain of combinations of variable values. We developed two types of hybrid models based on BIO_PORE mechanistic model and machine learning models. The models predict outflow concentrations of COD and nitrogenous fractions, from inflow concen- trations, operational conditions and treatment wetlands dimensions. The parallel method is a weighted sum of the two individual models run separately. The serial method is the result of the mechanistic model modulated by a weighted result of the machine learning model. The weights were computed based on the global fit of the hybrid model to the synthetic data, and are adjusted with the number of observations and features. The machine learning models were developed following a typical workflow of tuning and cross- validation based on the RMSE metric, and the selection of the final model was based on the combination of RMSE, MAPE and RSQ metrics obtained for the training and test sets. We saw that the metrics are sensitive to different characteristics of the fitting. But overall tree-based models performed best with lower variations across the folds, which we attributed to their ensemble structure. We obtained better perfor- mances in predicting outflow concentrations with the serial hybrid models than with the individual models. [SOURCE: Page_221]

Finally, in Chapter 7, on the application of hybrid models, we applied the methodologies to the dataset gathered previously. Considering the limited number of observations, we envisaged statistical models rather than machine learning models but they did not prove successful. The hybridisation of the NkC* model to a tree-based model led to better results than with the individual models. The inclusion of the quality weights during the training of the machine learning model leads to more reliable models in terms of methodology. But no visual proof of improvement was observable because the low weight of the unsuit- able data, although not leading to their removal, still leads to having fewer observations for the training of the models. In the final results, the weight given to machine learning models was about half for the parallel method, and 1 for the serial method, showing their non negligible improvement. From the predictions of outflow concentrations, we used optimisation to estimate back the best design per pollutant. The limit in [SOURCE: Page_221]

198 Thèse accessible à l'adresse : https://theses.insa-lyon.fr/publication/2025ISAL0042/these.pdf © [S. H. Y. Guillaume Ruty], [2025], INSA Lyon, tous droits réservés [SOURCE: Page_221]

this approach is the number of pieces of information (features) needed to apply the models. We calculated the uncertainties associated with the predictions using uncertainty propagation. With the chosen ranges of variation, the optimal design ensures a compliant removal of the limiting pollutant only half of the time, and that a 95% compliance requires much greater areas. Therefore, in practice even the largest design cor- responding to the limiting pollutant does not allow a compliance with all treatment objectives. Considering a larger systemic scope, we looked into optimising the design as a compromise between all the pollutants based on their treatment objectives and water destinations. [SOURCE: Page_222]

We saw overall that the unification of knowledge relies on the specific points of view and approaches that aim to characterise treatment wetlands and wastewater treatment. This unification by the aggre- gation of symbolic representations and by the hybridisation of numerical models helped gain a deeper understanding of the limits of individual approaches, and define a more reliable design prediction. [SOURCE: Page_222]

9.2      Perspectives This thesis is the start to further research on symbolic and numerical modelling. We identified the following scientific nodes: [SOURCE: Page_222]

• the aggregation of interdisciplinary knowledge in the context of integrated projects in water man- agement. From the development of an ontology in order to conciliate knowledge of different natures, we found that the process of construction itself allows one to gain more understanding. Therefore, we believe that methodologies should be developed to better involve the recipient stakeholders in the construction, similarly to participatory methods and serious games. [SOURCE: Page_222]

• gathering data on treatment wetlands and Nature-based Solutions. More means could be put in communicating data, notably based on the common data exchange format we proposed. Research could be done in assessing how to gather and compare data, between the need for universalisation and standardisation, and the observation of a high plurality, complexity and heterogeneity of situations. [SOURCE: Page_222]

• including the quality weight in the training of machine learning models. This improvement has been implemented for many models already, but several algorithms in the caret R package do not include the option of including case weights yet. [SOURCE: Page_222]

• the model hybridisations adapted to treatment wetlands contexts, in particular, hybrid models that integrate both symbolic and numerical representations. Because of the lack of data, we must rely on current knowledge and causality, so mechanistic model must keep a key role of regulator similar to embedded models or physics-informed neural networks. In particular for the data-driven model, research could focus on developing a structure that integrates categorical information and causality from phenomena, mobilising knowledge graphs and genetic programming. [SOURCE: Page_222]

Appendix A [SOURCE: Page_256]

State of the art supplements [SOURCE: Page_256]

A.1       NkC* equation proof The tank in series model was first developed by MacMullin and Weber in 1935. This model is based on a mass balance between the inlet and outlet of the wetland. The mass of pollutant at a section i at a given dis- tance in the filter depends on the mass entering M in,i , the mass leaving M out,i and the mass degraded M r,i . [SOURCE: Page_256]

dM i (t) = M i−1 (t) − M i (t) − M r,i (t) dt The following assumptions are made: [SOURCE: Page_256]

• a permanent regime such that the mass does not vary: [SOURCE: Page_256]

0 = M i−1 (t) − M i (t) − M r,i (t) [SOURCE: Page_256]

and [SOURCE: Page_256]

0 = C in (t)Q in (t) − C out (t)Q out (t) − M r,i (t) [SOURCE: Page_256]

• a degradation rate following a first-order kinetics k v (aggregating all processes mentioned in CWM$_1$), such that: M r (t) = − k v,i Vi C in (t) with k v,i the volumetric removal coefficient at a section of water vol- ume θ i Vi with θ i the water content and Vi the volume of the section. [SOURCE: Page_256]

0 = C i−1 (t)Q i−1 (t) − C i (t)Q i (t) − k v,i θ i Vi C i (t) [SOURCE: Page_256]

• a constant inflow rate Q (neglecting evapotranpiration and precipitation): [SOURCE: Page_256]

0 = QC i−1 (t) − QC i (t) − k v,i θ i Vi C i (t) [SOURCE: Page_256]

that rewrites as [SOURCE: Page_256]

C i (t)      Q             1 =            = C i−1 (t) Q + Vi k v,i 1 + k v,i θ i Vi Q [SOURCE: Page_256]

• equal volumes Vi = V between N theoretical tanks [SOURCE: Page_256]

• equal water content/porosity between theoretical tanks: θ i = ² [SOURCE: Page_256]

• equal kinetic rates between theoretical tanks: k v,i = k v [SOURCE: Page_256]

Such that, defining the wetland as a series of N sections (or tanks), the model writes: [SOURCE: Page_256]

C N (t)       1 =(            )N C 0 (t)    1 + k v ²V QN [SOURCE: Page_256]

• a homogeneously distributed background mass that does not react (hence concentration C star ): M i−1 = m i−1 − m∗ , M i = m i − m∗ and M r,i = m r,i − m∗ [SOURCE: Page_256]

Operating a change of variable to include the background (residual) concentration C ∗ : [SOURCE: Page_257]

C N (t) − C ∗        k v ²V − N = (1 +       ) C 0 (t) − C ∗        QN Then, from the relation between areal and volumetric removal coefficients k a = k v h² and V = hS: [SOURCE: Page_257]

ka S N C N (t) = C ∗ + (C 0 (t) − C ∗ )(1 −       ) QN [SOURCE: Page_257]

A.2       Arrhenius simplified law Removal kinetics are known to be temperature dependent, assuming higher values as temperature in- creases. The Van’t Hoff-Arrhenius law expresses the temperature dependence of the kinetic rate of chemi- cal transformation: Ea k = k o × e RT with : k is the reaction term, T the temperature in K, E a the apparent energy of activation, in mol.L−1 , R = 8.314 the gas constant, in J.K −1 .mol −1 (or Boltzmann constant). This law has been simplified in Metcalf and Eddy (2003), into a new one that takes a reference tem- perature to determine the reaction kinetic constant k as a function of temperature. The variation of the equilibrium constant with changes in temperature is taken into account: [SOURCE: Page_257]

d(lnk)   Ea = dT      RT 2 It is then integrated between the limits T$_1$ and T$_2$ . Since most wastewater treatment operations and processes are carried out at or near ambient temperature, the quantity k ET1a T$_2$ can be assumed to be a B constant C for practical purposes: [SOURCE: Page_257]

k^2     Ea ln(      )=        (T$_2$ − T$_1$ ) = C(T$_2$ − T$_1$ ) k^1    RT$_1$ T$_2$ [SOURCE: Page_257]

k^2 = e C(T$_2$ −T$_1$ ) k^1 And then, defining θ = eC , yielding: [SOURCE: Page_257]

k^2 = θ (T$_2$ −T$_1$ ) k^1 θ is actually locally computed on a given range of temperatures, but in practice this locally determined value is used for a greater range of temperatures, ie. assumed constant although it varies with tempera- ture. If T$_1$ is taken equal to 20 degree Celsius and T$_2$ becomes a variable, its becomes: [SOURCE: Page_257]

k T = k 20 θ (T −20) A linearised version can be obtained: [SOURCE: Page_257]

log(k T$_2$ ) − log(k T$_1$ ) = log(θ ) T$_2$ − T$_1$ So θ can then be calculated as θ = 10slope . [SOURCE: Page_257]

Appendix B [SOURCE: Page_258]

Symbolic representation supplements [SOURCE: Page_258]

B.1       Concentrations and attributes The parameters that result from and represent a sum of different components are defined below: [SOURCE: Page_258]

Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) : [SOURCE: Page_258]

• A commonly used gross measurement of the concentration of biodegradable organic impurities in wastewater. The amount of oxygen, expressed in milligrams per litre (mg/L), required by bacteria while stabilizing, digesting, or treating organic matter under aerobic conditions is de- termined by the availability of material in the wastewater to be used as biological food and the amount of oxygen used by the microorganisms during oxidation. (USEPA 2002) • The amount of oxygen that is required to biochemically convert organic matter into inert sub- stances; an indirect measure of the amount of biodegradable organic matter present in the water or wastewater (WHO 2006) • Amount of oxygen required to oxidize organic matter (biodegradable) with a biological process (oxidation of biodegradable organic matter by bacteria). The biological oxygen demand (BOD) is an index of water pollution that assesses the biodegradable fraction of the carbonaceous pol- lution load in wastewater, and is usually calculated after 5 days at 20°C and in darkness: it is then called BOD$_5$. (Glossaire OiEau) [SOURCE: Page_258]

Chemical oxygen demand (COD) : [SOURCE: Page_258]

• A measure of oxygen use equivalent to the portion of organic matter that is susceptible to oxi- dation by a strong chemical oxidizing agent. (USEPA 2002) • Oxygen consumption by strong chemical oxidants to oxidize organic and inorganic substances in water. The chemical oxygen demand (COD) is used to assess the pollution load of wastewater. (Glossaire OiEau) [SOURCE: Page_258]

Total Kjeldahl Nitrogen (TKN) : An analytical method for determining total organic nitrogen and ammo- nia. (USEPA 2002) [SOURCE: Page_258]

Dissolved Oxygen (DO) : [SOURCE: Page_258]

• The oxygen dissolved in water, wastewater, or other liquid, usually expressed in milligrams per liter (mg/L), parts per million (ppm), or percent of saturation. (USEPA 2002) • Parameter governing most of biological processes in aquatic ecosystems. The concentration of dissolved oxygen is the result of the following physical, chemical and biological factors: ex- changes at the air-ocean interface; dissemination and mixing in the water body; use in chemical oxidation reactions (natural or anthropogenic); use by aquatic organisms for breathing (which includes bacterial degradation of organic matter in a broad sense) and for nitrification; in situ production by photosynthesis. (Glossaire OiEau) [SOURCE: Page_258]

Appendix C [SOURCE: Page_262]

Data for modelling supplements [SOURCE: Page_262]

C.1       Detailed database The detailed database implemented is described in Figure C.1 and presents the relations between the tables and the columns associated. Primary keys are specified first, then external keys that establish the link to other tables. The names are written without abbreviations nor determiners. The standard used is the snake_case with lower cases and underscores, but we kept acronyms with capital letters. [SOURCE: Page_262]

C.2       Correlations The correlations between the different variables in the dataset on horizontal and vertical flow treatment wetlands are shown in Figure C.2. The intensity go from negative correlations in orange, to no correlation in white, and to positive correlations in blue. They vary slightly as unsuitable observations are included or not, and as the missing data are imputed using MICE pmm method. [SOURCE: Page_262]

C.3       Chauvenet check As regards statistical methods, the Z-score is usually used to identify outliers, characterising observations by their distance to the mean value expressed as the number of standard deviations, or by the expected number of outliers based on the number of observations. We used another similar method, the Chauvenet criterion which provides the probability of obtaining each observation based on a fitted distribution. The Chauvenet criterion has led to labelling more observations as ”doubtful” and ”unsuitable”, compared to the Z-score (Figure C.3); however, we consider this difference to be negligible. We would suggest use of the Chauvenet criterion, which provides a probability (i.e. a ”quantification of uncertainty”) that is more easily interpretable (aligning with Muhr et al. (2023)) and better grasps the continuity between typical and outlier values than the Z-score. [SOURCE: Page_262]

Appendix D [SOURCE: Page_266]

Numerical representation supplements [SOURCE: Page_266]

D.1       BIOPORE saturation-inhibition coefficients In COMSOL Multiphysics software, the concentrations must be expressed in mol/m^3 , implying that K should also be converted to the same units. To do so, K is divided by the molar mass of the species. As an example, K OH is the saturation-inhibition coefficient for S O , set at 0.2 mgO$_2$ /L, ie. 0.2/(2MO ) = 0.00625 mol/m^3 . For COD however, multiple molar masses can correspond since it is a set of molecules that can be oxidised with O$_2$. Langergraber et al. (2007) uses C5H7O2N (glucose) as an adequate characterising biomass composition for COD in activated sludge. Then, 160 g of O$_2$ are needed to oxidise 113 g of glucose, such that K in mgCOD/L would be assumed as K in mg − glucose/L, then can be converted to mol − glucose/m^3 by dividing by M glucose , and mol − O$_2$ /m^3 by multiplying by 160/113=1.416. However, it would also be possible to directly divide the initial value K by MO$_2$ without preliminary conversion of K to moles of glucose. [SOURCE: Page_266]

Appendix E [SOURCE: Page_268]

Real case application supplements [SOURCE: Page_268]

E.1       NkC* calibration The values of the first-order kinetic rate k (in m/yr) are calibrated by optimising the RMSE (and RSQ). The values reported below show a large discrepancy depending on whether the optimisation is based on the effluent load (information due to the water flow rate is included) or on the effluent concentration: [SOURCE: Page_268]

P rediction                  BOD              COD                  N H$_4$                  TN                TP C out          100 − 106           63 − 68               7 − 10                4−5             8 − 12 L out          570 − 575               459           136 − 293           187 − 193           78 − 80 [SOURCE: Page_268]

The 95th percentile values of k are close to the calibrated values for the prediction of L out , but (except for NH$_4$ and TN) the optimised values of k for C out differ by an order of magnitude from the 50th per- centile. The variance of the predicted values of the test data set is also quite high (Figure E.1). Therefore, considering that the k values from the literature are based on a larger dataset and have been determined specifically for biodegradation, we prefer to use these values rather than the calibrated values, which may account for variance due to other factors. [SOURCE: Page_268]

Figure E.1: Observed versus predicted outflow concentrations by the calibrated NkC* model, with k = 9.73 [SOURCE: Page_268]

E.2       Uncertainties Observation uncertainties The fact that the data set used consists of mean concentrations over different time periods is the main source of uncertainty. We do not have access to the co-variation of the outflow concentration with the in- flow concentration, nor with temperature, pH, conductivity over the period, etc. Therefore, we do not try to incorporate the uncertainties directly into the models. As indicated in the state of the art, an individual prediction can be considered accurate and precise, while being off-track or uncertain. The characteristics may vary over time, leading to different predictions, and uncertainties have been associated with model [SOURCE: Page_268]

parameters (values of kinetic rates, assumptions) and variable values (mean concentrations). In particular, the data-driven models have been trained on mean concentrations, but the associated standard deviations are not negligible, see Figure E.2. In particular, they increase with concentrations, indicating heteroscedas- ticity. [SOURCE: Page_269]

NkC* The NkC* model takes as inputs C in , Q, d and S. C in and Q are pre-sizing variables, i.e. their variability observed in the real data is too large to be taken into account in pre-sizing. Pre-sizing is not based on ex- treme rainfall events or peaks in inflow concentrations. We have used the Monte Carlo simulation method to propagate uncertainties from the inputs to the predictions of the outflow concentration, as described in workflow E.3. The variables involved are: [SOURCE: Page_269]

• the mean inflow concentrations, they follow a lognormal distribution with a standard deviation based on the values provided in the dataset. [SOURCE: Page_269]

• the inflow rate, which follows a lognormal distribution with an arbitrary standard deviation of 0.5 [SOURCE: Page_269]

• the kinetic rates, which we considered to follow a normal distribution with an arbitrary standard deviation of 1. Their variation may be correlated with water or seasonal temperature, so temperature is considered indirectly. [SOURCE: Page_269]

## FOLIO ADMINISTRATIF

THESE . . . . . . . .. .DE . . . .L’INSA . . . . . . .. .LYON,        MEMBRE . . . . ... .........       DE......... .. . .... L’UNIVERSITE           DE....... .. .. .. .. .. .... LYON [SOURCE: Page_271]

NOM : GUILLAUME RUTY                                                                     DATE de SOUTENANCE : 10/06/2025 [SOURCE: Page_271]

Prénoms : Sophie Hai Yen Marie [SOURCE: Page_271]

TITRE : Model hybridisation for reliable decision-making [SOURCE: Page_271]

NATURE : Doctorat                                                                        Numéro d’ordre : 2025ISAL0042 [SOURCE: Page_271]

École Doctorale : Chimie [SOURCE: Page_271]

Spécialité : Génie des procédés [SOURCE: Page_271]

RÉSUMÉ : In the context of global change, cities are moving towards more sustainable and resilient water practices. Nature-based solutions contribute to integrated water management approaches by locally managing water volumes and treating pollution, while bringing biodiversity and supporting socio-economic dynamics to the urban landscape at a reasonable cost. These solutions are flourishing around the world under different terminolo- gies and lack guidelines for their implementation. This challenge is addressed by the MULTISOURCE project, within which this thesis aims at the technical aspect of providing a pre-sizing of technological units developed for wastewater treatment. In particular, treatment wetlands face a lack of understanding of the relationship between the designs and the treatment processes involved, and a lack of comparable data on the systems. Current design models are simple and conservative, while data-driven models are unreliable. This thesis proposes, as a first step, the development of an ontology to clarify terminological ambiguities, to unify knowledge on treatment wetlands and to better identify their main characteristics in terms of pollutant removal. The second step of this work proposes to homogenise data quality checks through a methodology for data validation with a quantitative assessment of the quality of the observations. In the third step, two method- ologies of hybridisation of mechanistic and data-driven models are developed to provide design estimates based on both knowledge and data. Finally, this methodology is applied to the validated data set and design optimisation methods are developed to address the uncertainty inherent in decision making. [SOURCE: Page_271]

MOTS-CLÉS : Symbolic representation, ontology, hybrid modelling, mechanistic, empirical, decision-support [SOURCE: Page_271]
